name: Nephrotic Syndrome — Minimal Change Disease (MCD)
description: Podocyte injury causing massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia; most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children

frequency.us: ~2/100,000 children/year; ~80% of nephrotic syndrome in young children; peak age 2–6 yrs
frequency.global: ~2/100,000 children/year globally; ~80% of childhood nephrotic syndrome; higher rates in Asia (3–7/100,000)
frequency.sources: Kidney Int 2012;81:1094; NAPRTCS 2011; ISKDC original studies

diagnosis: Urinalysis (heavy proteinuria), serum albumin, lipid panel; kidney biopsy if atypical or steroid-resistant (shows effacement of foot processes on EM)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Corticosteroids (prednisone) — first-line; remission in ~90% of children • Relapsing/steroid-dependent disease: mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, levamisole (off-label), rituximab • Steroid-resistant MCD: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus preferred over cyclosporine); RAAS blockade for proteinuria management
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Anti-nephrin antibodies identified as causative in a subset of MCD/podocytopathies (NEJM 2024) — nephrin- directed therapies under early development ▶ Obinutuzumab (anti-CD20) — Phase 2/3 trial in idiopathic nephrotic syndrome including MCD (Roche MAJESTY/POSTERITY program) ▶ Inebilizumab, ianalumab — B-cell depleting agents in early investigation ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — adjunctive antiproteinuric role; emerging evidence in pediatric nephrotic syndrome

name: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) — Primary/Idiopathic
description: Glomerular scarring affecting some glomeruli focally and segmentally; most common cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children

frequency.us: ~1/100,000 children; 20–30% of childhood nephrotic syndrome; highest incidence in Black children (~3×)
frequency.global: ~1/100,000 children overall; significant racial/ethnic variation; higher in West African and Hispanic populations
frequency.sources: NAPRTCS 2011; JASN 2016;27(4); Kitiyakara et al., CJASN 2019

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (light microscopy, IF, EM); podocin/NPHS2 genetic testing; circulating permeability factor assay; eGFR

treatment.standardOfCare: • Corticosteroids (prednisone) — first-line for primary/idiopathic FSGS; complete/partial remission in ~40–50% • Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) — for steroid-dependent or steroid-resistant disease • Mycophenolate mofetil — steroid-sparing; used in relapsing/refractory disease • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — antiproteinuric; mainstay for all FSGS regardless of immunosuppression • LDL apheresis — for circulating permeability factor– mediated FSGS refractory to other therapy Methods • Rituximab (off-label) — anti-CD20; increasingly used for refractory steroid-dependent FSGS; evidence from pediatric cohorts
treatment.emerging: Near-Approval / Late-Stage Investigational ▶ Sparsentan (Filspari) — oral dual endothelin A/AT1R antagonist (Travere Therapeutics); sNDA under FDA review for FSGS (PDUFA date April 13, 2026; extended from Jan 2026); Phase 3 DUPLEX trial showed significant proteinuria reduction and lower ESKD rates vs. irbesartan; Phase 2 DUET (ages 8–75) met primary endpoint; EPPIK trial includes pediatric FSGS; would be first FDA- approved FSGS-specific therapy if approved; already FDA/EMA approved for IgAN Investigational ▶ Inaxaplin (VX-147; Vertex Pharmaceuticals) — oral first- in-class APOL1 channel inhibitor; FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designation + Rare Pediatric Disease Designation for APOL1-mediated FSGS; Phase 2a (NEJM 2023) showed 47.6% UPCR reduction; now in Phase 3 AMPLITUDE trial (NCT05312879) including adolescents ages 10–17; interim analysis at Week 48 may support accelerated approval in US ▶ Obinutuzumab — anti-CD20 type II antibody; more complete B-cell depletion than rituximab; case series/trials in steroid-resistant NS ▶ Povetacicept (Alpine Immune Sciences) — APRIL/BAFF dual inhibitor; Phase 2 in proteinuric kidney disease ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., dapagliflozin) — renoprotective; growing evidence in proteinuric CKD including pediatric populations; not FSGS-specific but increasingly used adjunctively

name: FSGS — Genetic/Monogenic
description: Hereditary podocyte dysfunction causing FSGS; caused by mutations in NPHS1, NPHS2, WT1, TRPC6, INF2, and >50 other genes

frequency.us: ~30% of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) cases have monogenic cause; higher yield in infants
frequency.global: ~30% of SRNS globally have monogenic etiology; >60 causative genes identified; higher in consanguineous populations
frequency.sources: NEJM 2013;369:1995; Bierzynska et al. JASN 2017; Trautmann et al. Kidney Int 2018

diagnosis: Comprehensive genetic panel (podocyte genes); kidney biopsy; EM for foot process morphology; family history and inheritance pattern

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — antiproteinuric; mainstay regardless of genotype • Supportive care — management of edema, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, nutrition • Immunosuppression generally ineffective — steroids/calcineurin inhibitors not recommended for monogenic FSGS • IMPORTANT EXCEPTION: CoQ10-deficient FSGS (ADCK4, COQ6 mutations) — coenzyme Q10 supplementation may halt or reverse renal decline; critical to identify • Genetic counseling — essential for family planning and living donor selection • Renal transplant planning — excellent outcomes; recurrence risk very low for most monogenic subtypes (<5%) Investigational (Genotype-Specific) ▶ Inaxaplin (VX-147; Vertex Pharmaceuticals) — for APOL1 high-risk genotype (G1/G2 homozygous or compound heterozygous); AMPLITUDE Phase 3 trial (NCT05312879) now includes adolescents 10–17 years; FDA Breakthrough Therapy + Rare Pediatric Disease Designation; Phase 2a showed ~48% UPCR reduction (NEJM 2023) ▶ Gene therapy approaches — early-stage research for NPHS1 (nephrin) and NPHS2 (podocin) deficiencies ▶ Antisense oligonucleotides / mRNA approaches — preclinical for podocin mutations ▶ Sparsentan — under FDA review for FSGS broadly (PDUFA April 2026); DUET trial included patients with FSGS-associated podocyte gene mutations Emerging Supportive Therapies ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — renoprotective in proteinuric CKD; adjunctive use growing even in genetic forms

name: APOL1-Mediated Nephropathy
description: Kidney disease caused by high-risk APOL1 variants (G1/G2) in individuals of African ancestry; presents as FSGS, collapsing glomerulopathy, or focal global glomerulosclerosis. APOL1 expressed in podocytes causes cell injury under second-hit triggers (infection, interferon, hemodynamic stress). Autosomal recessive — two risk alleles required for high phenotypic risk.

frequency.us: ~13% of Black adults carry 2 APOL1 risk alleles; ~35–50% of FSGS in Black children attributable to APOL1 high-risk genotype; >7 million high-risk individuals in the US.
frequency.global: G1/G2 variants in ~15% of West Africans; rare in non-African populations.
frequency.sources: Genovese et al. Science 2010;329:841; Kopp et al. NEJM 2011;365:2183; Kasembeli et al. JASN 2015; Dummer et al. CJASN 2023

diagnosis: APOL1 genotyping (G1: rs73885319 + rs60910145; G2: rs71785313) — 2 risk alleles required for high-risk genotype Kidney biopsy — FSGS or collapsing variant on light microscopy; podocyte foot process effacement on EM Urinalysis — heavy proteinuria, nephrotic range; urine protein/creatinine ratio; eGFR, serum creatinine Exclude secondary causes: HIV, interferon exposure, SLE, sickle cell nephropathy Family history — screen first-degree relatives; autosomal recessive inheritance pattern

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — antiproteinuric; mainstay regardless of immunosuppression status • Corticosteroids — generally ineffective for APOL1- mediated FSGS; avoid unless MCD overlap suspected • Blood pressure control — target <130/80 mmHg; high cardiovascular-renal risk in this population • Avoid second-hit triggers — NSAIDs, contrast, uncontrolled infections, interferon-alpha • Genetic counseling — autosomal recessive; 2 risk alleles required; family screening recommended • Renal transplant — effective for ESKD; APOL1 high-risk donor kidneys associated with shorter graft survival; genotype donors of African ancestry Emerging / Investigational ▶ Inaxaplin (VX-147; Vertex Pharmaceuticals) — oral first- in-class APOL1 ion channel inhibitor; FDA Breakthrough Therapy + Rare Pediatric Disease Designation; Phase 2a (NEJM 2023): 47.6% UPCR reduction vs placebo; Phase 3 AMPLITUDE trial (NCT05312879) includes adolescents ages 10–17; interim Week 48 data may support accelerated approval 2025–2026 ▶ Interferon pathway inhibition — targeting APOL1 second- hit activation via type I IFN axis; anifrolumab under early investigation ▶ APOL1 mRNA / antisense silencing — preclinical; podocyte-targeted suppression of cytotoxic G1/G2 isoform production ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — renoprotective in proteinuric CKD; adjunctive use growing in APOL1 nephropathy; not APOL1-specific Methods

name: Membranous Nephropathy — Pediatric (PLA2R and non-PLA2R)
description: Immune complex deposition in subepithelial space causing nephrotic syndrome; secondary causes more common in children than adults

frequency.us: Rare; ~1–5% of pediatric nephrotic syndrome; secondary causes (HBV, SLE) predominate
frequency.global: Rare in high-income countries (~1–5% of pediatric NS); more prevalent in endemic HBV/HCV regions (Asia, Africa)
frequency.sources: JASN 2012;23:650; Debiec et al. NEJM 2004; Ronco & Debiec Nat Rev Nephrol 2012

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (IgG4 deposits, spike pattern on silver stain); anti-PLA2R antibody; HBV serology; ANA/dsDNA; urine protein

treatment.standardOfCare: • Treat underlying cause: HBV → antivirals (tenofovir, entecavir); SLE → immunosuppression; malignancy → tumor resection • Idiopathic/PLA2R-positive: watchful waiting (spontaneous remission ~30%); RAAS blockade for proteinuria • Rituximab — now widely considered first-line immunosuppression for PLA2R-positive MN (MENTOR and GEMRITUX trial evidence); replaces cyclophosphamide-based regimens in many centers • Cyclosporine/tacrolimus ± MMF — alternatives for rituximab-refractory or relapsing disease • Anti-PLA2R antibody titer monitoring guides treatment decisions
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Felzartamab (anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody) — Phase 2 M-PLACE trial showed efficacy in moderate-to-high-risk PLA2R-positive MN; Phase 3 underway ▶ Daratumumab (anti-CD38) — case series data for refractory PLA2R-positive MN ▶ Ofatumumab — for rituximab-resistant/intolerant patients (case series 2024) ▶ Obinutuzumab — under investigation (MAJESTY trial) ▶ Complement-targeted therapies (iptacopan, pelecopan) — Phase 2 trials; results inconclusive to date ▶ Expanding antigen panel (THSD7A, NELL-1, SEMA3B, EXT1/2) informs precision diagnosis

name: IgA Nephropathy
description: Most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide; IgA immune complex deposition in mesangium causing hematuria and variable proteinuria

frequency.us: ~1–2/100,000 children; most common glomerulonephritis in adolescents; ~10–20% of pediatric GN biopsies
frequency.global: ~1/100,000 globally; highest in East Asia (10–40/100,000 in Japan/China); most common GN worldwide
frequency.sources: KDIGO IgAN Guidelines 2021; Wyatt & Julian NEJM 2013; Roberts et al. AJKD 2020

diagnosis: Urinalysis (hematuria ± proteinuria); kidney biopsy (mesangial IgA on IF); Oxford MEST-C score; serum IgA; eGFR and proteinuria trend

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — cornerstone; target proteinuria <0.5 g/day • SGLT2 inhibitors — now recommended as part of CKD supportive bundle per 2025 KDIGO IgAN guideline • Systemic corticosteroids — for progressive disease with active inflammation despite optimized supportive care • Mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine — adjunct immunosuppression FDA-Approved Disease-Specific Therapies (2021–2025): • Targeted-release budesonide (Tarpeyo/Nefecon, Calliditas) — full FDA approval Dec 2023; reduces eGFR decline in adults with primary IgAN • Sparsentan (Filspari, Travere) — dual endothelin A/AT1R antagonist; full FDA approval Sept 2024 for IgAN; Phase 3 DUPLEX trial ongoing for FSGS (PDUFA Apr 2026) • Iptacopan (Fabhalta, Novartis) — Factor B / alternative complement pathway inhibitor; FDA accelerated approval Aug 2024; 38% UPCR reduction vs placebo at 9 months (APPLAUSE-IgAN Phase 3) Methods • Atrasentan (Vanrafia, Novartis) — first selective endothelin A receptor antagonist; FDA approved 2025 for IgAN • Sibeprenlimab (Voyxact, Otsuka) — anti-APRIL monoclonal antibody; FDA accelerated approval Nov 2025; 54% UPCR reduction vs placebo in VISIONARY Phase 3
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Povetacicept (BAFF/APRIL dual inhibitor) — Phase 2/3; RUBY-3 trial showing sustained UPCR and Gd-IgA1 reductions ▶ Felzartamab (anti-CD38) — Phase 2 IGNAZ trial interim results positive ▶ Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) — Phase 2 data: 25% relative UACR reduction vs placebo ▶ Telitacicept (BAFF/APRIL inhibitor) — Phase 3 ongoing ▶ Mezagitamab (anti-CD38) — Phase 2/3 ongoing ▶ Combination approaches under study per 2025 KDIGO guideline: layered pathway-directed therapy

name: IgA Vasculitis Nephritis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura)
description: Systemic small vessel vasculitis with IgA deposits causing palpable purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, and nephritis in children

frequency.us: ~10–20/100,000/year; most common systemic vasculitis in children; nephritis in 20–50%; peak age 4–6 yrs
frequency.global: ~10–20/100,000/year in Western countries; slightly lower in Asia; renal involvement in 20–50% globally
frequency.sources: Gardner-Medwin et al. Lancet 2002; Ozen et al. ARD 2010; EULAR/PRES/PRINTO criteria

diagnosis: Urinalysis; kidney biopsy if significant proteinuria or impaired renal function (mesangial IgA, similar to IgAN); skin biopsy; clinical criteria

treatment.standardOfCare: • Supportive care — fluid management, antihypertensives, analgesics for joint/abdominal symptoms • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — for persistent proteinuria • Corticosteroids (prednisone) — for moderate-severe nephritis; crescentic disease: pulse IV methylprednisolone • Mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine — for steroid- dependent or frequently relapsing nephritis • Cyclophosphamide — reserved for severe crescentic nephritis (Class III/IV histology)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ IgAN-directed therapies may benefit IgA vasculitis nephritis given shared pathophysiology (Gd-IgA1 axis); trials generally have excluded pediatric IgAV ▶ Rituximab — case reports/series for refractory crescentic IgAV nephritis ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — adjunctive antiproteinuric benefit in proteinuric IgAV nephritis; emerging use ▶ 2024 KDIGO IgAV guideline aligns IgAV nephritis management with IgAN framework

name: MPGN — Complement-mediated
description: Glomerulonephritis with mesangial and endocapillary hypercellularity; driven by dysregulation of alternative complement pathway

frequency.us: Rare; <5% of pediatric glomerulonephritis biopsies; complement-mediated recognized with genetic testing
frequency.global: Rare globally; <5% of pediatric GN; increasing recognition with improved complement genetic testing panels
frequency.sources: Smith et al. CJASN 2019; Servais et al. JASN 2007; C3 Glomerulopathy Consensus Report KI 2013

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy; complement studies (C3, C4, CH50, AP50); CFH/CFI/C3/CFB genetic panel; anti-CFH antibodies; electron microscopy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Eculizumab (anti-C5) — for complement dysregulation confirmed by genetic testing or low C3/low C4 pattern; evidence base primarily from aHUS but used off-label for complement-driven MPGN Methods • Ravulizumab — extended dosing alternative to eculizumab • RAAS blockade — antiproteinuric • Plasma infusion/fresh frozen plasma — for CFH or CFHR deficiency (rare) • Mycophenolate mofetil ± steroids — for immune complex- driven component • Meningococcal vaccination — mandatory before complement inhibitor therapy FDA-Approved (2025) ▶ Pegcetacoplan (Empaveli, Apellis) — FDA approved July 2025 for IC-MPGN (patients aged ≥12 years); first approved therapy for this indication; proximal C3 inhibitor
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Iptacopan (Factor B inhibitor) — Phase 2/3 data in complement-mediated kidney disease ▶ Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor) — Phase 2 trials ▶ Personalized complement pathway targeting based on genetic complement profiling

name: MPGN — Immune Complex
description: Glomerulonephritis with MPGN pattern driven by chronic antigen-antibody complex deposition; secondary to infections, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal proteins

frequency.us: Uncommon; secondary causes (HBV, HCV, SLE, endocarditis) more common; primary rare in pediatrics
frequency.global: Uncommon; incidence declining with HBV vaccination; secondary MPGN dominant globally; prevalence varies by infection burden
frequency.sources: Sethi & Fervenza NEJM 2012; Appel et al. JASN 2005; KDIGO GN Guidelines 2012

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (IF showing IgG/IgM/C3); identify underlying cause: ANA, ANCA, complement, HBV/HCV serology, cryoglobulins, SPEP

treatment.standardOfCare: • Treat underlying cause — antivirals for HCV (DAAs: sofosbuvir-based regimens; often curative); antibiotics for chronic bacterial infection; chemotherapy for lymphoproliferative disease • RAAS blockade — antiproteinuric management • Immunosuppression (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) — for autoimmune-driven IC-MPGN (SLE, Sjögren) • Cryoglobulinemia-associated: rituximab + antiviral (if HCV+) as primary therapy
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Pegcetacoplan (Empaveli) — FDA approved July 2025 for primary IC-MPGN (idiopathic, not secondary); relevant for complement-amplified secondary IC-MPGN under investigation ▶ B-cell depleting agents for cryoglobulinemia — obinutuzumab (superior B-cell depletion vs rituximab) under investigation

name: C3 Glomerulopathy (C3GN)
description: Glomerulonephritis with dominant C3 deposition and absent/minimal immunoglobulin, caused by alternative complement pathway dysregulation

frequency.us: Very rare; <1/1,000,000; distinguished from DDD by EM findings; genetic and acquired complement disorders
frequency.global: Very rare globally; <1/1,000,000; distinct from DDD on electron microscopy; both genetic and acquired complement dysregulation
frequency.sources: Pickering et al. KI 2013; Servais et al. JASN 2012; C3G Consensus Report KI Suppl 2013

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (dominant C3 on IF, absence of Ig); complement pathway workup (C3, C4, factor H/I/B/properdin); genetic panel; anti-CFH antibodies

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade — antiproteinuric and antihypertensive; first-line supportive • Mycophenolate mofetil ± low-dose steroids — for progressive C3G; modest evidence base • Plasma therapy (FFP infusion or plasma exchange) — for CFH deficiency or anti-CFH antibodies Methods • Eculizumab — off-label; limited and variable efficacy in C3G (better evidence for dense deposit disease); response predicted by terminal complement activation markers • Meningococcal vaccination — mandatory if complement inhibitor used • Renal transplant for ESKD (risk of recurrence ~50%) FDA-Approved (July 2025) ▶ Pegcetacoplan (Empaveli, Apellis) — FDA approved July 2025 for C3 glomerulopathy (aged ≥12 years); FIRST ever approved therapy for C3G; proximal C3/C3b inhibitor; subcutaneous twice-weekly self-administration; approval based on Phase 2/3 data showing proteinuria reduction and complement suppression
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Iptacopan (Factor B inhibitor, Novartis) — Phase 2/3 ongoing in C3G; APPELHANSEN trial ▶ Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor, Alexion) — Phase 2 trials ongoing ▶ Complement genetic panel — essential for patient stratification and precision therapy selection

name: Dense Deposit Disease (DDD / MPGN Type II)
description: Rare MPGN variant with highly electron-dense ribbon-like deposits in GBM; caused by C3 nephritic factor or complement gene mutations

frequency.us: Extremely rare; ~2–3 cases/million; median onset childhood/adolescence; C3 nephritic factor in majority
frequency.global: ~2–3/million globally; most data from European registries; North American Complement- Mediated TMA Registry
frequency.sources: Appel et al. JASN 2005; Bomback & Appel KI 2010; Smith et al. CJASN 2014

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy with EM (pathognomonic dense deposits); C3NeF; C3, factor H levels; complement genetic panel; fundoscopy (drusen)

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade — antiproteinuric; mainstay • Plasma infusion for CFH deficiency — replaces absent complement regulatory proteins • Mycophenolate mofetil — for progressive disease; modest evidence • Eculizumab — variable efficacy in DDD (evidence less robust than in aHUS); may benefit patients with documented terminal complement activation • Renal transplant (high recurrence risk ~80–90%; allograft loss common) FDA-Approved (July 2025) ▶ Pegcetacoplan (Empaveli, Apellis) — FDA approved July 2025 for C3G including DDD (aged ≥12 years); FIRST approved disease-specific therapy; proximal C3/C3b complement inhibitor
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Iptacopan (Factor B inhibitor) — Phase 2/3 in C3G/DDD ▶ Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor) — Phase 2 trials ▶ C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF) quantification guides complement inhibitor selection ▶ Monoclonal antibody targeting C3 convertase stabilization — investigational Methods

name: Anti-GBM Disease (Goodpasture) — Pediatric
description: Autoimmune disease with anti-GBM antibodies attacking type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes; pulmonary-renal syndrome

frequency.us: Very rare in children; <0.5/million/year; mostly adolescents; pulmonary involvement less common than adults
frequency.global: Very rare globally; <0.5/million/year; predominantly adult disease; European multicenter study reports <5% pediatric cases
frequency.sources: Cui et al. Medicine 2015; Johnson et al. KI 1985; Levy et al. QJM 2001

diagnosis: Anti-GBM antibody (ELISA/CLIA); ANCA (concurrent positivity in ~30%); kidney biopsy (linear IgG on IF, crescentic GN); chest imaging; pulmonary function

treatment.standardOfCare: • Emergency plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) — removes circulating anti-GBM antibodies; 14 exchanges over 2–3 weeks; most urgent intervention • Cyclophosphamide + high-dose corticosteroids (pulse IV methylprednisolone → oral prednisone) — concurrent immunosuppression to halt antibody production • Dialysis support — if AKI requires renal replacement therapy • Renal transplant — after antibody clearance (typically ≥6– 12 months of undetectable anti-GBM titers) • Lung protection — oxygen supplementation; avoid pulmonary hemorrhage triggers (smoking cessation, treat infections)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Rituximab — for refractory or relapsing anti-GBM disease; case reports/series ▶ Imlifidase (IdeS) — IgG-cleaving enzyme; experimental compassionate use to rapidly remove anti-GBM IgG when plasmapheresis cannot be performed urgently ▶ CAR-T/B-cell depleting approaches — very early stage ▶ Dual anti-GBM + ANCA positivity (~10–30% of cases) — influences treatment duration (longer immunosuppression needed for ANCA component)

name: Lupus Nephritis — Pediatric (Class I–VI)
description: Renal involvement in childhood-onset SLE; more severe and rapid progression than adult SLE nephritis; ISN/RPS classification I–VI

frequency.us: Pediatric SLE: ~0.5– 0.6/100,000/year; nephritis in 50– 80% of pediatric SLE; Class III/IV most common
frequency.global: Pediatric SLE: ~0.3– 0.9/100,000/year globally; nephritis in up to 80%; higher prevalence in Asian, Hispanic, Black populations
frequency.sources: Tarr et al. ARD 2012; CARRA Registry 2019; ACR/EULAR SLE Classification Criteria 2019

diagnosis: Urinalysis, urine protein:creatinine; ANA, anti- dsDNA, complement (C3/C4); kidney biopsy for class; CBC, renal function; SLEDAI score

treatment.standardOfCare: • Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) + hydroxychloroquine + corticosteroids — first-line induction for Class III/IV LN (Euro-Lupus or high-dose MMF regimen) • Cyclophosphamide (NIH high-dose or Euro-Lupus low- dose IV) — alternative induction for severe/proliferative disease; preferred for Class IV with crescents • Voclosporin (Lupkynis, Aurinia) — calcineurin inhibitor; FDA approved Jan 2021 for adult LN; used with MMF + steroids; increasing use in older adolescents (AURORA 1 & 2 trials; KDIGO 2024-endorsed) • Belimumab (Benlysta, GSK) — anti-BLyS/BAFF; FDA approved Dec 2020 for LN; IV or SC; used as add-on to standard of care; adolescent data emerging • RAAS blockade — Class I/II or proteinuric background • Hydroxychloroquine — standard background therapy for all LN classes FDA-Approved (October 2025) ▶ Obinutuzumab (Gazyva, Genentech/Roche) — anti-CD20 type II monoclonal antibody; FDA approved Oct 2025 for active adult LN receiving standard therapy; REGENCY Phase 3 superiority vs placebo + SOC; pediatric trial Methods (POSTERITY) ongoing for adolescents with Class III/IV LN
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ CAR-T cell therapy (anti-CD19) — early case series showing deep B-cell depletion and LN remission; Phase 1/2 trials ongoing ▶ Anifrolumab (anti-IFN-α receptor) — approved for SLE; potential role in LN under investigation ▶ Finerenone, SGLT2 inhibitors — adjunctive renal protection per KDIGO 2024 CKD bundle ▶ Ustekinumab (IL-12/23), iberdomide — investigational for refractory LN

name: ANCA-associated Vasculitis Nephritis (GPA / MPA)
description: Necrotizing crescentic GN caused by anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies; part of systemic small-vessel vasculitis

frequency.us: Rare; ~1–2/million/year; GPA more common than MPA in pediatrics; mean age ~12–14 years
frequency.global: ~1–2/million/year in children; European registries report slightly higher rates; GPA predominates over MPA in pediatric cohorts
frequency.sources: Cabral et al. Pediatrics 2009; EULAR/PRES recommendations 2010; ARPAKid Registry

diagnosis: ANCA (PR3/MPO by ELISA); kidney biopsy (pauci-immune crescentic GN); chest CT; ENT evaluation; eGFR; urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Rituximab — preferred induction agent for GPA/MPA over cyclophosphamide in most adults and older children; equivalent or superior remission rates (RAVE/RITUXVAS trials); preferred in young women and relapsing disease • Cyclophosphamide (IV pulse or oral) + high-dose corticosteroids — alternative induction; preferred for severe alveolar hemorrhage or renal failure requiring dialysis • Azathioprine or rituximab — maintenance therapy; rituximab increasingly preferred for maintenance (MAINRITSAN trials) • Plasma exchange (PLEX) — previously standard for severe dialysis-requiring disease; PEXIVAS trial (2020) showed no benefit for renal survival or mortality; now NOT routinely recommended; reserved for concurrent anti- GBM antibodies • Mycophenolate mofetil — alternative maintenance agent FDA-Approved (Oct 2021) ▶ Avacopan (Tavneos, Amgen/ChemoCentryx) — C5a receptor antagonist; FDA approved Oct 2021 for GPA/MPA as adjunct to SOC; ADVOCATE Phase 3: non- inferior remission at 26 wks, superior sustained remission at 52 wks; reduces corticosteroid burden; increasingly incorporated into induction regimens
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Obinutuzumab — improved B-cell depletion vs rituximab; Phase 2/3 in ANCA vasculitis ▶ Imlifidase (IdeS) — for refractory ANCA nephritis with high IgG burden; investigational ▶ Complement pathway (C3/C5) — additional targets under study ▶ Pediatric-specific data limited; treatment extrapolated from adult trials with weight-based dosing Methods

name: Post-infectious / Post- streptococcal GN
description: Immune complex GN occurring 1–3 weeks after streptococcal or other bacterial infection; characterized by hematuria, edema, hypertension

frequency.us: Common; ~10/100,000/year; peak age 5–12 yrs; most common acute GN in North American children
frequency.global: Very common in developing countries; ~10/100,000/year in high- income countries; major cause of GN in re
frequency.sources: Carapetis et al. Lancet Infect Dis 2005; Rodriguez-Iturbe & Musser JASN 2008; Eison et al. Pediatrics 2011

diagnosis: Urinalysis (hematuria, RBC casts); ASO titer; streptozyme; low C3 (transiently); throat/skin culture; kidney biopsy rarely needed

treatment.standardOfCare: • Supportive management — primary approach; most cases self-limited • Salt and fluid restriction — for hypertension and edema • Antihypertensives (calcium channel blockers, hydralazine, loop diuretics) — for symptomatic hypertension • Diuretics (furosemide) — for fluid overload and edema • Antibiotics — eradicate residual streptococcal infection (penicillin, amoxicillin); does NOT alter renal course but prevents spread • RAAS blockade — for persistent proteinuria in recovery phase • Dialysis — for severe AKI with oliguria/fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics (rare, <1%)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ No disease-specific investigational therapies; prognosis excellent in children (>95% full recovery) ▶ Atypical/non-resolving PSGN — consider complement evaluation (rare overlap with C3G or aHUS) ▶ IgA-dominant PIGN (staphylococcal) — emerging recognition as distinct entity; management similar but may require immunosuppression in refractory cases

name: Thin Basement Membrane Nephropathy
description: Diffuse thinning of GBM on EM causing persistent microscopic hematuria; benign in most cases; allelic with Alport syndrome (COL4A3/A4)

frequency.us: Common; ~1% of general population; majority of asymptomatic isolated hematuria in children
frequency.global: ~1% globally; autosomal dominant inheritance; majority of isolated hematuria in school-age children worldwide
frequency.sources: Pierides et al. KI 2009; Haas et al. AJKD 2009; KDIGO GN Guidelines 2012

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy with EM (GBM <150–200 nm); COL4A3/A4 genetic testing; urinalysis; family history of hematuria; exclude Alport

treatment.standardOfCare: • No treatment typically required — benign prognosis in most pediatric cases; isolated hematuria • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — initiate if proteinuria develops (>300 mg/day) or if blood pressure rises • Annual monitoring — urinalysis, blood pressure, eGFR, urine protein/creatinine ratio • Genetic counseling — essential; COL4A3/COL4A4 heterozygous mutations overlap with autosomal dominant Alport (TBMN-Alport spectrum); family screening recommended • Avoid nephrotoxins — NSAIDs, contrast media, aminoglycosides • Renal biopsy — not always required; EM finding of diffuse thinning (<250 nm); necessary to distinguish from early Alport
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Reclassification ongoing — 2025 guidance recognizes TBMN/heterozygous Alport as a spectrum; SGLT2 inhibitors under investigation for COL4A3/4 heterozygous mutations with proteinuria ▶ No novel disease-specific therapies approved or in late- stage trials Methods

name: HBV-Associated Membranous Nephropathy — Pediatric
description: Membranous nephropathy caused by hepatitis B viral antigen-antibody immune complex deposition in subepithelial space

frequency.us: Rare in US (low HBV prevalence); mostly in immigrant populations from endemic regions
frequency.global: Major cause of childhood membranous nephropathy in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa; declining with HBV vaccination programs
frequency.sources: Lin et al. Kidney Int 1990; KDIGO HBV Guidelines 2018; WHO HBV vaccination data

diagnosis: HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBc; kidney biopsy (HBsAg/HBeAg deposits on IF); liver function; viral load; anti-PLA2R (usually negative)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Antiviral therapy — cornerstone; tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF — preferred in adolescents for renal/bone safety); entecavir as alternative • RAAS blockade — for proteinuria management • Avoid immunosuppression unless under antiviral cover — risk of HBV reactivation; if required (e.g., severe class V), ensure antiviral prophylaxis started ≥1 week prior • HBeAg seroconversion — associated with spontaneous remission of nephropathy (~30%); antiviral therapy accelerates seroconversion • Monitor HBsAg, HBeAg, HBV DNA, ALT, renal function, proteinuria throughout
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Functional cure strategies for HBV (cccDNA silencing, capsid assembly modulators, RNAi) — if HBV eliminated, nephropathy expected to resolve; trials ongoing ▶ Rituximab — for antiviral-resistant or refractory proteinuric disease under antiviral cover; limited case reports ▶ TAF over TDF preferred in young patients and those with renal or bone concerns — increasing adoption

name: Antiphospholipid Syndrome Nephropathy
description: Thrombotic microangiopathy of renal vessels caused by antiphospholipid antibodies; occurs as primary APS or in association with SLE

frequency.us: Rare in children; mostly adolescent females; APS in ~20% of pediatric SLE; renal in ~25% of APS
frequency.global: Rare globally; predominantly adolescent females; APS in pediatric SLE varies 10–35% across registries
frequency.sources: Avcin et al. Arthritis Rheum 2008; Levy et al. Lupus 2004; PAPS collaborative data

diagnosis: Antiphospholipid antibodies (aCL, anti-β2GPI, lupus anticoagulant) ×2 positive 12 weeks apart; kidney biopsy (TMA pattern); anti-dsDNA, ANA

treatment.standardOfCare: • Anticoagulation — warfarin (target INR 2.5–3.5 for arterial thrombosis; 2.0–3.0 for venous); LMWH as bridge or in pregnancy • Hydroxychloroquine — reduces thrombotic events and aPL titers; recommended for all SLE-related APS • RAAS blockade — for hypertension and proteinuria (hypertensive nephrosclerosis component) • Aspirin — adjunctive antiplatelet for arterial events; combined with anticoagulation in high-risk patients • Blood pressure control — stringent targets (<130/80 mmHg) Note: DOACs (rivaroxaban, apixaban) — NOT recommended for triple-positive aPL (LAC + anti-cardiolipin + anti-β2GPI); warfarin preferred; DOACs may be used for double/single positivity with venous-only events after shared decision-making
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Eculizumab — for catastrophic APS (CAPS) and refractory TMA; evidence from case series and small cohorts; increasingly accepted in CAPS ▶ Rituximab — for refractory APS or aPL-positive SLE nephritis; emerging evidence ▶ Belimumab — for SLE-APS overlap; BLISS trials included LN patients with aPL positivity Methods ▶ Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) — for APS nephropathy with chronic vascular injury; investigational; some case series ▶ Complement inhibition — aPL activates complement; anti- C5 strategies under investigation

name: Alport Syndrome — X-linked (COL4A5)
description: Most common hereditary nephritis; mutations in COL4A5 causing progressive nephritis, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities in males

frequency.us: ~1/5,000–10,000; accounts for ~1% of pediatric ESKD; X-linked most common (85% of Alport); males severely affected
frequency.global: ~1/5,000–10,000 globally; predominant in European-descent populations; ESKD by 25 yrs in 50% of affected males
frequency.sources: Kashtan et al. JASN 2013; European Alport Registry; Jais et al. JASN 2003

diagnosis: Urinalysis (hematuria ± proteinuria); audiogram; ophthalmology exam; kidney biopsy (EM: GBM lamellation/thinning); COL4A5 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril) / ARBs (losartan) — initiated at first sign of microalbuminuria/proteinuria; ESCAPE trial and Alport registry data show significant delay to ESKD; 2022 KDIGO Alport guideline recommends ACEi/ARB in ALL males with hematuria + family history regardless of proteinuria level • KDIGO 2022 Alport Guidelines — landmark update; recommends early ACEi/ARB even before proteinuria; tier-based approach: Tier 1 (persistent proteinuria) → mandatory; Tier 2 (microalbuminuria) → strong recommendation; Tier 3 (isolated hematuria, high-risk genotype) → consider • BP control to <50th percentile (or CKD target <75th %ile) — essential for renal preservation • Low-protein diet — adjunct in advanced CKD stages • Kidney transplant — highly effective; no recurrence of Alport nephritis in graft (no type IV collagen made); ESKD median age ~25–35 yr in untreated males; anti-GBM disease in transplant rare (<5%) • Hearing aids — for sensorineural hearing loss; audiological surveillance annually • Ophthalmological monitoring — anterior lenticonus, macular flecks; annual slit-lamp exam
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Sparsentan (FILSPARI) — dual ET-A/AT-II antagonist; DUPLEX trial includes Alport patients; ACEi/ARB- refractory proteinuria; investigational ▶ Lademirsen (anti-miR-21) — microRNA-21 inhibitor targeting TGF-β fibrotic pathway; Phase 2 (NCT02855268); Alport-specific; halted 2023 for strategic reasons; mechanism validated ▶ Bardoxolone methyl — Nrf2 activator; improves GFR in CKD; Phase 3 CARDINAL trial in Alport (NCT03019185); completed; modest eGFR improvement ▶ COL4A5 gene therapy — AAV delivery to podocytes/GBM; preclinical (mouse models); long-term goal ▶ Stem cell therapy — mesenchymal stem cells reducing fibrosis; preclinical Methods

name: Alport Syndrome — Autosomal Recessive (COL4A3/A4)
description: Biallelic mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 causing severe nephritis similar to X-linked Alport; affects males and females equally

frequency.us: ~15% of Alport syndrome cases in US; typically presents in first decade with rapid ESKD progression
frequency.global: ~15% of all Alport globally; ESKD in adolescence/young adulthood; consanguineous families at higher risk
frequency.sources: Jais et al. JASN 2003; Gross et al. JASN 2012; Kashtan Ped Nephrol 2010

diagnosis: COL4A3/COL4A4 genetic testing; kidney biopsy (EM: GBM thinning and lamellation); audiogram; ophthalmology; family history

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — same indications as X-linked Alport; KDIGO 2022 guidelines apply equally; early initiation at microalbuminuria stage; AR Alport often has earlier, more severe course than X-linked in males • BP control — CKD targets; combination antihypertensive as needed • Monitoring — proteinuria (monthly initially), eGFR (every 3–6 months), hearing (annually), ophthalmology (annually) • Kidney transplant — curative; no recurrence; ESKD typically earlier than X-linked (median ~20s); living-related donor evaluation requires COL4A3/A4 carrier status testing (heterozygous carriers have favorable outcomes but need long-term follow-up) • KDIGO 2022 note: COL4A3/A4 heterozygous carriers ("thin basement membrane nephropathy spectrum") now recognized as having ~30% lifetime CKD risk; ACEi warranted if proteinuria develops Emerging (same pipeline as X-linked Alport) ▶ Lademirsen, bardoxolone methyl, sparsentan — see X- linked Alport; trials include all COL4 genotypes ▶ COL4A3/A4 gene therapy — autosomal recessive inheritance makes gene therapy more straightforward than X-linked; preclinical

name: Alport Syndrome — Autosomal Dominant
description: Heterozygous COL4A3/COL4A4 mutations causing variable nephritis; often milder than AR form; previously called familial hematuria

frequency.us: Underdiagnosed; heterozygous COL4A3/A4 mutations in ~1/200 population; significant CKD in 30– 40%
frequency.global: ~1/200 globally carry heterozygous COL4A3/A4 mutations; 30–40% develop proteinuria/CKD; likely most common inherited GN
frequency.sources: Gross et al. JASN 2018; Savige et al. AJKD 2016; Deltas et al. Ped Nephrol 2013

diagnosis: COL4A3/COL4A4 genetic testing; urinalysis; family history of hematuria; kidney biopsy (may show GBM thinning or lamellation)

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — KDIGO 2022: same tier-based approach as other Alport forms; heterozygous COL4A3/A4 mutations; milder course than X-linked or AR; ESKD in ~15–30% of affected individuals (often adult onset) • BP management — standard CKD targets • Genetic counseling — AD inheritance; 50% transmission risk; test at-risk family members • Monitoring — same surveillance as other Alport forms; hearing and ophthalmology involvement less common than X-linked • Kidney transplant — if ESKD reached; excellent outcomes; no recurrence Emerging ▶ Same investigational pipeline as X-linked Alport (lademirsen, bardoxolone methyl, sparsentan)

name: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome — Finnish Type (NPHS1)
description: Mutations in NPHS1 encoding nephrin causing massive proteinuria from birth; originally described in Finnish population

frequency.us: ~1/50,000 in US; Finnish prevalence ~1/8,200; presents at birth with massive proteinuria and anasarca
frequency.global: ~1/50,000 globally; highly prevalent in Finland (~1/8,200); high carrier frequency in Finnish population (~1/200)
frequency.sources: Kestila et al. Mol Cell 1998; Holmberg & Jalanko Ped Nephrol 2014; Jalanko et al. Ped Nephrol 2009

diagnosis: Neonatal urinalysis (massive proteinuria); NPHS1 genetic testing; kidney biopsy (diffuse mesangial sclerosis pattern); serum albumin; AFP elevated antenatally

treatment.standardOfCare: • Albumin infusions — frequent (often daily/alternate day) to maintain serum albumin ≥20 g/L and minimize complications; mainstay of supportive management Methods • IV albumin + IV furosemide — manages massive edema; goal serum albumin ≥15–20 g/L • Nephrectomy (bilateral) — key management decision; unilateral or bilateral; removes massive protein loss; timing individualized; usually performed before transplant or when protein losses unmanageable; bilateral nephrectomy + dialysis bridge to transplant • Nutrition — high-protein diet (2–3 g/kg/day); vitamin D, trace element supplementation; nasogastric/gastrostomy tube feeding commonly required • Thyroid hormone supplementation — thyroxine loss in urine causes hypothyroidism; levothyroxine replacement standard • Anticoagulation — hypercoagulable state; prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin often used • Prophylactic antibiotics — pneumococcal vaccine + penicillin prophylaxis; high infection risk • Kidney transplant — definitive treatment; NPHS1 mutations → no nephrin in native kidneys; ~25% risk of recurrent nephrotic syndrome post-transplant due to anti- nephrin antibodies; rituximab used for post-transplant recurrence • ACEi/ARBs — reduces proteinuria; used pre- nephrectomy/transplant Emerging ▶ Anti-nephrin antibody detection — NEJM 2024 data demonstrate circulating anti-nephrin antibodies in subset of NPHS1 patients; rituximab targets this mechanism; potential monitoring tool ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-NPHS1) — podocyte-targeted; preclinical; NPHS1 promoter-driven expression challenging due to size

name: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome — NPHS2 (podocin)
description: Autosomal recessive mutations in NPHS2 (podocin) causing steroid- resistant nephrotic syndrome in infancy or early childhood

frequency.us: ~10–15% of childhood steroid- resistant nephrotic syndrome in US; onset 3 months to 5 years
frequency.global: 10–15% of childhood FSGS/SRNS globally; prevalent in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and European populations
frequency.sources: Boute et al. Nat Genet 2000; Weber et al. Nat Genet 2000; Ruf et al. JASN 2004

diagnosis: NPHS2 genetic testing; kidney biopsy (FSGS or minimal change on LM); steroid trial confirms resistance; EM (foot process effacement)

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — partial antiproteinuric effect; less responsive than MCD/primary FSGS; use in all NPHS2 patients with proteinuria • Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) — limited efficacy vs. primary FSGS; some NPHS2 genotypes (especially R138Q homozygous) are steroid-resistant AND CNI-resistant; genotype guides expectations • Dietary management — protein supplementation; edema management • Kidney transplant — standard treatment for ESKD; recurrence risk much lower than primary FSGS (NPHS2- associated FSGS rarely recurs unless compound heterozygous with one non-truncating mutation); R229Q variant in one allele increases recurrence risk • Genetic testing — critical before transplant to stratify recurrence risk; donor evaluation Methods • Steroids — generally ineffective (steroid-resistant NS by definition in most); brief trial acceptable per KDIGO 2021 NS guidelines Emerging ▶ Podocyte stabilization strategies — coenzyme Q10, antioxidants for mitochondrial podocytopathies (indirect benefit) ▶ Anti-nephrin antibody monitoring — subset may have immune overlay; rituximab considered ▶ mRNA therapy for NPHS2 — restoring podocin; preclinical concept

name: Pierson Syndrome (LAMB2)
description: Biallelic LAMB2 mutations causing congenital nephrotic syndrome + microcoria (fixed miosis) + neurodevelopmental impairment

frequency.us: Extremely rare; <200 cases
frequency.global: Extremely rare globally; <200 cases reported in literature; severe early-onset NS with microspherophakia and retinal dystrophy
frequency.sources: Zenker et al. Nat Genet 2004; Matejas et al. KI 2010; Pierson review Ped Nephrol 2012

diagnosis: LAMB2 genetic testing; ophthalmology (microcoria, retinal abnormalities); kidney biopsy (FSGS/DMS); neonatal urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal replacement therapy — ESKD in infancy/early childhood; peritoneal dialysis preferred in infants; nasogastric feeding + intensive nutrition support during dialysis phase • Kidney transplant — ESKD treatment; renal outcomes good post-transplant (LAMB2 not expressed in donor kidney in pathologic form); timing when weight/size permits (typically ≥8–10 kg) • Ophthalmological management — microcoria is pathognomonic; does not worsen post-transplant; manage refractive errors; amblyopia prevention; specialist ophthalmology follow-up lifelong • Neurological monitoring — hypotonia, developmental delay in severe forms; physiotherapy, occupational therapy • Nutritional support — intensive supplementation in nephrotic phase and dialysis; growth promotion • Supportive NS management — albumin infusions, diuretics, anticoagulation as for other congenital NS Emerging ▶ LAMB2 gene therapy — very early concept; basement membrane protein delivery challenges; preclinical

name: Galloway-Mowat Syndrome
description: Heterogeneous group of conditions (WDR73, KEOPS complex genes, etc.) causing congenital nephrotic syndrome + microcephaly + neurological disease

frequency.us: Very rare; multiple genetic causes; poor prognosis with early ESKD and neurodevelopmental impairment
frequency.global: Very rare globally; caused by mutations in >20 genes (OSGEP, WDR73, NUP107, etc.); universal poor prognosis
frequency.sources: Braun et al. NEJM 2017; Colin et al. JASN 2014; Galloway- Mowat review Ped Nephrol 2019

diagnosis: Genetic panel (WDR73, OSGEP, TP53RK, etc.); brain MRI; kidney biopsy; developmental assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal replacement therapy — ESKD typically in infancy to early childhood; peritoneal dialysis; intensive nutritional support • Kidney transplant — feasible for renal component; extra- renal manifestations (microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, seizures) impact candidacy and outcomes; center-by-center evaluation; controversial given multi- organ severity in many genotypes • Neurological management — antiepileptic drugs for seizures; seizure control challenging; anticonvulsant optimization Methods • Nutritional support — nasogastric/gastrostomy feeding; protein and caloric supplementation • Physical/occupational/speech therapy — developmental support • Genetic testing — multiple genes (WDR4, TP53RK, TPRKB, OSGEP, LAGE3, GON7, etc.); genotype- phenotype correlation informs prognosis and transplant decision • Genetic counseling — autosomal recessive in most; prenatal diagnosis available Emerging ▶ tRNA modification pathway — multiple GMS genes encode KEOPS complex; translational regulation pathway; research stage ▶ No disease-modifying therapies available

name: Denys-Drash Syndrome (WT1)
description: WT1 missense mutations causing diffuse mesangial sclerosis, Wilms tumor predisposition, and 46XY DSD (male pseudohermaphroditism)

frequency.us: Rare; ~150 cases reported
frequency.global: Extremely rare globally; ~150 total reported cases; autosomal dominant de novo WT1 mutations; near-universal Wilms tumor risk
frequency.sources: Pelletier et al. Cell 1991; Breslow et al. Cancer 2000; Lehnhardt et al. Ped Nephrol 2011

diagnosis: WT1 genetic testing; kidney biopsy (diffuse mesangial sclerosis); gonadal evaluation (karyotype, pelvic ultrasound); Wilms tumor surveillance

treatment.standardOfCare: • Nephrectomy — CRITICAL: bilateral prophylactic nephrectomy recommended given near-universal Wilms tumor risk (>90% lifetime); timing debated but most centers recommend before age 2–3 years or at diagnosis; pathological specimens required • Dialysis + kidney transplant — after bilateral nephrectomy; peritoneal dialysis bridge; transplant once oncologically clear; excellent renal outcomes post-transplant (no disease recurrence) • Wilms tumor surveillance — prior to nephrectomy: ultrasound every 3 months; MRI for better characterization • Wilms tumor treatment if present — nephrectomy + chemotherapy (actinomycin D, vincristine ± doxorubicin per COG/SIOP protocols); radiation for high-stage disease • DSD management — gonadal dysgenesis; gonadectomy (streak gonads at high risk of gonadoblastoma); hormonal management; psychosocial counseling; multidisciplinary DSD team • Steroid-resistant NS — supportive; ACEi/ARB for proteinuria; steroid-resistant by definition; dialysis planning Emerging ▶ WT1 targeted therapies — understanding WT1 missense mutation effects on podocyte transcription; no targeted drugs yet ▶ Genotype-specific counseling — WT1 exon 8/9 mutations (zinc finger domain) associated with DDS; exon 9 splice site mutations → Frasier syndrome

name: Frasier Syndrome (WT1)
description: WT1 splice site mutations causing slowly progressive FSGS, male pseudohermaphroditism (46XY), and gonadoblastoma risk; milder than Denys-Drash

frequency.us: Very rare; WT1 intron 9 splice mutations; slower ESKD (adolescence/young adulthood); gonadoblastoma ~30%
frequency.global: Very rare globally; WT1 intron 9 donor site mutations; distinct from Denys-Drash; streak gonads with gonadoblastoma risk
frequency.sources: Barbaux et al. Nat Genet 1997; Pelletier et al. Cell 1991; Lehnhardt et al. Ped Nephrol 2011

diagnosis: WT1 genetic testing (intron 9); kidney biopsy (FSGS); karyotype; gonadal ultrasound; urinalysis and renal function monitoring

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • Gonadectomy — CRITICAL: streak gonads have high gonadoblastoma risk (30–60%); bilateral gonadectomy recommended at diagnosis; gonadoblastoma can transform to dysgerminoma • Kidney transplant — ESKD typically in adolescence/young adulthood (slower than DDS); no Wilms tumor risk in Frasier (unlike DDS); transplant after nephrectomy; good outcomes • Steroid-resistant NS management — ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria; progressive CKD; dialysis planning • Hormonal management — testosterone or estrogen replacement post-gonadectomy per gender identity; endocrinology comanagement • DSD psychosocial support — multidisciplinary team; gender identity counseling Emerging ▶ WT1 splice site research — Frasier caused by +KTS splice isoform imbalance; therapeutic splicing modulation investigated

name: Nail-Patella Syndrome (LMX1B)
description: Autosomal dominant LMX1B mutations causing nail dysplasia, absent/hypoplastic patella, iliac horns, glaucoma, and nephropathy in ~30–40%

frequency.us: ~1/50,000; nephropathy in 30– 40%; ESKD in ~10%; hematuria/proteinuria may appear in childhood
frequency.global: ~1/50,000 globally; COL5A1/LMX1B mutations; renal involvement in 30–40%; COL4A3/A4 involvement established
frequency.sources: Bongers et al. Nat Genet 2002; Sweeney et al. Am J Hum Genet 2003; NPS Consortium data

diagnosis: LMX1B genetic testing; kidney biopsy (EM: 'moth- eaten' GBM with collagen fibrils); X-ray (iliac horns, absent patella); ophthalmology (glaucoma)

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — first-line for proteinuria/hypertension; ~30–50% of NPS patients develop nephropathy; KDIGO CKD guidelines apply; early initiation at microalbuminuria • BP control — essential; renovascular and glomerular mechanisms • Monitoring — annual renal function, urinalysis, BP; ophthalmology (open-angle glaucoma in 30–50%); orthopedic surveillance (patella dislocation, elbow dysplasia) • Glaucoma treatment — topical beta-blockers, prostaglandin analogues; laser trabeculoplasty; trabeculectomy; regular IOP monitoring • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; NPS does not recur in graft (LMX1B mutation affects host cells, not donor); good outcomes • Orthopedic management — physiotherapy for patellar instability; surgical stabilization if required; skeletal surveillance Emerging ▶ LMX1B transcription factor research — podocyte- expressed; understanding downstream targets for therapy

name: Schimke Immuno- Osseous Dysplasia (SMARCAL1)
description: SMARCAL1 mutations causing spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, T-cell immunodeficiency, and progressive steroid-resistant FSGS; often fatal in childhood

frequency.us: Very rare; ~250 cases
frequency.global: Extremely rare globally; ~250 cases reported; SMARCAL1

diagnosis: SMARCAL1 genetic testing; kidney biopsy (FSGS); skeletal survey; lymphocyte immunophenotyping; T-cell function studies

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Hematopoietic stem cell
transplant — experimental Methods

name: CoQ10 Nephropathy (ADCK4 / COQ6)
description: Mitochondrial coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis defects causing steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome/FSGS that may respond to CoQ10 supplementation

frequency.us: Very rare; ADCK4 and COQ6 mutations; important treatable cause; pediatric onset typical
frequency.global: Very rare globally; both ADCK4 and COQ6 mutations reported; coenzyme Q10 supplementation may halt renal progression
frequency.sources: Ashraf et al. JASN 2013; Heeringa et al. JASN 2011; Lippa et al. Ped Nephrol 2018

diagnosis: Genetic testing (ADCK4, COQ6, COQ2, COQ8B); kidney biopsy (FSGS); urine organic acids; muscle CoQ10 levels; mitochondrial function testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Oral CoQ10 supplementation (ubiquinol or ubiquinone) — may dramatically halt or even reverse renal decline if initiated before significant fibrosis; dose 30 mg/kg/day; mechanism: restores mitochondrial electron transport chain function; ADCK4 mutations respond best • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — antiproteinuric; adjunctive • Renal transplant — if progressive to ESKD; post- transplant outcomes good Note — CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC PRIORITY: COQ2/COQ6/ADCK4 mutations represent the most treatment- responsive form of genetic FSGS; CoQ10 initiation before dialysis essential for renal recovery
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Optimized CoQ10 formulations (nanomicellar, liposomal) — improved bioavailability under study ▶ Gene therapy for ADCK4/PDSS2 — preclinical ▶ Mitochondrial-targeted antioxidants (MitoQ) — investigational ▶ Exogenous CoQ10 analogues — early stage

name: Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease (ARPKD — PKHD1)
description: PKHD1 mutations causing enlarged echogenic kidneys with collecting duct cysts + congenital hepatic fibrosis; presents perinatally or in childhood

frequency.us: ~1/20,000 in US; severe forms cause perinatal death from pulmonary hypoplasia; survivors face CKD and portal HTN
frequency.global: ~1/20,000 globally; PKHD1 mutations; most common recessive PKD; perinatal/neonatal mortality ~30–50% in most severe
frequency.sources: Zerres et al. Nat Genet 1994; Bergmann et al. JASN 2005; Guay-Woodford AJKD 2014

diagnosis: Prenatal/neonatal renal ultrasound (enlarged echogenic kidneys); PKHD1 genetic testing; liver ultrasound; liver biopsy (ductal plate malformation); MRI

treatment.standardOfCare: • Supportive management of renal disease — antihypertensives (ACEi/ARB preferred); proteinuria management; CKD staging and management per KDIGO guidelines • Antihypertensive therapy — critical; RAS blockade first- line; BP target <50th %ile for age • Biliary/hepatic management — congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF) universal; portal hypertension surveillance; beta- blockers for varices; endoscopy for variceal band ligation; TIPS for refractory portal hypertension; Caroli disease component (ductal plate malformations) • Urinary tract infection management — increased susceptibility; aggressive antibiotic treatment; prophylaxis if recurrent • Dialysis — peritoneal or hemodialysis for ESKD; PD may be limited by hepatosplenomegaly/ascites • Combined kidney-liver transplant — for patients with ESKD + severe portal hypertension/liver disease; timing Methods optimization critical; outcomes improving; isolated kidney transplant if liver disease mild • Neonatal management — bilateral enlarged echogenic kidneys; respiratory support for pulmonary hypoplasia in severe neonatal cases; oligohydramnios-related pulmonary complications • Growth support — growth hormone supplementation for growth failure in CKD
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Tolvaptan (Jynarque, Otsuka) — V2R antagonist; approved for ADPKD adults; PEDIATRIC TRIAL ONGOING (ORBIT trial, NCT02964599) for ARPKD; inhibits cAMP-driven cystogenesis; not yet approved for ARPKD or pediatric use; monitoring: liver toxicity, aquaretic effects ▶ mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, sirolimus) — reduce cyst growth in animal models; no sustained benefit in human PKD trials; not recommended outside trials ▶ HDAC inhibitors — preclinical for ARPKD ▶ PKHD1 gene therapy — hepatocyte-targeted; preclinical; complex gene (largest human gene)

name: Autosomal Dominant PKD — Pediatric Onset (ADPKD — PKD1/PKD2)
description: PKD1/PKD2 mutations causing bilateral renal cysts that typically present in adulthood but increasingly diagnosed in childhood with screening

frequency.us: ~1/1,000 overall; pediatric manifestations in ~2–5% including HTN, hematuria, cyst complications
frequency.global: ~1/1,000 globally (most common inherited renal disease); PKD1 (85%) and PKD2 (15%); pediatric manifestations in 2–5%
frequency.sources: Torres et al. Lancet 2007; CRISP Study; ADPKD Consensus Report 2015

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (cysts); MRI for detailed assessment; PKD1/PKD2 genetic testing; blood pressure monitoring; urinalysis; family history

treatment.standardOfCare: • Blood pressure management — ACEi/ARBs first-line; hypertension begins in childhood; ESCAPE trial shows BP target <50th percentile; early intervention reduces renal progression • Monitoring — annual BP, urinalysis, renal function; renal imaging (ultrasound every 3–5 years or per symptoms); avoid CT radiation in children • Avoid nephrotoxins — NSAIDs, contrast agents, aminoglycosides — limit; optimize hydration • High fluid intake — reduces vasopressin levels; delays cystogenesis; 2–3 L/m²/day; water preferred over juice/soda • Pain management — for renal cyst hemorrhage/infection; analgesics; drainage if severe • Psychosocial support — genetic condition; disclosure counseling; impact on child/family • Genetic counseling — PKD1 (chromosome 16) vs PKD2 (chromosome 4); PKD2 milder course; prenatal diagnosis; pre-implantation genetic testing available FDA-Approved (adults; pediatric under study) ▶ Tolvaptan (Jynarque, Otsuka) — FDA approved 2018 for adults with ADPKD at risk of rapid progression; TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials; slows TKV growth ~50%; not approved in pediatrics; hepatotoxicity monitoring required; PEDIATRIC trials planned; liver function tests mandatory Methods every 18 months; aquaretic side effects (nocturia, thirst); contraindicated in liver disease
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Tolvaptan pediatric trials — safety and PK studies in children underway; PREVENT-ADPKD trial; potential future approval ▶ mTOR inhibitors — no benefit demonstrated in adults; not recommended ▶ CFTR inhibitors — c-AMP pathway link; investigational ▶ Metformin — reduces cAMP via AMPK; Phase 2 TAME- PKD (NCT02656017); promising; off-label early use in some centers ▶ Tesevatinib (EGFR/Src inhibitor) — Phase 2 data; slows TKV progression ▶ KD025 (ROCK2 inhibitor) — anti-fibrotic; preclinical for PKD

name: Nephronophthisis — Infantile (NPHP2/INVS)
description: Most severe NPHP form; INVS mutations causing renal cysts and fibrosis presenting in first year of life with rapid progression to ESKD

frequency.us: Very rare; ESKD before age 2; accounts for small fraction of infantile ESKD in US registries
frequency.global: Very rare globally; INVS/NPHP2 mutations; situs inversus in ~25%; ESKD typically before 18 months
frequency.sources: Otto et al. Nat Genet 2003; Tory et al. JASN 2009; ESCAPE Trial data

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (small echogenic kidneys ± cysts); NPHP2/INVS genetic testing; kidney biopsy (tubular basement membrane disruption, interstitial fibrosis)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal replacement therapy — ESKD in infancy (typically within first year of life); peritoneal dialysis; aggressive nutritional support for growth • Kidney transplant — curative for renal disease; excellent outcomes; NPHP does not recur in graft; timing when size permits (≥8–10 kg); infantile NPHP has earlier ESKD than juvenile • Situs inversus management — universal in NPHP2/INVS; cardiac evaluation; no specific therapy but surgical planning for transplant • Hepatic fibrosis — present in NPHP2; liver surveillance, portal hypertension monitoring; combined kidney-liver transplant if severe • Nutritional support — NG/GT feeding; protein and caloric supplementation • Renin-angiotensin blockade — CKD management; BP control

name: Nephronophthisis — Juvenile (NPHP1)
description: Most common NPHP; NPHP1 deletion causing chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis with polydipsia, polyuria, anemia, and ESKD ~age 13

frequency.us: Most common genetic cause of ESKD in first 3 decades; ~1/50,000; NPHP1 deletion in ~25% of cases
frequency.global: ~1/50,000 globally; NPHP1 deletion most frequent cause; ESKD median age ~13 years; ciliopathy spectrum
frequency.sources: Saunier et al. Nat Genet 1997; Hildebrandt et al. Kidney Int 1997; Otto et al. JASN 2002

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (small normal-sized or slightly small echogenic kidneys); NPHP1 deletion by MLPA; genetic panel; retinal exam (Senior- Løken); kidney biopsy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal replacement therapy — ESKD typically by ~13–15 years (juvenile NPHP1); medullary cystic disease; progressive tubulointerstitial nephritis • Kidney transplant — gold standard; curative; no recurrence in graft; deceased or living donor; outcomes excellent • CKD management — ACEi/ARBs for hypertension and proteinuria; anemia management (EPO); mineral bone disease management; nutrition support; growth hormone for CKD-related growth failure Methods • Ophthalmological surveillance — Senior-Løken syndrome overlap (10–15% of NPHP1); annual exam for retinitis pigmentosa • CNS surveillance — cerebellar involvement in some NPH1 variant syndromes; MRI if neurological symptoms • Avoidance of nephrotoxins — NSAIDs, contrast Emerging ▶ No disease-modifying therapy available for NPHP1 ▶ mTOR pathway — NPHP proteins modulate mTOR/Hedgehog; mTOR inhibitors investigated; no clinical benefit established ▶ CEP290/CC2D2A gene therapy concepts — preclinical; ciliary protein delivery challenging

name: Nephronophthisis — Adolescent (NPHP3)
description: NPHP3 mutations causing NPHP with ESKD in adolescence (~age 19); may have extrarenal features (liver fibrosis, retinal dystrophy)

frequency.us: Rare; ESKD in late adolescence; less common than NPHP1; NPHP3 mutations
frequency.global: Rare globally; NPHP3 mutations cause adolescent-onset NPHP; liver and heart involvement reported
frequency.sources: Olbrich et al. Nat Genet 2003; Tory et al. JASN 2009; NPHP registry data

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; NPHP3 genetic testing; liver function; retinal exam; kidney biopsy if uncertain

treatment.standardOfCare: • Same approach as juvenile NPHP1 — CKD management, ACEi/ARBs, RRT, transplant • ESKD typically in adolescence to young adulthood (NPHP3 milder than NPHP1) • Extra-renal surveillance — hepatic fibrosis (NPHP3- associated); situs inversus; cardiac malformations in some; retinal degeneration in Senior-Løken overlap • Kidney transplant — curative; no recurrence Emerging: No disease-modifying therapies available

name: Bardet-Biedl Syndrome — Renal (BBS)
description: Ciliopathy with primary cilia dysfunction causing obesity, rod-cone dystrophy, polydactyly, cognitive impairment, hypogonadism, and renal anomalies

frequency.us: ~1/100,000–160,000 in US; renal anomalies in ~53%; renal failure in ~5–10%
frequency.global: ~1/100,000–160,000 globally; higher in Arab and Bedouin populations; renal cysts and CAKUT in majority
frequency.sources: Forsythe et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2013; BBS International Registry; Beales et al. Nat Genet 1999

diagnosis: Clinical criteria (primary/secondary features); BBS genetic panel (20+ genes); renal ultrasound; retinal assessment; MRI brain; BMI monitoring

treatment.standardOfCare: • CKD/renal anomaly management — structural renal anomalies (cysts, horseshoe, dysplasia) common; ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria/HTN; CKD monitoring per KDIGO; avoid nephrotoxins • Obesity management — severe early-onset obesity is universal in BBS; dietary intervention; behavioral modification; multidisciplinary obesity clinic • Hypertension — antihypertensives per AAP guidelines; obesity-driven • Type 2 diabetes management — early-onset T2D in many; metformin; GLP-1 agonists • Retinal dystrophy — no proven therapy; low vision aids; genetic counseling; avoid vitamin A supplements (counterproductive in some BBS genotypes) • Hypogonadism — testosterone or estrogen replacement post-puberty; endocrinology comanagement • Developmental support — intellectual disability variable; speech/language therapy; occupational therapy • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; good outcomes; obesity management critical peri-transplant FDA-Approved (2020) Methods ▶ Setmelanotide (IMCIVREE, Rhythm Pharmaceuticals) — MC4R agonist; FDA approved June 2020 for obesity due to BBS (and other MC4R pathway deficiencies); weight loss of 10–15%; also improves hyperphagia; first pharmacotherapy specifically for BBS obesity; pediatric approval ≥6 years; SC daily injection Emerging ▶ Ciliary biology — BBS proteins form BBSome; downstream therapeutics targeting cAMP, Hedgehog, mTOR; research stage ▶ Gene therapy — large number of BBS genes; gene- specific approaches; preclinical

name: Joubert Syndrome — Renal (JBTS)
description: Ciliopathy with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia (molar tooth sign), hypotonia, oculomotor apraxia, and variable nephronophthisis or CAKUT

frequency.us: ~1/80,000–100,000 in US; nephropathy in ~35%; ESKD in ~20% by age 20
frequency.global: ~1/80,000–100,000 globally; >35 causative genes; molar tooth sign on MRI pathognomonic; renal involvement variable
frequency.sources: Romani et al. JASN 2013; Travaglini et al. Ped Nephrol 2013; JBTS International Consortium

diagnosis: Brain MRI (molar tooth sign pathognomonic); renal ultrasound; genetic panel (CEP290, TMEM67, CC2D2A, etc.); retinal exam; developmental assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • Nephronophthisis component — CKD management; ACEi/ARBs; dialysis and transplant for ESKD; kidney transplant does not affect neurological manifestations • Respiratory management — neonatal/infant apnea/hyperpnea ("manta ray" breathing); supplemental oxygen; caffeine for apnea; CPAP; most respiratory symptoms improve with age • Developmental and neurological support — cerebellar vermis aplasia/hypoplasia ("molar tooth sign"); gross motor delay; physiotherapy; occupational therapy; speech therapy; intellectual support • Ophthalmological — oculomotor apraxia, retinal dystrophy; visual rehabilitation; low vision aids • Liver surveillance — hepatic fibrosis in JBTS7/RPGRIP1L and others; portal hypertension monitoring • Genetic testing — >40 genes identified (CEP290, TMEM67/MKS3, AHI1, NPHP1, RPGRIP1L, etc.); genotype informs prognosis Emerging ▶ No disease-modifying therapies available ▶ Ciliopathy pathway research — primary cilia biology; Hedgehog/mTOR modulation; preclinical

name: Meckel-Gruber Syndrome
description: Lethal ciliopathy (MKS1, TMEM216, CEP290, etc.) causing renal cystic dysplasia, occipital encephalocele, polydactyly; incompatible with life

frequency.us: ~1/13,000–140,000 (wide variation by population); lethal; prenatal diagnosis critical
frequency.global: 1/13,000 in some Finnish populations; 1/140,000 in others; MKS1, TMEM67, CEP290 common mutations; universally lethal
frequency.sources: Mecke & Passarge Neuropediatrics 1971; Barisic et al. Eur J Hum Genet 2015; MKS Consortium

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound (renal cysts + encephalocele + polydactyly); fetal MRI; genetic panel for MKS genes; autopsy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Lethal condition — Meckel-Gruber syndrome is uniformly lethal (encephalocele + bilateral renal cystic dysplasia + polydactyly); stillbirth or death in early neonatal period • Prenatal diagnosis — ultrasound diagnosis possible from 11–14 weeks gestation; MRI for confirmation; genetic testing (MKS1, TMEM216, CEP290, etc.) • Perinatal palliative care — counseling for comfort-focused care; neonatology consultation; no curative intervention available Methods • Bereavement support — family counseling; autopsy for genotype-phenotype correlation • Genetic counseling — autosomal recessive; 25% recurrence risk; prenatal diagnosis in subsequent pregnancies; preimplantation genetic testing available

name: Senior-Løken Syndrome
description: Ciliopathy combining nephronophthisis with early- onset retinal dystrophy (Leber congenital amaurosis or retinitis pigmentosa); NPHP1/4/5 mutations

frequency.us: Rare; ~1/1,000,000 in US; retinal dystrophy may precede renal disease by years
frequency.global: ~1/1,000,000 globally; NPHP genes (NPHP1, NPHP4, NPHP5, CEP290); retinal degeneration onset before renal failure
frequency.sources: Senior et al. Am J Ophthalmol 1961; Otto et al. Nat Genet 2005; Tory et al. JASN 2009

diagnosis: Retinal exam + ERG (retinal dystrophy); renal ultrasound (NPHP pattern); genetic panel (NPHP1, NPHP4, NPHP5/IQCB1, CEP290); kidney biopsy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Nephronophthisis management — same as NPHP1 for renal component; ACEi/ARBs; CKD monitoring; dialysis; kidney transplant (curative for renal disease; renal outcomes excellent) • Retinal dystrophy — Leber congenital amaurosis or retinitis pigmentosa spectrum; no curative therapy; low vision rehabilitation; dark-adapted glasses; vitamin A supplementation (caution: variable benefit/harm by genotype; discuss with ophthalmologist) • Ophthalmological monitoring — early electroretinogram (ERG) for functional assessment; OCT for structural monitoring; genetic ophthalmology specialist • Genetic counseling — multiple causative genes (NPHP5/IQCB1, NPHP6/CEP290, NPHP1, etc.); autosomal recessive; variable retinal/renal severity by gene Emerging ▶ CEP290 antisense oligonucleotide (sepofarsen, ProQR) — for CEP290-associated retinal dystrophy (LCA10); Phase 2/3 ILLUMINATE trial; intravitreal injection; improves visual acuity in some patients; ongoing trials ▶ Gene therapy for LCA (non-CEP290) — voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna, Spark) FDA approved 2017 for RPE65 mutations (not Senior-Løken); model for future CEP290 delivery

name: Oro-Facial-Digital Syndrome Type I — Renal
description: X-linked dominant ciliopathy (OFD1) with oral, facial, and digit anomalies; females affected (lethal in males); renal cysts in ~15–20%

frequency.us: ~1/250,000 in US; renal cysts minor feature; X-linked; typically affects females
frequency.global: ~1/250,000 globally; X- linked; caused by OFD1 mutations; renal cysts in ~15–20%; CNS features prominent
frequency.sources: Ferrante et al. Nat Genet 2006; Thauvin-Robinet et al. Orphanet 2011; OFDS1 Registry

diagnosis: OFD1 genetic testing; renal ultrasound; clinical oral/digital/facial assessment; brain MRI (Joubert-like features in some)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal cyst management — similar to ADPKD management when cysts present; ACEi/ARBs for hypertension/proteinuria; nephrology monitoring; dialysis and kidney transplant for ESKD • Oral abnormalities — cleft lip/palate repair; dental management; frequent dental evaluation; jaw anomalies • Cerebral involvement — partial agenesis of corpus callosum; Dandy-Walker malformations; neurodevelopmental monitoring; seizure management; anti-epileptics as needed • Digital anomalies — polydactyly, syndactyly; orthopedic surgical correction • Speech therapy — for oral and neurological components Methods • Genetic counseling — X-linked dominant; lethal in males; almost exclusively females affected; OFD1 gene mutation; prenatal testing available Emerging ▶ No disease-modifying therapies; supportive multidisciplinary management

name: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex — Renal (AML / cysts)
description: TSC1/TSC2 mutations causing renal angiomyolipomas and cysts; risk of hemorrhage from large AMLs and progression to CKD

frequency.us: ~1/6,000 in US; renal involvement in >80%; AMLs and cysts nearly universal; RCC risk increased
frequency.global: ~1/6,000 globally; TSC1/TSC2 mutations; renal AMLs in >80% by adulthood; cystic disease common; RCC in ~2–3%
frequency.sources: Northrup & Krueger Ann Neurol 2013; TSC Consensus Conference 2012; Curatolo et al. Lancet 2008

diagnosis: Renal MRI (AMLs — fat signal); TSC1/TSC2 genetic testing or clinical criteria; MRI surveillance every 1–3 years; urinalysis; eGFR

treatment.standardOfCare: • Everolimus (Afinitor) — mTOR inhibitor; FDA approved for growing TSC-associated AMLs ≥3 cm (EXIST-2 trial); reduces AML volume significantly; also approved for SEGA and renal cell tumors in TSC • Sirolimus — alternative mTOR inhibitor; off-label use in pediatric TSC-AML • Selective embolization (transarterial embolization) — for acute hemorrhage from AML (Wunderlich syndrome) or growing lesions not controlled on mTOR inhibitors • Nephron-sparing surgery — when embolization fails or for diagnostic uncertainty • RAAS blockade — for proteinuria and hypertension • Annual renal MRI surveillance — per ITSC guidelines from age 1 (recommended every 1–3 years)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Nab-sirolimus (Fyarro) — FDA approved 2021 for malignant PEComa; off-label interest in TSC-AML ▶ Longer-term mTOR inhibitor use — emerging data on prevention of renal functional decline ▶ Autologous stem cell approaches — very early for severe multi-organ TSC; not renal-specific ▶ Combination strategies (mTOR + CDK inhibitors) — preclinical

name: Von Hippel-Lindau — Renal Cysts (pediatric onset)
description: VHL mutations causing renal cysts and early-onset clear cell RCC; pediatric surveillance important for at-risk family members

frequency.us: ~1/36,000 in US; renal cysts from childhood; RCC in 24–45% by 5th decade
frequency.global: ~1/36,000 globally; VHL mutations; renal cysts childhood onset; RCC rare but reported in pediatric age; surveillance essential
frequency.sources: Lonser et al. Lancet 2003; Maher & Kaelin JASN 1997; VHL Alliance guidelines 2020

diagnosis: VHL genetic testing; annual renal MRI from age 8–10 in VHL families; abdominal ultrasound; ophthalmology; CNS imaging (hemangioblastomas)

treatment.standardOfCare: • VHL renal surveillance — annual renal imaging (MRI preferred; ultrasound for children to minimize radiation); screen for clear cell RCC (common in VHL); kidney cysts usually asymptomatic in childhood • Nephron-sparing surgery — for renal cell carcinoma when lesion ≥3 cm; partial nephrectomy; active surveillance for lesions <3 cm (watchful waiting); minimize nephron loss given bilateral/multifocal RCC risk • Systemic VHL surveillance — annual MRI brain/spine (hemangioblastomas); ophthalmology (retinal hemangioblastomas); biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines); pancreatic endocrine tumor screening Methods • Multidisciplinary VHL center care — neurosurgery, ophthalmology, endocrinology, nephrology, urology, genetic counseling FDA-Approved (2021) — MAJOR ADVANCE ▶ Belzutifan (WELIREG, Merck) — HIF-2α inhibitor; FDA approved August 2021 for VHL-associated RCC, CNS hemangioblastomas, and pancreatic NETs (adults); LITESPARK-004 Phase 2 trial: 49% ORR for VHL-RCC; pediatric data emerging; blocks HIF-2α driven tumor growth; oral once-daily tablet; can eliminate need for surgery in some cases; anemia (common SE); monitor Hgb Emerging ▶ Belzutifan pediatric studies — ongoing; pharmacokinetics in adolescents; dose finding ▶ PT2977 (successor HIF-2α inhibitors) — next-generation compounds ▶ Anti-VEGF approaches — bevacizumab for retinal hemangioblastomas; intravitreal injection

name: Medullary Cystic Kidney Disease (UMOD / MUC1)
description: UMOD or MUC1 mutations causing chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis and gout in adolescents/young adults; now classified as ADTKD

frequency.us: Rare; UMOD and MUC1 mutations; hyperuricemia/gout often precedes renal failure by decades
frequency.global: Rare globally; UMOD most common cause; MUC1 expansion mutations; autosomal dominant; gout in young adults characteristic
frequency.sources: Hart et al. Nat Genet 2002; Kirby et al. Nat Genet 2013; Devuyst & Pirson Ped Nephrol 2008

diagnosis: UMOD/MUC1 genetic testing; renal ultrasound (may appear normal or small); uric acid; kidney biopsy (tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis); family history

treatment.standardOfCare: • CKD management — ACEi/ARBs for hypertension/proteinuria; KDIGO CKD stages; monitoring eGFR, proteinuria, BP; typically adult onset (teens–40s) but includes pediatric cases • Gout management — hyperuricemia universal in UMOD mutations; allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) first-line; febuxostat alternative; dietary purine restriction; adequate hydration • Avoid nephrotoxins — NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides; NSAIDs particularly harmful given tubulointerstitial damage • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; no disease recurrence in graft; excellent outcomes; gout resolves post-transplant • Genetic counseling — autosomal dominant; UMOD (uromodulin) or MUC1 mutations; genotyping important since MUC1 mutation missed by standard sequencing (VNTR repeat); specialized MUC1 sequencing recommended Emerging ▶ 4-PBA (4-phenylbutyrate) — chemical chaperone; promotes UMOD protein folding and secretion; Phase 2 trial ongoing for ADTKD-UMOD; reduces intracellular UMOD accumulation; potentially disease-modifying ▶ BRD4 inhibitors — targets MUC1-STAT pathway in ADTKD-MUC1; preclinical

name: Autosomal Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease (ADTKD — MUC1, HNF1B, REN)
description: Umbrella term for hereditary tubulointerstitial nephridites caused by MUC1, UMOD, HNF1B, REN, or SEC61A1 mutations; progressive CKD

frequency.us: Collectively rare; HNF1B most common in US; ADTKD covers multiple genes with dominant inheritance
frequency.global: Rare globally; HNF1B most prevalent cause; MUC1 and UMOD also recognized; slowly progressive to ESKD
frequency.sources: Bingham & Ellard Ped Nephrol 2012; ADTKD Consortium data; Eckardt et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2013

diagnosis: Genetic panel (MUC1, UMOD, HNF1B, REN); renal ultrasound; uric acid; liver function (HNF1B); pancreas assessment (HNF1B-related MODY5)
