treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • CKD management — KDIGO stages; ACEi/ARBs for hypertension; monitoring schedule; nutrition; avoid nephrotoxins • Gout treatment — allopurinol for UMOD variant; specific to UMOD subtype; see MCDK/UMOD entry • Kidney transplant — curative; no recurrence; excellent outcomes; all ADTKD subtypes • Genetic counseling — dominant inheritance; multiple genes (UMOD, MUC1, REN, HNF1B) • REN (renin) mutations — severe neonatal anemia, hypo- RAS-related; sodium supplementation, blood transfusion, erythropoietin in infancy/early childhood • HNF1B — complex phenotype (renal cysts, diabetes MODY5, genital tract malformations); multidisciplinary management • KDIGO 2019 ADTKD guidelines — framework for management Emerging ▶ 4-PBA — for ADTKD-UMOD (see MCDK/UMOD); Phase 2 ongoing ▶ BRD4/MUC1 pathway — ADTKD-MUC1; investigational

name: HNF1B Nephropathy / 17q12 Microdeletion Syndrome
description: HNF1B mutations/17q12 deletion causing renal cysts and diabetes (MODY5), with variable renal dysplasia, CAKUT, hyperuricemia, and cholestasis

frequency.us: ~1/10,000–20,000 in US; 17q12 deletion in ~50%; highly variable phenotype (renal + pancreatic/hepatic)
frequency.global: ~1/10,000–20,000 globally; HNF1B mutations and 17q12 microdeletion; MODY5 diabetes common co-feature
frequency.sources: Bingham & Ellard Ped Nephrol 2012; Bellanne-Chantelot et al. JASN 2004; 17q12 Deletion Consortium

diagnosis: HNF1B genetic testing or chromosomal microarray; renal MRI/ultrasound; OGTT (MODY5 diabetes); liver/pancreas imaging; uric acid; urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal cyst/dysplasia management — CKD monitoring; ACEi/ARBs for hypertension and proteinuria; may present as neonatal/fetal echogenic kidneys; ESKD in subset (variable) • Diabetes (MODY5) management — insulin-dependent diabetes; NOT responsive to sulfonylureas; insulin therapy; endocrinology co-management; onset typically adolescence/young adulthood • Genital tract abnormalities — Müllerian agenesis/bicornuate uterus in females; cryptorchidism in males; reproductive counseling; gynecology/urology referral • Liver/biliary abnormalities — cholestasis in some; hepatology monitoring • Electrolyte monitoring — hypomagnesemia common (tubular Mg wasting); oral magnesium supplementation • Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency — supplemental pancreatic enzymes if present • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; no recurrence; excellent outcomes • Genetic counseling — 50% de novo; MODY5 inheritance; family screening; array CGH for 17q12 deletion (whole gene deletion common) Methods

name: Renal Agenesis — Unilateral
description: Absence of one kidney due to failure of ureteric bud induction; compensatory hypertrophy of contralateral kidney occurs

frequency.us: ~1/1,000–2,000 births in US; contralateral kidney anomalies in ~30%; higher in males
frequency.global: ~1/1,000–2,000 births globally; most common in males; associated with CAKUT syndromes and chromosomal anomalies
frequency.sources: Westland et al. Ped Nephrol 2011; Sanna-Cherchi et al. JASN 2013; CAKUT Consortium

diagnosis: Prenatal or postnatal ultrasound; DMSA scan to confirm absence vs. ectopia; VCUG if VUR suspected; blood pressure; urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Monitoring — blood pressure annually; urinalysis + protein/creatinine ratio annually from early childhood; eGFR monitoring; avoid nephrotoxins; renal ultrasound every 3–5 years for contralateral compensatory hypertrophy • BP management — ACEi/ARBs at first sign of hypertension or microalbuminuria; compensatory hyperfiltration promotes glomerulosclerosis • Contralateral kidney protection — avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast; aggressive hydration when ill; careful use of nephrotoxic medications • Diet — avoid excessive protein and sodium intake; DASH principles • CAKUT evaluation — unilateral agenesis frequently associated with other CAKUT anomalies (VUR, contralateral UPJ obstruction); voiding cystourethrogram if UTI; renal ultrasound protocol • Genetic counseling — HNF1B, PAX2, RET mutations in subset; chromosomal microarray if other anomalies present • Long-term counseling — ~40% lifetime risk of hypertension; ~10–15% CKD risk; contact sports counseling (protective padding; kidney guard for high- contact sports)

name: Renal Agenesis — Bilateral (Potter Sequence)
description: Complete absence of both kidneys causing oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, Potter facies, and limb deformities; lethal without intervention

frequency.us: ~1/4,000–5,000 births in US; lethal perinatally from pulmonary hypoplasia; amnioinfusion experimental
frequency.global: ~1/4,000–5,000 births globally; potters sequence inevitable; outcomes improving with fetal interventions (amnioinfusion) experimentally
frequency.sources: Granger et al. Ped Nephrol 2012; Thomas & Frias Ped Rev 2009; NEJM 2023 (amnioinfusion trial)

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound (absent kidneys, severe oligohydramnios); MRI fetal; autopsy confirmation postnatal

treatment.standardOfCare: • Potter sequence — bilateral renal agenesis is uniformly fatal without intervention; pulmonary hypoplasia from oligohydramnios; no kidney function • Experimental renal agenesis — infant dialysis programs at highly specialized centers (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, etc.); peritoneal dialysis from birth possible • Palliative care — standard approach; neonatology and palliative medicine counseling for families; compassionate care protocol • Prenatal counseling — renal agenesis diagnosed by fetal MRI; detailed counseling on prognosis; options discussion • Amniotic fluid instillation — experimental prenatal therapy to improve lung development; investigational trials underway (CHOP/Cincinnati) • If survival achieved (dialysis protocol): kidney transplant goal; requires sufficient pulmonary development; PD access placed surgically; rare long-term survivors reported Emerging ▶ Prenatal amniotic fluid supplementation (FAST trial) — serial amnioinfusions to restore lung development; Phase Methods 2 investigational trials; potential to improve pulmonary hypoplasia and enable neonatal survival to dialysis ▶ Xenotransplantation — pig-to-human kidney; neonatal application highly investigational

name: Renal Hypoplasia
description: Small kidney(s) with reduced nephron number but normal architecture; unilateral or bilateral; may progress to CKD

frequency.us: ~1/500 births (any degree) in US; bilateral hypoplasia major cause of childhood CKD in US (CKiD data)
frequency.global: ~1/500 births globally; bilateral hypoplasia in ~0.5– 1/10,000; leading cause of CKD in childhood worldwide
frequency.sources: Sanna-Cherchi et al. JASN 2012; CKiD Study; Westland et al. CJASN 2014

diagnosis: Prenatal/postnatal ultrasound; kidney size measurement; GFR assessment; DMSA scan (differential function); blood pressure; proteinuria

treatment.standardOfCare: • CKD monitoring — staged per KDIGO; renal function surveillance from diagnosis; BP monitoring; urinalysis; proteinuria • Antihypertensive therapy — ACEi/ARBs preferred; hyperfiltration injury prevention in solitary or hypoplastic kidney • UTI prevention/treatment — increased susceptibility; low threshold for antibiotic treatment; VCUG if UTI to assess for VUR • Growth monitoring — CKD-associated growth failure; growth hormone therapy if growth failure established • Nutrition — adequate protein and caloric intake; salt restriction if hypertensive • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; bilateral severe hypoplasia may lead to childhood ESKD; excellent post- transplant outcomes

name: Renal Dysplasia
description: Abnormal renal parenchymal development with disorganized architecture, primitive ducts, and metaplastic cartilage; may be cystic or non-cystic

frequency.us: Most common renal structural anomaly; bilateral dysplasia major cause of pediatric CKD in NAPRTCS
frequency.global: Most common structural renal anomaly globally; component of many CAKUT phenotypes; bilateral disease leading cause of ESKD
frequency.sources: NAPRTCS 2011; Harambat et al. Ped Nephrol 2012; CKiD Study design CJASN 2008

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (echogenic, disorganized architecture); DMSA (poor function); VCUG (associated VUR); genetic evaluation for syndromic causes

treatment.standardOfCare: • Serial ultrasound — baseline at diagnosis then every 3– 12 months depending on severity; assess for involution (MCDK) vs. progression (cystic dysplasia) • CKD management — KDIGO stages; ACEi/ARBs; bilaterally dysplastic kidneys lead to ESKD; unilateral tolerated if contralateral normal • Hypertension management — frequent comorbidity; standard antihypertensives • UTI management — voiding VCUG to exclude VUR; recurrent UTIs; antibiotic prophylaxis if VUR present • Proteinuria monitoring — annual urine protein/creatinine ratio • Dialysis and transplant — for severe bilateral dysplasia; peritoneal dialysis; transplant when size/weight permit • Genetic evaluation — CAKUT panel genes (RET, PAX2, HNF1B, BMP4, etc.) for bilateral dysplasia; chromosomal microarray for syndromic cases

name: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney (MCDK)
description: Complete replacement of one kidney with non- communicating cysts and no functional parenchyma; contralateral kidney compensates

frequency.us: ~1/4,000 births in US; unilateral most common; involution by age 5 in most cases
frequency.global: ~1/4,000 births globally; predominantly unilateral; bilateral lethal; European registry data consistent with US rates
frequency.sources: Kuwertz-Broeking et al. Arch Dis Child 2004; Rabelo et al. Ped Nephrol 2015; MCDK Registry

diagnosis: Prenatal/postnatal ultrasound; DMSA (confirms non-function); VCUG (15– 20% have contralateral VUR); blood pressure

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Observation — most MCDK involute completely by 2–5
years; serial ultrasound every 6–12 months until involution
confirmed; no intervention required for asymptomatic
involuting MCDK Methods • Contralateral kidney surveillance — compensatory hypertrophy; monitor for VUR (VCUG in first year if UTI or additional anomalies); hypertension; proteinuria • BP monitoring — annually from age 5; hypertension develops in ~15–20% • Nephrectomy — reserved for: persistently enlarging MCDK after age 2, hypertension, suspected Wilms in a cystic mass, symptoms (pain, UTI) • Renal tumor risk — very small increased risk of RCC or Wilms in MCDK; reassurance; nephrectomy if concerning features • Long-term follow-up — even after involution: annual BP, urinalysis, creatinine through adolescence

name: Renal Involvement in VACTERL / CHARGE Syndrome
description: Structural renal anomalies (agenesis, horseshoe, VUR, hydronephrosis) occurring as part of VACTERL or CHARGE association

frequency.us: VACTERL ~1/10,000–40,000 US; CHARGE ~1/8,500–10,000 US; renal anomalies in ~50% VACTERL
frequency.global: VACTERL ~1/10,000– 40,000 globally; CHARGE ~1/8,500–10,000; European registries consistent with US data
frequency.sources: Solomon et al. Birth Defects Res 2018; Issekutz et al. Am J Med Genet 2005; CHARGE Consortium

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis; renal ultrasound; VCUG; chromosomal microarray (CHARGE: CHD7 gene); echocardiogram; spine imaging

treatment.standardOfCare: • Renal anomaly management — 50–80% of VACTERL have renal anomalies (horseshoe, agenesis, dysplasia, VUR); manage per specific anomaly type; CKD monitoring • VUR management — VCUG screening; antibiotic prophylaxis; see VUR entry • Multidisciplinary care — VACTERL is multi-system; card iology (cardiac anomalies), GI surgery (esophageal atresia/TE fistula, anorectal malformations), orthopedics (vertebral/limb), nephrology coordination • Nephrology surveillance — annual BP, urinalysis, creatinine; early referral if CKD develops • CHARGE syndrome (CHD7) — renal anomalies in 20– 40%; same CKD monitoring approach; hearing loss management; ophthalmology; genetics

name: Duplex Kidney / Ureteral Duplication
description: Incomplete or complete ureteral duplication with two separate collecting systems draining one kidney; upper pole prone to obstruction/ectopia

frequency.us: ~1/500 population in US; most common renal anomaly; females more affected; upper pole ureterocele ~20%
frequency.global: ~1/500 globally; most common congenital urinary tract anomaly; duplicated systems with ureterocele higher in females
frequency.sources: Privett et al. Br J Urol 1976; Siomou et al. Ped Nephrol 2011; AAP UTD guidelines 2011

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound; postnatal ultrasound; VCUG (lower pole VUR); MAG3 renogram (differential function); MRI urography

treatment.standardOfCare: • Observation — majority of duplex/ureteral duplication are asymptomatic and managed conservatively • UTI management — upper pole ureterocele often obstructs and causes UTIs; antibiotic prophylaxis for febrile UTI; culture-directed antibiotics for breakthrough UTIs • Ureterocele management — depends on location and function: small orthotopic ureterocele → observation; obstructing ureterocele → endoscopic puncture (first-line); ectopic ureterocele with non-functioning upper pole → upper pole heminephrectomy or complete nephroureterectomy • VUR management — lower pole often refluxes in duplex systems; antibiotic prophylaxis; endoscopic injection (Deflux); ureteral reimplantation for breakthrough infections • Imaging — renal ultrasound + VCUG + MAG3 renal scan to assess function and drainage Methods

name: Antenatal Hydronephrosis
description: Dilatation of the renal pelvis identified on prenatal ultrasound; most common prenatal finding; etiologies range from transient to obstructive

frequency.us: ~1–5% of pregnancies have antenatal hydronephrosis; majority resolves; SFU grading standard
frequency.global: ~1–5% of all pregnancies globally; most common prenatal anomaly detected on ultrasound; majority (50–70%) resolves spontaneously
frequency.sources: Nguyen et al. Ped Nephrol 2010; Lee et al. Urology 2006; SFU Classification System

diagnosis: Serial prenatal ultrasound; postnatal ultrasound at 48– 72 hours and 4–6 weeks; MAG3 renogram; VCUG; APD measurement (SFU grade)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) grading — Grades 1–4; Grade 1–2 transient physiological in majority (>70% resolves spontaneously) • Postnatal evaluation — renal ultrasound at 48–72 hours and again at 1 month; severe prenatal ANH warrants earlier postnatal scan • VCUG — for bilateral ANH, severe grades, or febrile UTI to rule out VUR/PUV • MAG3 diuretic renography — assess differential renal function and obstruction (UPJ/UVJ) • Antibiotic prophylaxis — amoxicillin in neonates with moderate-severe ANH pending workup; trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole for older infants; prophylaxis duration per SFU/AAP guidance • Surgical intervention — UPJ obstruction with <40% differential function or progressive dilatation → pyeloplasty; see UPJ/UVJ entries • Observation — mild ANH (APD <10 mm at term) → outpatient follow-up; most resolve

name: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction (UPJO)
description: Obstruction at junction of renal pelvis and ureter causing hydronephrosis; intrinsic (aperistaltic segment) or extrinsic (crossing vessel)

frequency.us: ~1/1,500 births in US; most common cause of significant antenatal hydronephrosis; males > females
frequency.global: ~1/1,500 births globally; bilateral in 10–40%; most common cause of upper tract obstruction requiring intervention
frequency.sources: Hussain et al. Ped Nephrol 2014; Sutherland et al. J Urol 2008; EAU Pediatric Guidelines 2021

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; MAG3 renogram (obstruction pattern, split function); VCUG (exclude VUR); MRI urography for complex cases

treatment.standardOfCare: • Observation vs. surgery decision — based on: differential renal function (DRF <40% = surgical threshold in most centers), drainage on MAG3 (T½ >20 min), progressive hydronephrosis, recurrent UTIs, symptoms (pain) • Pyeloplasty — gold standard surgical repair; laparoscopic or robotic-assisted dismembered Anderson-Hynes pyeloplasty; >95% success rate; preserves renal function; outpatient or 23-hour stay • Antibiotic prophylaxis — for significant hydronephrosis pending surgery or during observation • Serial MAG3 renography + ultrasound — every 3–6 months during observation; post-pyeloplasty scan at 3–6 months • Endopyelotomy — alternative to open/laparoscopic repair in selected adolescents; lower success rate; less preferred in pediatrics • Congenital UPJ — most common cause; extrinsic compression (crossing vessel) in ~20%

name: Ureterovesical Junction Obstruction
description: Obstruction at junction of ureter and bladder causing hydroureteronephrosis; includes primary megaureter and obstructed ectopic ureter

frequency.us: ~1/5,000 births in US; primary megaureter ~20% of antenatal hydronephrosis referrals
frequency.global: ~1/5,000 births globally; spontaneous resolution in majority; surgical correction when obstruction is significant
frequency.sources: Liu et al. Ped Nephrol 2014; Baskin et al. J Urol 1994; EAU Pediatric Urology Guidelines 2021

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (dilated ureter and pelvis); MAG3 renogram; VCUG (exclude VUR); MRI urography

treatment.standardOfCare: • Observation — many UVJ obstructions (megaureter) resolve spontaneously, especially primary non-refluxing type; serial ultrasound • Antibiotic prophylaxis — during observation period; febrile UTI management • Surgical intervention — ureteral reimplantation with tapering (for obstructed megaureter); indications: Methods declining renal function (<40% DRF), recurrent febrile UTIs despite prophylaxis, progressive dilatation, symptoms • Timing — most centers delay surgery until 12–18 months if no deterioration; neonatal surgery if severe obstruction and infected • MAG3 renography — differential function and drainage assessment; key for surgical decision • Temporary ureteral stent or cutaneous ureterostomy — for urgent decompression in infected obstruction

name: Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR) — Primary
description: Retrograde urine flow from bladder to ureter/kidney due to incompetent ureterovesical junction; predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal scarring

frequency.us: ~1% general US population; 30–40% of children post-febrile UTI; familial in ~30%
frequency.global: ~1% globally; highest in white European-descent children; lower in Black and Asian children; resolves spontaneously in most
frequency.sources: Smellie et al. BMJ 1975; Tekgül et al. Eur Urol 2015; RIVUR Trial 2014

diagnosis: VCUG (gold standard); DMSA (renal scarring); MAG3 renogram; grading I– V; urodynamics if bladder dysfunction suspected

treatment.standardOfCare: • Low-grade VUR (I–II) — observation alone; antibiotic prophylaxis not routinely recommended by 2011 AAP guidelines; parental education on UTI recognition; prompt treatment of febrile UTIs • Higher-grade VUR (III–V) / recurrent febrile UTIs — antibiotic prophylaxis (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or nitrofurantoin); RIVUR trial (2014): prophylaxis reduces UTI recurrence but not renal scarring in uncomplicated VUR; benefit greatest in bladder/bowel dysfunction • Bladder/bowel dysfunction (BBD) — treat aggressively; BBD worsens VUR outcomes; timed voiding, fiber, anticholinergics for OAB component • Endoscopic injection (Deflux/dextranomer-hyaluronic acid) — minimally invasive; 70–80% resolution for Grade II–III; 50–60% for Grade IV; office/day surgery procedure; avoids open surgery • Open ureteral reimplantation (Cohen or Politano- Leadbetter) — >95% success rate; reserved for failed Deflux, Grade V, anatomical abnormalities; gold standard • Robotic-assisted ureteral reimplantation — increasingly used; comparable outcomes to open; shorter stay • Spontaneous resolution — Grade I 80%, Grade II 75%, Grade III 50%, Grade IV 25%, Grade V 15% per year Emerging ▶ Circumcision — reduces UTI risk in uncircumcised males with VUR; reduces breakthrough UTIs ▶ DMSA scan — 4–6 months post-febrile UTI to detect renal scarring; guides management intensity

name: Vesicoureteral Reflux — Secondary
description: VUR caused by elevated intravesical pressure (neurogenic bladder, PUV, dysfunctional voiding) rather than intrinsic ureterovesical junction abnormality

frequency.us: Prevalence depends on underlying bladder pathology; higher grade VUR than primary
frequency.global: Prevalence determined by underlying pathology globally; neurogenic bladder and PUV major drivers; surgical correction often required
frequency.sources: EAU Pediatric Guidelines 2021; AAP 2011 UTI guidelines; VCUG referral criteria

diagnosis: VCUG; urodynamics; identify and treat underlying cause; DMSA for scarring; renal function

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Treat underlying cause — neurogenic bladder (clean
intermittent catheterization, anticholinergics, Botox),
bladder outlet obstruction (PUV ablation), posterior
urethral valves; VUR often resolves when primary cause
corrected Methods • CIC for neurogenic bladder — clean intermittent catheterization maintains low bladder pressures; prevents high-pressure VUR • Same antibiotic prophylaxis/surgical considerations as primary VUR if persistent • Bladder pressure management — anticholinergics; intravesical onabotulinumtoxinA for neurogenic DO • Ureteral reimplantation — only after bladder dysfunction maximally treated and only if VUR persists

name: Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV)
description: Obstructing folds in posterior male urethra causing bilateral hydronephrosis, bladder dysfunction, and CKD; most severe obstructive uropathy in males

frequency.us: ~1/5,000–8,000 male births in US; ~15–20% of pediatric ESKD; most severe LUTO in males
frequency.global: ~1/5,000–8,000 male births globally; European registry data similar; ESKD in 15–20% despite early ablation
frequency.sources: Nassr et al. Ped Nephrol 2017; NAPRTCS 2011; ERA-EDTA Registry; PUV Long-term Study

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound (bilateral hydronephrosis, thick-walled bladder, keyhole sign); VCUG (confirms valves); cystoscopy; MAG3; creatinine nadir predicts outcome

treatment.standardOfCare: • Valve ablation — endoscopic cystoscopic ablation (resection or vaporization) of posterior urethral valves; performed urgently/semi-urgently after initial stabilization; primary definitive treatment • Initial stabilization — urethral catheter decompression; treat electrolyte abnormalities and AKI; IV fluids; antibiotics if UTI/urosepsis • Renal function monitoring — PUV is leading cause of congenital obstructive uropathy ESKD; 30–50% reach ESKD by adolescence/young adulthood; serial eGFR, proteinuria, BP • ACEi/ARBs — for hypertension and proteinuria; nephroprotective • VUR management — present in 50% of PUV; antibiotic prophylaxis; usually resolves after valve ablation • Bladder dysfunction management — myogenic bladder damage persists after valve ablation; timed voiding; CIC if elevated PVR; anticholinergics cautiously (may worsen retention) • Nocturnal polyuria — renal concentrating defect common in PUV; desmopressin rarely helpful; fluid management education • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; bladder must be evaluated and optimized pre-transplant; bladder augmentation may be needed; excellent outcomes possible

name: Prune Belly Syndrome (Eagle-Barrett)
description: Triad of absent abdominal musculature, cryptorchidism, and urinary tract anomalies (megaureter, megacystis, renal dysplasia) exclusively in males

frequency.us: ~1/35,000–50,000 male births in US; CKD in ~30%; spectrum from lethal to mild
frequency.global: ~1/35,000–50,000 male births globally; near-universal male; triad of abdominal wall, cryptorchidism, urinary anomalies
frequency.sources: Woodhouse et al. Br J Urol 1982; Hassett et al. J Urol 2012; PBS Consortium data

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound; postnatal evaluation: renal ultrasound, VCUG, MAG3; abdominal wall assessment; orchidopexy evaluation

treatment.standardOfCare: • Urological reconstruction — complex, individualized; urethroplasty for urethral stenosis; orchidopexy for cryptorchidism (bilateral, intra-abdominal); ureteral reconstruction (for severely dilated ureters with infection) • Antibiotic prophylaxis — for recurrent UTIs; culture- directed treatment of febrile UTIs • Clean intermittent catheterization — if bladder dysfunction with elevated PVR • Abdominal wall reconstruction — abdominoplasty for cosmesis and core stability; improves pulmonary mechanics; typically deferred until 6–12 months Methods • Pulmonary management — absent abdominal musculature causes respiratory compromise; chest physiotherapy; treat pulmonary hypoplasia if present • CKD monitoring — renal dysplasia common; ACEi/ARBs; serial renal function; dialysis/transplant for ESKD • Cryptorchidism — orchidopexy early (within first year) to preserve fertility potential and reduce malignancy risk

name: Horseshoe Kidney
description: Fusion of lower poles of both kidneys across midline; associated with UPJO and VUR; usually incidental finding

frequency.us: ~1/400–600 US population; most common fusion anomaly; UPJO in 15–30%; Turner/trisomy 18 association
frequency.global: ~1/400–600 globally; consistent prevalence worldwide; associated with multiple congenital syndromes
frequency.sources: Glodny et al. J Urol 2009; Weizer et al. J Urol 2003; EAU Pediatric Guidelines

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (bridging isthmus); MAG3 renogram (exclude obstruction); VCUG; CT/MRI for complex anatomy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Observation — most horseshoe kidneys asymptomatic; incidental finding; no treatment needed • UTI management — increased susceptibility due to altered drainage; urine culture; antibiotic treatment; VCUG to evaluate for VUR • Urolithiasis management — increased stone risk (urinary stasis, altered urodynamics); hydration; stone analysis; metabolic stone evaluation; ESWL (reduced efficacy in horseshoe kidneys); ureteroscopy; PCNL adapted technique • Hypertension management — ACEi/ARBs if hypertension develops; routine BP monitoring • UPJ obstruction — present in 30%; pyeloplasty if indicated (robot-assisted or laparoscopic) • Wilms tumor surveillance — horseshoe kidney has slight increased risk; ultrasound if suspicious lesion • Renal cell carcinoma — increased risk long-term; imaging surveillance in adults

name: Ectopic Kidney
description: Kidney located outside normal renal fossa (pelvic, iliac, thoracic, crossed fused ectopia); associated with VUR and UPJO

frequency.us: ~1/900–1,000 in US; pelvic ectopia most common; crossed fused ectopia ~1/7,500
frequency.global: ~1/900–1,000 globally; often incidental; malrotation typical; complications include obstruction and infection
frequency.sources: Bauer Urol Clin NA 1975; Glodny et al. J Urol 2009; Walsh Campbell's Urology

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; MAG3 renogram; VCUG; CT/MRI for complex anatomy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Observation — most ectopic kidneys function normally; no intervention needed • Hypertension monitoring — annual BP; ectopic kidneys may have anomalous vasculature contributing to renovascular hypertension • UTI management — some ectopic kidneys have drainage impairment; prompt antibiotic treatment; VCUG for VUR • Urolithiasis — similar to horseshoe kidney; hydration; stone management • Pelvic ectopic kidney — important surgical landmark; counsel families; surgical planning for any abdominal/pelvic procedures

name: Urethral Stricture — Pediatric
description: Narrowing of urethra causing voiding dysfunction, UTIs, and upper tract dilatation; can be congenital, traumatic, or iatrogenic in children

frequency.us: Rare in children without prior surgery; iatrogenic post- hypospadias repair most common cause
frequency.global: Rare globally without prior instrumentation; congenital anterior urethral valves uncommon; surgical trauma predominant cause
frequency.sources: Snodgrass & Prieto J Urol 2009; EAU Pediatric Guidelines 2021; Duel et al. J Urol 1998

diagnosis: Uroflowmetry; VCUG; urethrogram; cystoscopy; urinary tract ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • Urethral dilation — first-line for short strictures; bougie or catheter-based; temporary relief; high recurrence • Urethroscopy + direct vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU) — for short (≤2 cm) strictures; cold-knife or laser incision; 50–60% success for first treatment; decreasing success with repeated procedures Methods • Urethroplasty — gold standard for recurrent/long strictures; anastomotic repair or substitution (buccal mucosal graft); 85–95% success rate; preferred over repeated dilation/DVIU • Urine culture — treat infection before instrumentation • Trauma evaluation — bulbar urethral stricture in boys often post-straddle injury; PFUI (pelvic fracture urethral injury) in pelvic trauma • Posterior urethral valves — separate etiology; managed with valve ablation

name: Bladder Exstrophy — Renal Complications
description: Bladder exstrophy causes continuous urinary tract anomalies with frequent renal complications (VUR, hydronephrosis, CKD from recurrent infections/obstruction)

frequency.us: ~1/30,000–50,000 US births; renal complications in majority without optimal management; VUR universal
frequency.global: ~1/30,000–50,000 births globally; complex reconstruction required; renal outcomes depend on early surgical management
frequency.sources: Mitchell & Bägli J Urol 1996; Gearhart & Mathews J Urol 2000; Exstrophy-Epispadias Complex Consortium

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; MAG3; VCUG; eGFR; urinalysis; urodynamics post- reconstruction

treatment.standardOfCare: • Primary surgical closure — staged reconstruction: primary bladder closure within 72 hours of birth (with or without osteotomy); epispadias repair at 6–12 months; bladder neck reconstruction after bladder capacity achieved (typically 4–5 years) • Modern staged approach vs. complete primary repair (CPR) — complete primary repair at birth increasingly used in specialized centers; comparable outcomes • Continence surgery — bladder neck reconstruction (Mitchell, Young-Dees-Leadbetter); urinary continence achieved in 50–80% by age 5–6 • Bladder augmentation — if bladder capacity insufficient post-reconstruction; ileocystoplasty • CIC — often required post-bladder neck repair for complete emptying • Renal monitoring — VUR present in most; antibiotic prophylaxis; upper tract surveillance • Orthopedic — pelvic osteotomy facilitates closure; physiotherapy; normal ambulation expected

name: Cloacal Anomalies — Renal Involvement
description: Complex cloaca in females causes renal anomalies (fusion, ectopia, agenesis, hydronephrosis) in ~50%; renal function critical for outcomes

frequency.us: ~1/50,000 US females; renal anomalies in ~50%; complex surgical reconstruction needed
frequency.global: ~1/50,000 females globally; spectrum from simple to complex; renal function crucial determinant of surgical approach and timing
frequency.sources: Levitt & Peña Semin Ped Surg 2010; Rich et al. J Pediatr Surg 1988; ARM-Net Registry

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; MRI pelvis and abdomen; VCUG; MAG3; cystoscopy and genitoscopy; genetic evaluation

treatment.standardOfCare: • Multidisciplinary surgical reconstruction — complex staged repair; initial colostomy and mucus fistula at birth; mobilization of common channel; separation of urinary, genital, and GI tracts; typically 12–18 months of age • Urological reconstruction — vaginal reconstruction; ureteral reimplantation if VUR; bladder reconstruction; Malone appendicovesicostomy (MACE) for neurogenic bladder • Renal anomalies — 30–50% have associated CAKUT; renal ultrasound and CKD monitoring • Clean intermittent catheterization — neurogenic bladder common due to sacral deficiency; CIC essential • GI/colorectal management — bowel management program; constipation prevention critical; Malone antegrade colonic enema (MACE) procedure for bowel continence Methods • Gynecological follow-up — vaginal stenosis; Müllerian anomalies; fertility counseling in adolescence • Psychosocial support — lifelong multidisciplinary team

name: Neurogenic Bladder — Spina Bifida / Myelomeningocele
description: Bladder dysfunction from spinal cord defect causing detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, high bladder pressures, VUR, and upper tract damage

frequency.us: ~3–4/10,000 births with NTD in US (folate fortification reduced NTD rates); neurogenic bladder in ~90% of MMC
frequency.global: Globally 1–10/10,000 births; highest in South Asia; NTD rates declining with folate supplementation programs
frequency.sources: Khoshnood et al. BMJ 2015; Mitchell et al. Birth Defects Res 2004; MOMS Trial NEJM 2011

diagnosis: Urodynamics (high-pressure bladder, detrusor overactivity, DSD); renal ultrasound; VCUG; MAG3; urinalysis; creatinine; annual assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • Clean intermittent catheterization (CIC) — cornerstone; every 3–4 hours; prevents overdistension, reduces infection, protects upper tracts; started from infancy to avoid bladder damage • Anticholinergic medications — oxybutynin (oral or intravesical), tolterodine, solifenacin; reduces detrusor overactivity and high bladder pressures; intravesical oxybutynin better tolerated (fewer systemic effects) • Renal + bladder ultrasound surveillance — every 6–12 months; identify hydronephrosis, VUR, poor bladder compliance early • Urodynamics — annually from birth or at diagnosis; leak point pressure, bladder compliance, capacity; guides CIC and medication adjustments • VUR management — antibiotic prophylaxis; reimplantation if needed after bladder optimization • Upper tract protection — goal bladder storage pressure <40 cmH2O; compliance monitoring FDA-Approved Pediatric: • OnabotulinumtoxinA (BOTOX, Allergan/AbbVie) — FDA approved 2021 for pediatric neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) in children ≥5 years; 100–200 units intravesical injection into detrusor; urodynamics-guided; improves compliance, reduces incontinence, protects upper tracts; duration 6–12 months; retreatment as needed; LANDMARK approval for pediatric urology • Bladder augmentation (enterocystoplasty) — ileocystoplasty or sigmoid cystoplasty; for refractory neurogenic bladder with inadequate capacity despite CIC + medications + Botox; Mitrofanoff appendicovesicostomy for continent catheterizable channel; bladder neck closure if needed • Mitrofanoff principle — appendicovesicostomy; umbilical or abdominal stoma for CIC; facilitates independent catheterization in adolescents • Malone antegrade colonic enema (MACE) — for neurogenic bowel component • Spinal cord monitoring — surveillance for tethered cord; neurosurgery comanagement; untethering when indicated Emerging Methods ▶ Sacral neuromodulation — InterStim; less established in myelomeningocele vs. non-neurogenic OAB; investigational in this population ▶ Beta-3 adrenergic agonist (mirabegron) — approved for adults/OAB; pediatric neurogenic bladder trials ongoing; alternative to anticholinergics ▶ Stem cell therapy for spinal cord injury — very early stage

name: Neurogenic Bladder — Sacral Agenesis
description: Sacral agenesis causes variable neurogenic bladder; bowel and bladder dysfunction; associated with maternal diabetes

frequency.us: Rare; ~1/25,000 births in US; maternal diabetes risk factor; partial sacral agenesis more common than complete
frequency.global: Rare globally; ~1/25,000; partial agenesis more frequent; renal/bladder phenotype variable by level of sacral involvement
frequency.sources: Boemers et al. J Urol 1994; Wilmshurst et al. Dev Med Child Neurol 2012; EAU Ped Guidelines

diagnosis: Spinal MRI; urodynamics; renal ultrasound; VCUG; MAG3 renogram; electromyography (EUS)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Same CIC + anticholinergics framework as myelomeningocele neurogenic bladder • Urodynamics — critical given variable bladder phenotype; sacral agenesis spectrum (Type I–IV per Renshaw); Type I (partial unilateral sacral) often mild; Type IV (total sacral agenesis) severe • OnabotulinumtoxinA — same indications as spina bifida neurogenic bladder • Anorectal malformations — frequent comorbidity; bowel management program; constipation management critical (distended rectum worsens bladder dysfunction) • Screening for associated anomalies — maternal diabetes association; cardiac, vertebral, GI anomalies • Bladder augmentation — if conservative measures fail; same surgical principles • MRI sacral/spinal — defines anatomy; surgical planning

name: Dysfunctional Elimination Syndrome
description: Combination of bladder and bowel dysfunction causing urinary urgency, frequency, incontinence, constipation, and VUR/UTIs in neurologically normal children

frequency.us: Common; ~30% of children referred for UTI workup in US; peak age 5–10 years; females predominate
frequency.global: Common globally; difficult to estimate true prevalence; behavioral and anatomic factors play varying roles across populations
frequency.sources: Vande Walle et al. Eur J Ped 2012; Austin et al. J Urol 2016; ICCS Standardization Report

diagnosis: History and voiding diary; uroflowmetry (staccato or plateau pattern); post-void residual; renal/bladder ultrasound; VCUG; urodynamics if needed

treatment.standardOfCare: • Timed/scheduled voiding — every 2–3 hours; prevents bladder overdistension; cornerstone of management • Bowel management — treat constipation aggressively (dietary fiber, fluids, polyethylene glycol/MiraLax); constipation universally worsens bladder dysfunction (pelvic floor competition) • Pelvic floor biofeedback — for dyssynergia/DSD; teaches relaxation of external sphincter during voiding; highly effective; typically 4–8 sessions • Anticholinergics — oxybutynin for OAB component if behavioral therapy insufficient; start low dose • VUR management — DES worsens VUR outcomes; treat DES first before considering surgery for VUR • Urotherapy — specialist nurse education; bladder diary; voiding diaries; behavioral modification • Urodynamics — for complex/refractory cases; rule out occult neurogenic bladder • Screen for associated stressors — constipation, anxiety, school bathroom avoidance; psychosocial support

name: Overactive Bladder —
description: Urinary urgency with or without incontinence, with frequency and nocturia, in neurologically normal children; detrusor overactivity on urodynamics

frequency.us: Common; ~5–10% of school- age US children; spontaneous resolution typical; peak age 5–7 years
frequency.global: ~5–10% of school-age children globally; ICCS criteria used internationally; spontaneous resolution in majority
frequency.sources: Norgaard et al. J Urol 1998; Neveus et al. ICCS Standardization 2010; Hoebeke et al. Eur Urol 2010

diagnosis: History and voiding diary; uroflowmetry; post-void residual; renal ultrasound; urinalysis; urodynamics if refractory

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • Behavioral therapy first-line — timed voiding; bladder training; double voiding; fluid management (avoid caffeine, citrus); constipation treatment; urotherapy education • Anticholinergic medications — oxybutynin extended- release (first-line pharmacotherapy); tolterodine; solifenacin (approved for OAB in children ≥5 yr in some countries); darifenacin; side effects: dry mouth, constipation, cognition (oxybutynin IR has most CNS effects; prefer ER formulations) • Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) — adult approved; pediatric OAB trials (NICE, EU approval pending for pediatric use); fewer anticholinergic side effects; off-label use increasing; favorable tolerability • Urodynamics — for refractory OAB to exclude neurogenic etiology • Constipation treatment — essential; MiraLax; fiber; disimpaction if needed Emerging ▶ OnabotulinumtoxinA (BOTOX) — FDA approved for pediatric NDO ≥5 yr (2021); off-label in non-neurogenic pediatric OAB; evidence growing; typically reserved for refractory cases ▶ Sacral neuromodulation (InterStim Micro) — FDA approved for OAB in adults; increasing pediatric data in refractory non-neurogenic OAB ≥16 yr; office-level evaluation with external stimulation trial

name: Nocturnal Enuresis — Refractory
description: Involuntary voiding during sleep in children ≥5 years; primary (never dry) or secondary; refractory defined as failure of standard treatments

frequency.us: Common; ~15% of 5-year-olds in US; ~1–2% of adolescents; spontaneous resolution 15%/year
frequency.global: ~5–15% of 5-year-olds globally; widely prevalent; ICCS defines primary/secondary forms; spontaneous resolution consistent worldwide
frequency.sources: Neveus et al. Acta Paediatr 2010; Forsythe & Redmond Dev Med Child Neurol 1974; ICCS Guidelines 2020

diagnosis: Voiding diary; renal/bladder ultrasound; urinalysis; urine osmolality; consider sleep study (OSA); assess bladder capacity; constipation evaluation

treatment.standardOfCare: • Alarm therapy — bedwetting alarm (enuresis alarm); first- line for motivated families; 70–80% cure rate; conditioning response; typically 8–12 weeks; most effective when combined with behavioral support • Desmopressin (DDAVP) — synthetic vasopressin analogue; reduces nighttime urine production; oral tablet (Nocdurna for adults; standard DDAVP for children) or intranasal spray (less preferred due to hyponatremia risk); 60–70% response; use for short-term (camp, sleepovers) or as maintenance; hyponatremia risk — restrict fluid intake after dosing; monotherapy or combined with alarm • Combined alarm + desmopressin — superior to either alone for refractory enuresis; recommended for non- responders • Behavioral interventions — bladder training; timed voiding; constipation treatment; star charts • Treat constipation — constipation in 30–50% of enuretic children; must treat concurrent constipation • Anticholinergics — oxybutynin added to desmopressin for OAB component; helps ~30% of refractory cases Methods • Exclude organic causes — diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, sleep apnea, spinal cord abnormality, urinary infection; urinalysis, glucose, and post-void residual Emerging ▶ Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) — combined with desmopressin for refractory nocturnal polyuria + OAB; pediatric trials; off-label

name: Hinman Syndrome (Non- neurogenic Neurogenic Bladder)
description: Acquired voiding dysfunction with features of neurogenic bladder but no neurological lesion; severe detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia, VUR, and renal damage

frequency.us: Rare; ~1% of children with severe voiding dysfunction referred to US tertiary centers; males predominate
frequency.global: Rare globally; behavioral and psychological overlay on dysfunctional voiding; recognized in all healthcare settings
frequency.sources: Allen JAMA 1977; Hinman & Bauman J Urol 1973; Khen- Dunlop et al. J Urol 2006

diagnosis: Urodynamics (high-pressure dyssynergia); renal ultrasound; VCUG; MRI spine (exclude lesion); psychiatric/psychological assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • CIC (clean intermittent catheterization) — essential for elevated post-void residual; prevents hydronephrosis; cornerstone • Anticholinergics — for OAB/detrusor overactivity component; oxybutynin; solifenacin • Biofeedback pelvic floor rehabilitation — central component; treats learned sphincter dyssynergia; typically 6–12 sessions • Psychosocial evaluation and therapy — Hinman-Allen syndrome has psychological overlay in many cases; child psychiatry/psychology referral; address family dynamics and anxiety • Constipation treatment — aggressive; MiraLax; bowel program • Urodynamics — essential for diagnosis confirmation and monitoring; high PVR, trabeculated bladder, absent neurological lesion • Renal monitoring — CKD possible from long-standing high-pressure bladder; ACEi/ARBs; renal function surveillance • Bladder augmentation — last resort for severe bladder damage despite maximum conservative therapy

name: Cystinosis — Nephropathic (CTNS)
description: Lysosomal cystine transport defect causing intracellular cystine accumulation; renal Fanconi syndrome in infancy progressing to ESKD by ~10 years untreated

frequency.us: ~1/100,000–200,000 in US; CTNS mutations; most common metabolic cause of renal Fanconi in children
frequency.global: ~1/100,000–200,000 globally; higher in Brittany, France (1/26,000); Northern European founder mutation common
frequency.sources: Gahl et al. NEJM 2002; Town et al. Nat Genet 1998; Cystinosis Registry European Network

diagnosis: Leukocyte cystine measurement (elevated); CTNS genetic testing; slit- lamp (corneal crystals); kidney biopsy (cystine crystals); urine amino acids/phosphate/glucose (Fanconi)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Cysteamine (Cystagon — immediate release; Procysbi — delayed-release, twice-daily dosing) — cystine-depleting agent; dramatically slows progression to ESKD; initiated at diagnosis regardless of renal function; Procysbi FDA approved 2013 (improved tolerability, 12-hourly vs. 6- hourly) • Electrolyte and phosphate supplementation — for Fanconi syndrome (phosphate, potassium bicarbonate, sodium bicarbonate, vitamin D, carnitine) • Rickets management — phosphate + calcitriol • Renal transplant — at ESKD; does NOT cure extrarenal disease (cystine continues to accumulate in transplanted organs) Methods • Cysteamine eye drops — for corneal crystals; separate formulation required (Cystadrops — EU approved; compounded in US) • Multidisciplinary follow-up — ophthalmology (corneal crystals), endocrine (thyroid, growth, diabetes), neurology (swallowing, cognition), muscle
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Gene therapy (lentiviral CTNS) — Phase 1/2 trials (UCLA; NCT03897361); autologous HSCT with gene-corrected cells; most advanced pipeline for cystinosis ▶ Rapamycin (sirolimus) — mTOR pathway dysregulated in cystinosis; preclinical/early clinical data ▶ Cysteamine prodrugs — improved CNS penetration for neurological cystinosis ▶ Stem cell therapy — investigational for muscle/swallowing manifestations

name: Lowe Syndrome / Oculocerebrorenal Syndrome (OCRL)
description: X-linked OCRL1 mutations causing congenital cataracts, intellectual disability, and renal Fanconi syndrome; exclusively affects males

frequency.us: ~1/500,000 in US; X-linked; intellectual disability and cataracts distinguish from other Fanconi causes
frequency.global: ~1/500,000 globally; X- linked; OCRL mutations; Fanconi syndrome onset in infancy; neurological involvement uniform
frequency.sources: Loi et al. Cell 1992; Bökenkamp & Ludwig Ped Nephrol 2011; Lowe Syndrome Association

diagnosis: OCRL genetic testing; urine amino acids/phosphate (Fanconi pattern); ophthalmology (cataracts, glaucoma); developmental assessment; leukocyte OCRL enzyme activity

treatment.standardOfCare: • Fanconi syndrome management — proximal tubular dysfunction; oral supplementation of: potassium (KCl), bicarbonate/citrate (Bicitra, Polycitra-K), phosphate, calcium, vitamin D; replace all wasted solutes • Citrate supplementation — prevents kidney stones (calcium oxalate/phosphate); Polycitra or potassium citrate • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — for proteinuria; partial effect; CKD progression management • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; renal disease alone is transplantable; extra-renal complications (intellectual disability, cataracts) persist; donor evaluation and informed consent around global prognosis • Ophthalmological — congenital cataracts present at birth; early surgical extraction (within weeks of birth); contact lens/glasses for aphakia; glaucoma (50%): topical beta- blockers, prostaglandins, trabeculectomy; lifelong ophthalmology • Neurological — intellectual disability universal; hypotonia; seizure management (anti-epileptics); developmental therapy; behavioral management (self-injurious behavior in ~50%) • Physical/occupational therapy — hypotonia management; motor development support • Nutrition — NG/GT feeding if swallowing difficulties; adequate caloric/protein intake

name: Dent Disease Type 1 (CLCN5)
description: X-linked CLCN5 mutations causing low-molecular weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and progressive CKD in males

frequency.us: Rare; ~1/30,000 males in US estimated; females carriers with mild proteinuria; ESKD in 30–80% of males
frequency.global: Rare globally; CLCN5 mutations; males primarily affected; European registries report ESKD by 30–50 yrs in 30–80%
frequency.sources: Thakker RV Nephron 2000; Wrong et al. QJM 1994; Dent Disease International Registry

diagnosis: Urine LMW proteins (beta-2 microglobulin, retinol-binding protein); urinalysis (proteinuria, hematuria); urine calcium; renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); CLCN5 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare:
• High fluid intake — dilutes calcium; reduces stone
formation; 2–3 L/m²/day; key preventive measure Methods • Thiazide diuretics — hydrochlorothiazide; reduces urinary calcium excretion; first-line anti-hypercalciuric; monitor electrolytes (hypokalemia risk); combined with citrate supplementation • Potassium citrate — prevents calcium stone formation; alkalinizes urine; supplement for metabolic acidosis component • Vitamin D and calcium — avoid excessive supplementation (worsens hypercalciuria); standard replacement only if deficient • Dietary sodium restriction — high sodium increases calcium excretion; reduce dietary NaCl • Phosphate supplementation — for hypophosphatemia when present; phosphate wasting variable in Dent 1 vs. 2 • ACE inhibitors — for proteinuria reduction; some benefit but limited evidence • Monitor urinary calcium, creatinine, phosphate, protein annually — guide supplementation • Kidney transplant — for ESKD (30–80% reach ESKD by adulthood); does not recur in graft Emerging ▶ mTOR pathway — CLCN5 (ClC-5) regulates receptor- mediated endocytosis; mTOR inhibitors investigated in animal models; no clinical data

name: Dent Disease Type 2 (OCRL)
description: OCRL mutations causing Dent disease phenotype (LMWP, hypercalciuria) with milder or absent Lowe syndrome neurological and ocular features

frequency.us: Rare; ~15% of all Dent disease from OCRL mutations; allelic with Lowe, milder phenotype
frequency.global: Rare globally; OCRL mutations; milder than classic Lowe syndrome; distinguished by absence of neurological features
frequency.sources: Hoopes et al. Am J Hum Genet 2005; Bökenkamp & Ludwig Ped Nephrol 2011

diagnosis: Urine LMW proteins; urine calcium; OCRL genetic testing; ophthalmology (subtle lens changes); developmental assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • Same management as Dent Disease Type 1 — high fluid intake, thiazide diuretics, potassium citrate, dietary NaCl restriction • Distinguish from Lowe Syndrome — OCRL mutations cause both Dent 2 (mild) and Lowe syndrome (severe); Dent 2 has kidney involvement WITHOUT significant ocular or neurological features; genotype-phenotype correlation imperfect • Fanconi syndrome management — if proximal tubular dysfunction more prominent than Dent 1; bicarbonate, phosphate, potassium supplementation • Ophthalmological exam — even though Dent 2 lacks overt cataracts, subclinical lenticular changes possible; annual slit-lamp exam recommended • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; favorable outcomes

name: Bartter Syndrome Type 1 (SLC12A1)
description: Antenatal/neonatal Bartter syndrome due to NKCC2 mutations; severe polyhydramnios, prematurity, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hypercalciuria

frequency.us: Rare; ~1/1,000,000 in US; most severe Bartter; antenatal polyhydramnios; nephrocalcinosis common
frequency.global: ~1/1,000,000 globally; SLC12A1 mutations; antenatal Bartter; dehydration, failure to thrive in neonates
frequency.sources: Simon et al. Nat Genet 1996; Nozu et al. J Hum Genet 2017; Bartter Syndrome Consortium

diagnosis: Urine/serum electrolytes (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated chloride excretion); renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); genetic testing (SLC12A1)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — prostaglandin inhibition; reduces polyuria and electrolyte wasting; most effective single agent; start at ~0.5–2 mg/kg/day; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl supplementation; may require high doses (2–4 mEq/kg/day) Methods • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduces potassium wasting; potassium-sparing; combined with KCl • Amiloride — potassium-sparing via ENaC block; alternative or adjunct • Sodium and fluid supplementation — especially in neonatal/antenatal Bartter; NG tube feeding; NaCl supplements • Magnesium supplementation — for hypomagnesemia if present (more common in Type 3) • ACEi/ARBs — reduces hyperaldosteronism-driven hypokalemia; adjunct therapy • Regular monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, Cl, Na, Mg), bicarb, renin, aldosterone; renal function; growth • Neonatal intensive care — most present with severe antenatal polyhydramnios + prematurity; NICU admission; IV electrolyte replacement before oral tolerated • Prostaglandin use timing — indomethacin initiated after stabilization; ibuprofen alternative if renal concerns • Outcome — medullary nephrocalcinosis common in all antenatal Bartter types; renal function typically preserved Emerging ▶ Chloride channel replacement — SLC12A1 (NKCC2) gene; no gene therapy available ▶ Vasopressin analogues — partial antidiuretic effect in some subtypes; investigational

name: Bartter Syndrome Type 2 (KCNJ1)
description: ROMK channel mutations; antenatal Bartter syndrome with neonatal hyperkalaemia (paradoxical) transitioning to hypokalaemia after neonatal period

frequency.us: Very rare; antenatal onset; transient hyperkalemia in neonatal period; KCNJ1 mutations
frequency.global: Very rare globally; KCNJ1 mutations; antenatal onset similar to Type 1; hyperkalemia distinguishes neonatal phase
frequency.sources: Simon et al. Cell 1996; Nozu et al. J Hum Genet 2017; Bartter Syndrome Consortium

diagnosis: Electrolytes (neonatal hyperkalemia → hypokalemia); antenatal/postnatal ultrasound; genetic testing (KCNJ1)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — prostaglandin inhibition; reduces polyuria and electrolyte wasting; most effective single agent; start at ~0.5–2 mg/kg/day; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl supplementation; may require high doses (2–4 mEq/kg/day) • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduces potassium wasting; potassium-sparing; combined with KCl • Amiloride — potassium-sparing via ENaC block; alternative or adjunct • Sodium and fluid supplementation — especially in neonatal/antenatal Bartter; NG tube feeding; NaCl supplements • Magnesium supplementation — for hypomagnesemia if present (more common in Type 3) • ACEi/ARBs — reduces hyperaldosteronism-driven hypokalemia; adjunct therapy • Regular monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, Cl, Na, Mg), bicarb, renin, aldosterone; renal function; growth Methods • Neonatal hyperkalemia early — KCNJ1/ROMK mutations paradoxically cause neonatal hyperkalemia before evolving to hypokalemia in infancy; important to recognize and not treat the transient hyperkalemia aggressively • Otherwise identical management to Type 1 antenatal Bartter • Nephrocalcinosis monitoring — medullary; renal ultrasound annually

name: Bartter Syndrome Type 3 (CLCNKB)
description: ClC-Kb chloride channel mutations; most clinically variable Bartter type; ranges from classic Bartter to Gitelman-like phenotype

frequency.us: ~1/500,000 in US; most common Bartter type; variable onset infancy to adolescence
frequency.global: ~1/500,000 globally; CLCNKB mutations; most frequent Bartter variant; variable severity and age of onset
frequency.sources: Simon et al. Nat Genet 1997; Nozu et al. J Hum Genet 2017; Bartter Syndrome Consortium

diagnosis: Serum/urine electrolytes (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria variable); genetic testing (CLCNKB); renal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — prostaglandin inhibition; reduces polyuria and electrolyte wasting; most effective single agent; start at ~0.5–2 mg/kg/day; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl supplementation; may require high doses (2–4 mEq/kg/day) • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduces potassium wasting; potassium-sparing; combined with KCl • Amiloride — potassium-sparing via ENaC block; alternative or adjunct • Sodium and fluid supplementation — especially in neonatal/antenatal Bartter; NG tube feeding; NaCl supplements • Magnesium supplementation — for hypomagnesemia if present (more common in Type 3) • ACEi/ARBs — reduces hyperaldosteronism-driven hypokalemia; adjunct therapy • Regular monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, Cl, Na, Mg), bicarb, renin, aldosterone; renal function; growth • Classic presentation — hypokalemia, hypochloremia, metabolic alkalosis; typically diagnosed in infancy/early childhood; milder than antenatal forms • Hypomagnesemia more prominent — MgCl₂ or Mg oxide supplementation important • Indomethacin — mainstay; may need lifelong use; monitor renal function • Overlap with Gitelman syndrome — CLCNKB mutations can mimic Gitelman phenotype; genetic testing essential

name: Bartter Syndrome Type 4 (BSND / CLCNKA+B)
description: Barttin or digenic ClCKA+B mutations causing severe antenatal Bartter syndrome with sensorineural hearing loss

frequency.us: Very rare; antenatal presentation; deafness distinguishes from other Bartter types; BSND mutations
frequency.global: Very rare globally; BSND mutations (barttin subunit); deafness co-feature; most severe electrolyte imbalances
frequency.sources: Birkenhager et al. Nat Genet 2001; Nozu et al. J Hum Genet 2017; Bartter Consortium

diagnosis: Electrolytes; audiogram (SNHL); genetic testing (BSND or both CLCNKA and CLCNKB); antenatal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — prostaglandin inhibition; reduces polyuria and electrolyte wasting; most effective single agent; start at ~0.5–2 mg/kg/day; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl supplementation; may require high doses (2–4 mEq/kg/day) Methods • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduces potassium wasting; potassium-sparing; combined with KCl • Amiloride — potassium-sparing via ENaC block; alternative or adjunct • Sodium and fluid supplementation — especially in neonatal/antenatal Bartter; NG tube feeding; NaCl supplements • Magnesium supplementation — for hypomagnesemia if present (more common in Type 3) • ACEi/ARBs — reduces hyperaldosteronism-driven hypokalemia; adjunct therapy • Regular monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, Cl, Na, Mg), bicarb, renin, aldosterone; renal function; growth • Sensorineural hearing loss — bilateral, severe/profound; early hearing aids; cochlear implant evaluation; deaf education planning; ENT audiology comanagement • Most severe antenatal Bartter form — combines renal (Bartter) + cochlear (BSND encodes barttin expressed in stria vascularis) manifestations • Early neonatal management — IV electrolytes; intensive supplementation; NG tube feeding • Long-term electrolyte management — chronic; significant supplementation required; compliance monitoring

name: Bartter Syndrome Type 5 / Antenatal (CASR)
description: Activating CASR mutations causing neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism-like or Bartter-like syndrome with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis

frequency.us: Very rare; CASR gain-of- function mutations; AD hypocalcemia distinguishable from Bartter phenotype
frequency.global: Very rare globally; CASR activating mutations; heterozygous mutations cause autosomal dominant hypocalcemia type 1
frequency.sources: Watanabe et al. Nat Genet 2002; Nozu et al. J Hum Genet 2017

diagnosis: Calcium, PTH, electrolytes; CASR genetic testing; renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); urinary calcium

treatment.standardOfCare: • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — prostaglandin inhibition; reduces polyuria and electrolyte wasting; most effective single agent; start at ~0.5–2 mg/kg/day; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl supplementation; may require high doses (2–4 mEq/kg/day) • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduces potassium wasting; potassium-sparing; combined with KCl • Amiloride — potassium-sparing via ENaC block; alternative or adjunct • Sodium and fluid supplementation — especially in neonatal/antenatal Bartter; NG tube feeding; NaCl supplements • Magnesium supplementation — for hypomagnesemia if present (more common in Type 3) • ACEi/ARBs — reduces hyperaldosteronism-driven hypokalemia; adjunct therapy • Regular monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, Cl, Na, Mg), bicarb, renin, aldosterone; renal function; growth • Hypocalcemia management — CRITICAL: activating CaSR mutations cause hypocalcemia PLUS Bartter-like salt-wasting; calcium and vitamin D supplementation Methods carefully titrated; aggressive calcium supplementation risks nephrocalcinosis • Calcimimetics (cinacalcet) — CONTRAINDICATED in activating CASR mutations (would worsen hypocalcemia); important drug-disease interaction awareness • PTH monitoring — suppressed PTH is expected; do not treat with PTH analogs without specialist guidance • Calcitriol + calcium — judicious supplementation; avoid over-supplementation Emerging ▶ CaSR antagonists (calcilytics) — investigational for activating CASR Bartter/hypocalcemia; NPS2143 and related compounds; Phase 2 research stage

name: Gitelman Syndrome (SLC12A3)
description: Autosomal recessive SLC12A3 mutations causing thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter defect; hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria

frequency.us: ~1/40,000 in US; most common inherited tubular disorder; adolescent presentation with muscle cramps, fatigue
frequency.global: ~1/40,000 globally; SLC12A3 mutations; widespread in Southern European, Chinese, Taiwanese populations
frequency.sources: Simon et al. Nat Genet 1996; Gitelman Alliance data; Blanchard et al. KI 2015

diagnosis: Serum electrolytes (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis); urinary calcium (low); renin/aldosterone; genetic testing (SLC12A3)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Magnesium supplementation — ESSENTIAL; hypomagnesemia universal and symptomatic (muscle cramps, fatigue, tetany); oral MgCl₂ or Mg oxide; divided doses to improve absorption; target serum Mg >0.6 mmol/L; IV Mg for severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia • Potassium supplementation — oral KCl; dietary potassium-rich foods; target K >3.0 mmol/L; chronic supplementation often required • Low dietary sodium — paradoxically reduces urinary potassium wasting via reduced distal delivery • Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — potassium-sparing; reduces K wasting; effective adjunct; monitor for hyperkalemia • Amiloride — potassium-sparing; highly effective in Gitelman (blocks ENaC downstream); some experts prefer over spironolactone • Indomethacin — less effective than in Bartter; limited role; used occasionally for residual symptoms • RAAS blockade — ACEi/ARBs occasionally used for additional potassium sparing; limited evidence • Monitoring — serum K, Mg, creatinine, BP every 3–6 months; urine electrolytes annually Important: Avoid medications worsening hypomagnesemia/hypokalemia — aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, cisplatin, prolonged diuretics Emerging ▶ Eplerenone — selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; fewer anti-androgen side effects than spironolactone; increasingly preferred in adolescent males ▶ Magnesium transport research — SLC12A3 (NCCT) loss- of-function; SLC41A3 Mg transporter involvement studied

name: Fanconi Syndrome — Idiopathic
description: Generalized proximal tubular dysfunction causing glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, bicarbonaturia, and LMWP without identified cause

frequency.us: Rare as isolated idiopathic entity in US; most cases have underlying cause (cystinosis, Dent, Lowe, drugs)
frequency.global: Rare as primary globally; most cases secondary; heavy metals, chemotherapy, tenofovir major acquired causes
frequency.sources: Klootwijk et al. JASN 2015; Foreman Ped Nephrol 2019; Fanconi Syndrome review KI 2020

diagnosis: Urine amino acids, glucose, phosphate, uric acid, LMW proteins, bicarbonate; serum electrolytes; exclude secondary causes; genetic evaluation

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • Replace all wasted solutes — essential; guided by urine losses: - Oral bicarbonate/citrate (Polycitra, Bicitra) — metabolic acidosis; 1–3 mEq/kg/day - Oral phosphate — hypophosphatemia; 25–75 mg/kg/day in divided doses - Oral potassium — hypokalemia; KCl or Polycitra-K - Oral/IV sodium — hyponatremia • Vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) — for impaired 1- hydroxylation and phosphate deficiency-related bone disease; rickets prevention/treatment • Calcium supplementation — with vitamin D • Hydration — polyuria management; adequate fluid intake • Find underlying cause — idiopathic is a diagnosis of exclusion; evaluate for cystinosis (the most common cause in children — CTNS gene testing; slit-lamp exam for crystals), Wilson disease, galactosemia, hereditary fructose intolerance, Lowe syndrome, drug toxicity (tenofovir, expired tetracycline, cisplatin) • Treat underlying etiology when identified — cystinosis → cysteamine (see #70); Wilson → penicillamine/zinc; HFI → fructose elimination

name: Fanconi-Bickel Syndrome (SLC2A2)
description: SLC2A2 (GLUT2) mutations causing proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome plus glycogen accumulation in liver/kidney with hepatomegaly and growth retardation

frequency.us: Very rare; ~200 cases reported
frequency.global: Extremely rare globally; ~200 total cases; GLUT2 transport defect; hepatic and renal manifestations; diet management
frequency.sources: Santer et al. Nat Genet 1997; Oe et al. JIMD Rep 2011; Fanconi-Bickel Registry

diagnosis: Urine amino acids, glucose, phosphate (Fanconi pattern); blood glucose (postprandial hyperglycemia, fasting hypoglycemia); liver ultrasound; SLC2A2 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Galactose-restricted diet — galactose is GLUT2 substrate; restriction reduces accumulation; not fully effective but reduces hepatic glycogen accumulation • Uncooked cornstarch — prevents hypoglycemia between meals; slow-release glucose via GGCS pathway; given every 4–6 hours; same as GSD type I management • Fanconi syndrome replacement — oral bicarbonate, phosphate, potassium, vitamin D, calcium supplementation as for idiopathic Fanconi • Liver management — hepatomegaly with glycogen/galactose accumulation; monitor liver function; avoid hepatotoxins • Growth support — poor growth common; nutrition optimization; growth hormone if severe CKD develops • Monitor renal function — CKD progression variable; some patients develop ESKD; ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria

name: Tyrosinemia Type I — Renal Fanconi (FAH)
description: FAH mutations causing hepatic and renal tubular dysfunction; succinylacetone accumulation causes Fanconi syndrome and hepatic failure

frequency.us: ~1/100,000–120,000 in US; most common in Quebec (~1/16,000); FAH mutations; liver failure prominent
frequency.global: ~1/100,000–120,000 globally; highest in French- Canadian (Quebec) and Scandinavian populations
frequency.sources: Lindstedt et al. Lancet 1992; NTBC treatment trial; HT1 International Registry

diagnosis: Urine succinylacetone (pathognomonic); urine amino acids (Fanconi pattern); plasma tyrosine; liver function; AFP; FAH genetic testing; newborn screening in many countries

treatment.standardOfCare: • NTBC (nitisinone / Orfadin) — transforms disease; inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase; virtually eliminates toxic metabolite accumulation; initiated immediately at diagnosis or NBS positive result; dramatically reduces need for liver transplant • Low tyrosine / low phenylalanine diet — essential adjunct to NTBC; prevents tyrosinemia-related neurological crises Methods • Renal Fanconi management — phosphate, bicarbonate, electrolyte supplementation while Fanconi active (usually resolves with NTBC) • Newborn screening — mandatory; early treatment prevents severe disease • Liver transplant — for NTBC non-responders, established HCC, or late diagnosis with cirrhosis; curative for hepatic and renal disease
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Gene therapy (mRNA or viral vector for FAH gene) — Phase 1/2 investigational programs; potentially curative without liver transplant ▶ Base editing / prime editing — preclinical for FAH correction; highly precise ▶ NTBC dose optimization — ongoing studies (lower doses may reduce ophthalmologic adverse effects)

name: Hereditary Fructose Intolerance — Renal Fanconi (ALDOB)
description: ALDOB mutations causing fructose-1-phosphate accumulation; liver failure, hypoglycemia, and proximal renal tubular Fanconi syndrome after fructose exposure

frequency.us: ~1/20,000–30,000 in Europe (US less well characterized); Fanconi reversible with fructose restriction
frequency.global: ~1/20,000–30,000 in European populations; ALDOB mutations; reversible with dietary fructose avoidance
frequency.sources: Bouteldja & Timson J Inherit Metab Dis 2010; Baker & Winegrad Lancet 1970

diagnosis: Urine amino acids, glucose, phosphate (after fructose); hypoglycemia after fructose; liver enzymes; ALDOB genetic testing; enzyme assay (liver biopsy)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Strict dietary fructose/sucrose/sorbitol elimination — definitive and curative for renal Fanconi; complete elimination resolves or prevents renal tubular damage; sorbitol found in many medications and "sugar-free" products (hidden sources) • Dietitian support — careful food labeling; fructose-free diet education; hidden fructose sources (HFCS, fruit juices, certain vegetables) • Fanconi syndrome supplementation — if already established tubular damage: bicarbonate, phosphate, potassium, vitamin D, calcium (same as idiopathic Fanconi); improves with dietary elimination • Emergency management — hypoglycemia in acute fructose exposure; IV dextrose; glucagon • Medical alert bracelet — for IV fructose-containing solutions (avoid sucrose, sorbitol in IV medications) • Liver function monitoring — hepatomegaly with repeated exposures; LFTs; coagulopathy

name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 1 — Distal (ATP6V1B1 / ATP6V0A4)
description: Defective H+ excretion in distal tubule causing hyperchloremic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypocitraturia, nephrocalcinosis, and rickets

frequency.us: ~1/100,000 in US; AR forms with deafness (ATP6V1B1); distal RTA causing nephrocalcinosis if untreated
frequency.global: ~1/100,000 globally; AR forms more prevalent in consanguineous populations; sensorineural deafness subtype common in Middle East
frequency.sources: Karet et al. Nat Genet 1999; Alper JASN 2002; RTA Consensus Review Ped Nephrol 2021

diagnosis: Blood gas (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis); urine pH (inappropriately alkaline >5.5 during acidosis); urinary citrate; renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Oral alkali therapy — first-line and highly effective; potassium citrate (Polycitra-K, Urocit-K) preferred: treats acidosis AND replaces potassium AND prevents stones (citrate chelates calcium); dose 1–3 mEq/kg/day • Sodium bicarbonate — alternative if potassium overload concern; divided doses • Potassium supplementation — hypokalemia universal; potassium citrate provides both K+ and alkali; aggressive replacement in severe hypokalemia • Calcium supplementation + vitamin D — for metabolic bone disease (rickets); calcitriol for established rickets Methods • Stone prevention — citrate supplementation dramatically reduces nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis; lifelong therapy • Audiological evaluation — ATP6V1B1 mutations associated with sensorineural hearing loss; audiogram at diagnosis and annually; hearing aids if needed • Monitoring — serum electrolytes (K, HCO3, Cl), urine pH, urine calcium/creatinine ratio every 3–6 months; renal ultrasound annually for nephrocalcinosis Key goal: maintain serum HCO3 >22 mEq/L; urine pH should lower appropriately after ammonium chloride loading

name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 2 — Proximal (SLC4A4)
description: Defective bicarbonate reabsorption in proximal tubule; usually part of Fanconi syndrome; SLC4A4 mutations cause isolated proximal RTA with ocular anomalies

frequency.us: Rare in isolation in US; more common as part of Fanconi syndrome; SLC4A4 mutations rare
frequency.global: Rare globally in isolation; SLC4A4 mutations cause isolated proximal RTA with ocular features (glaucoma, cataracts)
frequency.sources: Igarashi et al. Nat Genet 1999; Ota et al. JASN 2013; RTA Consensus Review Ped Nephrol 2021

diagnosis: Blood gas (metabolic acidosis); urine pH (appropriately acidic at nadir); fractional excretion of bicarbonate elevated; genetic testing; ophthalmology for SLC4A4

treatment.standardOfCare: • Large-dose alkali therapy — MUCH larger doses needed than dRTA; 5–15 mEq/kg/day; proximal tubule wastes bicarbonate → need high doses to exceed renal threshold; potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate • Potassium supplementation — bicarb supplementation increases urinary K loss (alkalinization drives K excretion); supplement KCl or potassium citrate simultaneously • Thiazide diuretic — paradoxically reduces bicarbonate wasting by inducing volume contraction (increases proximal reabsorption); use cautiously with adequate K replacement • Phosphate supplementation — if hypophosphatemia present (especially in syndromic proximal RTA/Fanconi) • Treat underlying cause — isolated SLC4A4 mutations (rare); more commonly RTA2 part of Fanconi syndrome; diagnose and treat etiology • Vitamin D (calcitriol) — for bone disease/rickets component • Note: Urine pH paradoxically low in severe metabolic acidosis (below threshold); rises when alkali dose exceeds reabsorptive capacity

name: Renal Tubular Acidosis Type 4 — Hyperkalemic
description: Aldosterone deficiency or resistance causing hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia; may be due to hyporeninism, adrenal disorders, or tubular resistance

frequency.us: Most common RTA type overall in US; common in pediatric CKD; rarely primary in children
frequency.global: Most prevalent RTA globally in CKD context; primary form rare in children; obstructive uropathy and adrenal causes predominant
frequency.sources: Batlle & Haque Kidney Int 2012; Campese & Karubian AJKD 1990; RTA review Ped Nephrol 2021

diagnosis: Blood electrolytes (hyperkalemia + metabolic acidosis); plasma renin, aldosterone; urine pH; screen for obstruction; adrenal function tests

treatment.standardOfCare: • Treat underlying cause — most common: congenital adrenal hyperplasia, obstructive uropathy (PUV, VUR), CKD, calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, hypoaldosteronism, pseudohypoaldosteronism • Fludrocortisone — for mineralocorticoid deficiency forms (hypoaldosteronism, CAH-related); 0.05–0.2 mg/day; increases renal sodium retention and potassium excretion; effective for low-aldosterone types • Dietary potassium restriction — reduce dietary K to 1–2 mEq/kg/day • Patiromer (Veltassa) or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma) — potassium binders; adult approved; pediatric use growing for refractory hyperkalemia; oral; well- tolerated Methods • Sodium bicarbonate — corrects metabolic acidosis; also lowers serum K transiently via redistribution • Loop diuretics (furosemide) — increases urinary potassium excretion; volume-replete patients • ACEi/ARB — AVOID or reduce dose; worsens hyperkalemia and low aldosterone state • Treat obstructive uropathy — relief of obstruction often resolves RTA4

name: Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 1 (AGXT)
description: AGXT mutations causing hepatic overproduction of oxalate; oxalate deposition in kidneys and systemic organs causing nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, and ESKD

frequency.us: ~1–3/1,000,000 in US; ~1–2% of pediatric dialysis patients; infantile oxalosis rapidly fatal
frequency.global: ~1–3/1,000,000 globally; higher in consanguineous populations; European OHO registry; most severe primary hyperoxaluria
frequency.sources: Hoppe et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2011; Cochat & Rumsby NEJM 2013; OHO Registry data

diagnosis: Urine oxalate (markedly elevated); plasma oxalate; AGXT genetic testing; renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); kidney biopsy (oxalate crystals); liver enzyme assay

treatment.standardOfCare: • Lumasiran (Oxlumo, Alnylam) — RNAi; inhibits HAO1 (glycolate oxidase); FDA approved Nov 2020 for PH1 in all ages including infants; reduces urinary oxalate by ~65%; subcutaneous monthly (loading) then quarterly; ILLUMINATE-A (adults/children) and ILLUMINATE-B (infants/children <6 yr) Phase 3 trials • High fluid intake — ≥3 L/m²/day; dilutes urine oxalate • Oral citrate (potassium citrate) — inhibits calcium oxalate crystallization • Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) — for pyridoxine-responsive patients (~30%; AGXT p.Gly170Arg mutation); dose 5–20 mg/kg/day; test all patients at diagnosis • Combined liver-kidney transplant — definitive cure (corrects hepatic enzyme defect + replaces damaged kidney); increasingly replaced by lumasiran but still needed in advanced disease • Intensive hemodialysis — for established oxalosis to remove systemic oxalate deposits before transplant FDA-Approved (October 2023) ▶ Nedosiran (Rivfloza, Novo Nordisk) — RNAi; inhibits LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A); FDA approved Oct 2023 for PH1 (adults and children ≥9 yr) AND PH2; once- monthly subcutaneous injection; alternative RNAi mechanism to lumasiran; PHYOX2 Phase 3 trial
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Stirapentol — LDH inhibitor; early stage ▶ Oxalobacter formigenes (probiotic) — intestinal oxalate degradation; Phase 2/3; not yet approved ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-mediated AGXT correction) — preclinical/early clinical ▶ Next-gen RNAi (LCPI-003) — investigational

name: Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 2 (GRHPR)
description: GRHPR mutations causing glyoxylate reductase deficiency; less severe than PH1; oxalate and L- glycerate excretion elevated

frequency.us: Very rare; ~10% of PH cases; milder than PH1; ESKD less common
frequency.global: Very rare globally; GRHPR mutations; European OHO Registry reports ~10% of PH cases; milder renal progression
frequency.sources: Cramer et al. J Biol Chem 1999; Hoppe et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2011

diagnosis: Urine oxalate and L- glycerate; GRHPR genetic testing; renal ultrasound; plasma oxalate

treatment.standardOfCare:
• High fluid intake — ≥3 L/m²/day
• Oral citrate — inhibits calcium oxalate and calcium
oxalate monohydrate (whewellite) crystallization
• Dietary oxalate restriction — low-oxalate diet Methods • Isolated kidney transplant — for ESKD; oxaluria improves post-transplant but glyoxylate/glycerate overproduction continues; recurrence risk lower than PH1 • Monitor renal function — frequent eGFR and 24-hour urinary oxalate assessments FDA-Approved (October 2023) ▶ Nedosiran (Rivfloza, Novo Nordisk) — RNAi targeting LDHA; FDA approved Oct 2023 specifically for PH2 as well as PH1 (children ≥9 yr and adults); reduces urinary oxalate; once-monthly subcutaneous injection
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Lumasiran — mechanism targets HAO1 (upstream of GRHPR defect); potential role being explored but primary indication is PH1 ▶ CRISPR/gene therapy for GRHPR — preclinical ▶ Oxalobacter formigenes — investigational for all PH types

name: Primary Hyperoxaluria Type 3 (HOGA1)
description: HOGA1 mutations causing mild hyperoxaluria; rarely leads to ESKD; mostly associated with recurrent nephrolithiasis

frequency.us: Rarest PH; HOGA1 mutations; nephrolithiasis rather than ESKD; mildest course
frequency.global: Rarest PH type globally; HOGA1 mutations; milder phenotype; stone disease predominant; ESKD exceptional
frequency.sources: Belostotsky et al. Am J Hum Genet 2010; Hoppe et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2011
