diagnosis: Urine oxalate; HOGA1 genetic testing; renal ultrasound; stone composition analysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — ≥3 L/m²/day; dilutes urine oxalate • Oral citrate (potassium citrate) — inhibits calcium oxalate stone formation • Dietary oxalate restriction — low-oxalate diet • Nephron-sparing urologic stone management — ureteroscopy, ESWL, PCNL as appropriate; avoid open surgery when possible • Monitor renal function — PH3 generally milder; ESKD less common than PH1/PH2 but possible • Vitamin B6 — not effective (HOGA1 pathway not B6- responsive)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ RNAi approaches targeting HOGA1 pathway — preclinical; no clinical trials as of 2025 ▶ Nedosiran — mechanism via LDHA; theoretical relevance to PH3 pathway; not yet studied in PH3 ▶ Increased recognition of PH3 phenotype — natural history studies ongoing to clarify ESKD risk

name: Renal Glucosuria (SLC5A2)
description: Benign tubular glucose transport defect causing persistent glucosuria with normal blood glucose; SLC5A2 mutations (same as SGLT2)

frequency.us: ~0.2–0.6% of US population; benign in heterozygotes; homozygous SLC5A2 causes significant glycosuria
frequency.global: ~0.2–0.6% globally; SLC5A2 mutations; related to SGLT2 transporter; benign; linked to naturally low blood glucose
frequency.sources: Santer & Calado JASN 2010; Kleta et al. Diabetes 2004

diagnosis: Urinalysis (persistent glucose with normal blood glucose); multiple urine samples; SLC5A2 genetic testing; exclude diabetes mellitus

treatment.standardOfCare: • No specific treatment required — isolated benign renal glucosuria is a benign condition; no metabolic consequences; blood glucose is NORMAL (not diabetes) • Education and reassurance — emphasize normal blood glucose; not diabetes; benign prognosis; glucosuria detected incidentally on urinalysis • Differentiate from diabetes mellitus — blood glucose, HbA1c, fasting glucose normal; urine glucose elevated due to low renal threshold for glucose (SLC5A2 mutation) Methods • SGLT2 inhibitors — SLC5A2 (SGLT2) is the pharmacological target of SGLT2 inhibitor drugs; benign renal glucosuria is essentially the natural SGLT2 inhibited phenotype; no therapy needed • Annual monitoring — urinalysis; confirm no proteinuria develops; monitor weight/growth; recheck blood glucose if clinical concern for diabetes • Genetic counseling — autosomal dominant or recessive; SLC5A2 mutations; spectrum of severity

name: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus — X- linked (AVPR2)
description: AVPR2 mutations causing resistance to ADH/vasopressin in collecting duct; massive polyuria, polydipsia, and hypernatremia in male infants

frequency.us: ~1/250,000 US males; AVPR2 X-linked; neonatal hypernatremia if unrecognized; high morbidity
frequency.global: ~1/250,000 males globally; most cases in North America and Europe from founder mutations; AVPR2 gene
frequency.sources: Bichet et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2009; Robben et al. JASN 2006; NDI Foundation Registry

diagnosis: Urine osmolality (low despite high serum osmolality); water deprivation test + desmopressin (no response); AVPR2 genetic testing; MRI (absent posterior pituitary bright spot)

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — unrestricted; free water access critical; prevents dehydration/hypernatremia; mainstay especially in infants • Amiloride — potassium-sparing diuretic; blocks ENaC; reduces polyuria by ~50%; preferred over hydrochlorothiazide alone; mechanism: increases intracellular cAMP via Na+ reduction • Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) — paradoxical antidiuresis via volume contraction; often combined with amiloride; reduces urine output 30–50% • Indomethacin (or other COX inhibitor) — reduces prostaglandin-mediated antagonism of AVP; adds 30– 50% additional reduction when combined with diuretics; monitor renal function and GI toxicity; limit long-term use • Low-salt, low-protein diet — reduces obligate solute load; reduces urine output • Newborn screening / early diagnosis — prevents hypernatremia-related intellectual disability; early hydration critical Nomenclature Update (2022/2025): International expert consensus (Nat Rev Nephrol 2025; Levtchenko et al.) recommends the term "arginine vasopressin resistance" (AVP-R) instead of "nephrogenic DI" to better reflect pathophysiology and reduce stigma
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Pharmacological chaperones (AVPR2 antagonists as chaperones) — for class II misfolding mutations (90% of AVPR2 defects); tolvaptan-based chaperones show partial rescue in vitro; clinical development challenging due to competitive binding; relcovaptan (SR49059) was early candidate (halted due to CYP450 interactions); new chaperone candidates in development ▶ Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor) — case reports of reduced urine output in children via cGMP-AQP2 pathway; adult studies show no consistent benefit; results conflicting ▶ AVPR2 agonists — bypass misfolded receptor; activate downstream cAMP regardless of mutation class; preclinical data promising Methods ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-AVPR2) — preclinical; X-linked inheritance means gene delivery to collecting duct principal cells; early stage ▶ Metformin / statins — activate AQP2 independently of AVP; preclinical data; not established clinically

name: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus — Autosomal (AQP2)
description: AQP2 mutations affecting aquaporin-2 water channel; autosomal recessive (most) or dominant; milder than X- linked AVPR2 NDI

frequency.us: Rare; AQP2 mutations in ~10% of hereditary NDI; autosomal recessive or dominant forms
frequency.global: Rare globally; AQP2 mutations; both AR and AD inheritance; males and females equally affected
frequency.sources: Deen et al. Science 1994; Bichet et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2009

diagnosis: Urine osmolality; water deprivation test + desmopressin (no response); AQP2 genetic testing; serum electrolytes

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — unrestricted; free water access critical; prevents hypernatremic dehydration • Hydrochlorothiazide + amiloride combination — reduces urine output via volume contraction; same mechanism as X-linked NDI • Low-salt, low-protein diet — reduces solute load; reduces urine output • Indomethacin — adjunctive; reduces polyuria; monitor renal function; limit duration Nomenclature Update: International expert consensus recommends "arginine vasopressin resistance" (AVP-R) over "nephrogenic DI" (Levtchenko et al., Nat Rev Nephrol 2025)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Direct AQP2 channel activators — bypass both receptor and cAMP pathway; several small molecules identified in high-throughput screening; preclinical ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-AQP2) — autosomal recessive (AR) form has two defective copies; gene delivery more complex; early preclinical ▶ AQP2 trafficking enhancers — PGE2-EP4 agonists; secretin analogues; fluvastatin-secretin combination shown to increase AQP2 trafficking in mouse models; investigational ▶ mRNA therapy for AQP2 — hepatic or renal-targeted delivery; preclinical ▶ CRISPR/base editing — potentially curative for specific AQP2 mutations; very early

name: Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type 1 — Renal (NR3C2)
description: Autosomal dominant NR3C2 mutations causing renal mineralocorticoid resistance; salt-wasting nephropathy with elevated renin/aldosterone

frequency.us: Rare; renal type milder than systemic; neonatal salt-wasting presentation
frequency.global: Rare globally; NR3C2 mutations; mineralocorticoid receptor insensitivity; systemic (SCNN1B/G) form more severe
frequency.sources: Geller et al. NEJM 1998; Chang et al. Nat Genet 1996; Pseudohypoaldosteronism review JASN

diagnosis: Serum electrolytes (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia); markedly elevated renin and aldosterone; urinary sodium (salt wasting); NR3C2 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • High-dose sodium supplementation — massive salt wasting; NaCl 10–20 mEq/kg/day; NG supplementation in infants; often challenging; gradual reduction as patients mature and some improvement occurs with age (renal form improves; systemic form does not) • Renal form (NR3C2 heterozygous) — autosomal dominant; milder; improves with age; aldosterone supplementation sometimes used; NR3C2 is renal mineralocorticoid receptor • High-dose fludrocortisone — INEFFECTIVE in renal PHA1 (receptor is non-functional); avoid; only useful in adrenal insufficiency (secondary PHA) Methods • Monitor electrolytes — hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis; frequent monitoring in infancy; normalize by 1–2 years of age in renal form • Indomethacin — reduces urinary sodium wasting in some reports; adjunct • Differentiate from systemic PHA1 (SCNN1B/G mutations) — systemic form affects lung and sweat glands in addition to kidney; does not improve with age; see entry #93 systemic

name: Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type 2 / Gordon Syndrome (WNK1/4)
description: WNK1/4 or KLHL3/CUL3 mutations causing chloride shunting in distal nephron; hypertension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis with low renin/aldosterone

frequency.us: Rare; familial hyperkalemic hypertension; WNK1/WNK4 mutations; childhood to adulthood presentations
frequency.global: Rare globally; WNK kinase pathway mutations; European kindreds well-described; pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2
frequency.sources: Wilson et al. Science 2001; Boyden et al. Science 2012; Gordon Syndrome Registry

diagnosis: Serum electrolytes (hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis); blood pressure elevated; low renin and aldosterone; WNK1/WNK4/KLHL3/CUL3 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Thiazide diuretics — HIGHLY EFFECTIVE and essentially curative; hydrochlorothiazide 1–3 mg/kg/day; thiazides inhibit NCC (the sodium-chloride cotransporter that is constitutively overactivated by WNK1/4 mutations); normalizes hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypertension rapidly • Dietary potassium restriction — reduces hyperkalemia while establishing thiazide therapy • Dietary sodium restriction — adjunct; reduces chloride load • Monitoring — electrolytes normalize rapidly on thiazides; titrate dose to maintain normal K, HCO3, and BP • Note: Fludrocortisone is INEFFECTIVE (PHA2 is caused by excessive NCC activity, not aldosterone deficiency) • Genetic counseling — WNK1, WNK4, KLHL3, CUL3 mutations; autosomal dominant; family screening

name: Liddle Syndrome (SCNN1B/G)
description: Gain-of-function mutations in ENaC beta/gamma subunits causing constitutive sodium reabsorption; severe hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin/aldosterone in adolescents

frequency.us: Rare; important monogenic hypertension cause in US; autosomal dominant; SCNN1B/SCNN1G
frequency.global: Rare globally; autosomal dominant; ENaC gain-of-function; family histories of severe early hypertension and hypokalemia
frequency.sources: Liddle et al. Trans Assoc Am Physicians 1963; Shimkets et al. Cell 1994; Botero-Velez et al. NEJM 1994

diagnosis: Blood pressure (severe hypertension); electrolytes (hypokalemia); low renin and aldosterone; SCNN1B/G genetic testing; genetic family screening

treatment.standardOfCare: • Amiloride — HIGHLY EFFECTIVE; directly blocks ENaC (epithelial sodium channel, the upregulated channel in Liddle); normalizes hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis; 5–20 mg/day; first-line drug • Triamterene — alternative potassium-sparing diuretic; blocks ENaC directly; similar mechanism to amiloride; less commonly used • Low dietary sodium — reduces sodium retention and BP • Spironolactone/eplerenone — INEFFECTIVE in Liddle (spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist; Liddle has low aldosterone; ENaC is overactive independent of aldosterone; spironolactone does not block ENaC directly); common diagnostic pitfall • Monitoring — BP, serum K, HCO3 normalize with amiloride; follow lifelong • Genetic counseling — SCNN1B or SCNN1G mutations; autosomal dominant; gain-of-function ENaC Methods

name: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (HSD11B2)
description: HSD11B2 mutations causing cortisol to activate mineralocorticoid receptors; severe hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin/aldosterone; cortisol acts as mineralocorticoid

frequency.us: Rare; autosomal recessive; severe childhood hypertension with low renin/aldosterone; HSD11B2 mutations
frequency.global: Rare globally; HSD11B2 mutations; acquired form from licorice ingestion more common than genetic; Mediterranean distribution
frequency.sources: White et al. Lancet 1997; Mune et al. Nat Genet 1995; AME Syndrome Registry

diagnosis: Blood pressure; electrolytes (hypokalemia); low renin/aldosterone; urine cortisol:cortisone ratio (elevated); HSD11B2 genetic testing; exclude licorice use

treatment.standardOfCare: • Spironolactone / eplerenone — competitive mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism; blocks cortisol- driven mineralocorticoid receptor activation; reduces hypertension and hypokalemia; first-line pharmacotherapy • Low dietary sodium + high dietary potassium — adjunct BP control • Dexamethasone — suppresses ACTH-driven cortisol production; reduces cortisol available for receptor binding; used in some protocols • Amiloride — alternative if spironolactone not tolerated; direct ENaC block • Carbenoxolone — inhibits 11β-HSD2 (the deficient enzyme); experimental and not recommended due to toxicity • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; 11β-HSD2 expressed in kidney; transplant corrects the metabolic defect; hypertension resolves post-transplant; favorable outcomes • Monitoring — BP, K, HCO3, plasma renin, aldosterone (both low), cortisol/cortisone ratio in urine (elevated ratio diagnostic); serial renal function • Genetic counseling — HSD11B2 mutations; autosomal recessive; homozygous/compound heterozygous

name: Acute Tubulointerstitial Nephritis (ATIN) — Drug- induced
description: Immune-mediated tubular and interstitial inflammation triggered by medications (NSAIDs, antibiotics, PPIs, anticonvulsants, checkpoint inhibitors); AKI

frequency.us: ~10–15% of biopsied AKI in US; antibiotics and NSAIDs most common; checkpoint inhibitors emerging
frequency.global: ~10–15% of biopsied AKI globally; drug-induced predominant in high-income countries; infection- related in re
frequency.sources: Praga & González JASN 2010; Moledina & Perazella JASN 2017; ERA-EDTA ATIN data

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (interstitial infiltration with lymphocytes/eosinophils); eosinophiluria (variable); urinalysis (white cell casts); drug exposure history; eGFR trend

treatment.standardOfCare: • Identify and discontinue causative drug — CRITICAL; NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, PPIs, sulfonamides, vancomycin, checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD1/CTLA4 — increasingly recognized); drug withdrawal is first and most important step; renal recovery often begins within days– weeks • Corticosteroids — prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg) for 4–8 weeks then taper; most evidence from observational studies; AKI Collaborative recommends steroids for moderate-severe ATIN (creatinine >2× baseline) if no improvement 5–7 days after drug withdrawal; some evidence for checkpoint inhibitor-ATIN • Supportive care — IV hydration if dehydrated; electrolyte correction; avoid further nephrotoxins • Renal biopsy — for diagnosis confirmation, severity assessment, and treatment decisions especially if unclear etiology or no recovery • Monitor renal recovery — eGFR, urinalysis, urine eosinophils (variable sensitivity); follow-up 3 months post- recovery Emerging Methods ▶ Checkpoint inhibitor nephritis — anti-PD1/CTLA4 → ATIN increasingly common; steroid + mycophenolate for refractory cases; rituximab case reports; guidance from IKIUS 2023 consensus

name: Acute Tubulointerstitial Nephritis — Immune / Sarcoid-associated
description: Immune-mediated ATIN in absence of drug trigger; may be associated with sarcoidosis, SLE, Sjögren, IgG4-related disease, or idiopathic

frequency.us: Rare in children in US; sarcoidosis-associated ATIN more common in adolescents; IgG4-RD rare in pediatrics
frequency.global: Rare globally in children; sarcoidosis prevalence varies geographically; IgG4-related disease predominantly adult
frequency.sources: Drent et al. Lancet 2013; Jayne & Rasmussen Semin Nephrol 2014

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy; chest imaging (sarcoidosis); serum ACE; ANA, anti-Ro/La; serum IgG4; calcium (hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis); calcium in urine

treatment.standardOfCare: • Identify and treat underlying condition — systemic sarcoidosis, anti-TBM antibody disease, IgG4-related kidney disease, SLE, Sjögren syndrome; disease-specific therapy • Corticosteroids — prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg); 3–6 months tapering course; cornerstone for sarcoid- ATIN, anti-TBM, IgG4-RKD • IgG4-related kidney disease — rituximab increasingly used for steroid-sparing or refractory IgG4-RKD; excellent response (>90% remission); IgG4 levels monitor response • Hydroxychloroquine — sarcoidosis adjunct; steroid- sparing; monitor ophthalmological toxicity • ACEi/ARBs — for proteinuria component and CKD management • Renal biopsy — diagnostic and guides treatment intensity • Monitor IgG4 levels, ACE level, calcium (sarcoid); CBC; serial renal function

name: TINU Syndrome (Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis)
description: Autoimmune condition causing acute TIN + bilateral uveitis; predominantly affects adolescent females; modified CRP-peptide antibodies pathogenic

frequency.us: Rare; ~1–5% of TIN in US; median age ~15 years; females predominate; uveitis may precede nephritis
frequency.global: Rare globally; ~1–5% of TIN series worldwide; HLA association; relapsing uveitis common; TINU Consortium data
frequency.sources: Mandeville et al. Am J Ophthalmol 2001; Mackensen et al. JASN 2007; TINU Consortium 2020

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (interstitial nephritis); ophthalmology (bilateral anterior uveitis); anti-modified CRP antibodies; urinalysis; eGFR

treatment.standardOfCare: • Corticosteroids (systemic) — prednisone 1 mg/kg/day; required for most TINU (especially bilateral panuveitis); 3– 6 month course with taper; renal ATIN responds more readily than ocular component • Topical ophthalmological treatment — corticosteroid eye drops (prednisolone acetate); mydriatics (tropicamide, cyclopentolate) for posterior synechiae prevention; initial treatment for anterior uveitis • Ophthalmology co-management — CRITICAL; uveitis may persist or relapse independently of renal disease; can precede or follow renal disease; regular follow-up slit- lamp exams • Systemic immunosuppression for refractory uveitis — methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine; used for steroid-sparing in chronic recurrent uveitis • Uveitis-specific biologics — adalimumab (HUMIRA) FDA approved 2016 for non-infectious intermediate/posterior uveitis in adults; increasingly used in pediatric TINU; anti- TNF therapy for refractory cases • Renal monitoring — urinalysis, eGFR, beta-2 microglobulin (tubular marker) to monitor renal recovery

name: Chronic Tubulointerstitial Nephritis
description: Progressive interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy from multiple etiologies (chronic obstruction, chronic infections, analgesics, Chinese herbs, heavy metals, genetic); leads to CKD

frequency.us: Common end-stage pathway in US; aristolochic acid and heavy metal nephropathy uncommon in US children
frequency.global: Common end-stage pathway globally; aristolochic acid nephropathy major issue in Asia (Chinese herbs); heavy metals in industrial settings
frequency.sources: De Broe Kidney Int 2012; Pozdzik et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2013; ERA-EDTA ATIN data

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis); eGFR trend; urinalysis; renal ultrasound (small kidneys); identify and remove cause; heavy metal screening

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • Identify and treat underlying etiology — most important step; causes: analgesic nephropathy (NSAIDs), lithium toxicity, calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, chronic reflux nephropathy, obstructive uropathy, sickle cell, radiation nephritis, idiopathic • Remove offending agent — NSAID cessation, lithium reduction/substitution (valproate/quetiapine); CNI dose reduction; often prevents further progression • CKD management per KDIGO — ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria; BP control; anemia management (EPO); CKD-MBD management; dietary modifications • Electrolyte monitoring — tubulointerstitial disease causes tubular dysfunction; RTA may develop; monitor K, HCO3, phosphate, sodium; supplement as needed • Dialysis and transplant — for ESKD; no disease recurrence unless etiology not corrected (e.g., recurrent obstruction, active autoimmune) • Specific: Aristolochic acid nephropathy — irreversible; no treatment; avoid herbal supplements containing aristolochic acid

name: Hypercalciuria — Idiopathic
description: Excessive urinary calcium excretion without identifiable systemic cause; most common metabolic cause of nephrolithiasis in children

frequency.us: ~2–4% of US children; accounts for ~40–50% of calcium oxalate stones; familial in ~50%
frequency.global: ~2–4% globally in children with urolithiasis; genetic predisposition variable; dietary calcium intake modifies expression
frequency.sources: Moe & Pearle Nat Rev Nephrol 2011; Penido & Ukarapol Ped Nephrol 2012; ROKS Consortium

diagnosis: 24-hour or spot urine calcium:creatinine ratio; serum calcium, PTH, vitamin D; renal ultrasound; stone composition; genetic evaluation if refractory

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — dilutes urinary calcium; 2–3 L/m²/day; plain water preferred; first and most important measure • Dietary sodium restriction — high sodium intake drives urinary calcium excretion via NHE3 competition; <2 g/day sodium; reduces calcium excretion significantly • Dietary calcium — NORMAL intake recommended; calcium restriction paradoxically INCREASES calcium oxalate stone formation (reduces intestinal oxalate binding); do not restrict dairy • Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) — reduces urinary calcium reabsorption in distal tubule; first-line pharmacotherapy for symptomatic hypercalciuria; highly effective; combined with potassium citrate to prevent hypokalemia • Potassium citrate — prevents stones by chelating calcium; alkalinizes urine; reduces calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate crystallization; Urocit-K, Polycitra-K • Dietary oxalate restriction — for calcium oxalate stones; reduce spinach, nuts, chocolate, beets • Protein moderation — high animal protein increases urinary calcium and uric acid; moderate restriction Emerging ▶ Genetic hypercalciuria — CLDN14, CASR variants in some familial cases; precision management based on genotype Methods

name: Cystinuria (SLC3A1 / SLC7A9)
description: Defective renal and intestinal cystine transporter causing cystine stones; recurrent large stones, staghorn calculi, and progressive CKD

frequency.us: ~1/7,000 in US; ~5–7% of pediatric kidney stones; autosomal recessive; SLC3A1 (type A) and SLC7A9 (type B)
frequency.global: ~1/7,000 globally; higher in Libyan Jewish and Spanish populations; urological complications common
frequency.sources: Dello Strologo et al. JASN 2002; Calonge et al. Nat Genet 1994; Cystinuria Consortium

diagnosis: Urine cystine screening (nitroprusside test); 24-hour urine cystine quantification; stone analysis (hexagonal crystals); genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — CRITICAL; urine output >3 L/m²/day; dramatically reduces cystine supersaturation; cornerstone of management; distribute throughout day and night (nocturia/night drinking important) • Urinary alkalinization — potassium citrate; target urine pH 7.0–7.5; cystine solubility dramatically increases above pH 6.5; essential adjunct • Dietary sodium restriction — reduces cystinuria; sodium promotes renal cystine excretion • Dietary methionine/protein restriction — reduces cystine production; moderate animal protein restriction • D-penicillamine — thiol agent; forms mixed disulfide with cystine (more soluble); 2nd line due to toxicity (nephrotic syndrome, lupus-like, bone marrow); vitamin B6 co- supplementation; use for refractory cases • Tiopronin (Thiola) — thiol agent; better tolerated than D- penicillamine; forms cysteine-tiopronin disulfide; first- choice thiol agent; doses 10–50 mg/kg/day • Captopril — thiol group; reduces cystinuria; modest effect; used adjunctively • Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) — less effective for cystine stones (hard); ureteroscopy preferred; PCNL for large staghorn calculi • Genetic counseling — SLC3A1 (type A) or SLC7A9 (type B) mutations; autosomal recessive

name: Enteric Hyperoxaluria
description: Secondary hyperoxaluria from increased intestinal oxalate absorption in fat malabsorption (short bowel syndrome, IBD, bariatric surgery)

frequency.us: Common in pediatric short bowel syndrome in US; increasingly recognized in pediatric IBD
frequency.global: Common globally in short bowel syndrome and malabsorptive conditions; fat malabsorption key mechanism
frequency.sources: Asplin & Coe Kidney Int 1999; Kumar et al. Am J Kidney Dis 2011

diagnosis: 24-hour urine oxalate (elevated but less than PH1/2); serum oxalate; stool fat; intestinal workup; stone analysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Treat underlying GI disease — Crohn disease (medical therapy, bowel resection), short bowel syndrome, bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y, sleeve gastrectomy); reducing fat malabsorption reduces oxalate absorption • Dietary oxalate restriction — reduce spinach, nuts, beets, chocolate, wheat bran; low-oxalate diet • Dietary fat restriction — excess fat saponifies calcium, leaving oxalate free for absorption; low-fat diet critical • Oral calcium carbonate with meals — binds dietary oxalate in gut; prevents absorption; give WITH food not separately; 500–2000 mg with each meal • High fluid intake — dilutes urinary oxalate; target urine output >2 L/day • Potassium citrate — urinary alkalinization; reduces calcium oxalate crystallization • Cholestyramine — bile acid sequestrant; reduces oxalate absorption in fat malabsorption states; adjunct • Probiotics (Oxalobacter formigenes) — gut bacteria that degrade oxalate; investigational in clinical trials; not commercially available Methods • Pyridoxine (B6) — reduces endogenous oxalate synthesis; modest effect in enteric hyperoxaluria (larger effect in PH1)

name: Hyperuricosuria — Pediatric
description: Elevated uric acid excretion causing uric acid or mixed uric acid-calcium stones; associated with high animal protein intake, enzyme defects, or uricosuric drugs

frequency.us: ~5–10% of pediatric kidney stones in US; uric acid stones uncommon in children; Lesch- Nyhan association
frequency.global: ~5–10% of pediatric stones globally; uric acid stones more common in warm climates and with high protein intake
frequency.sources: Lesch & Nyhan Am J Med 1964; Moe et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2011; EAU Urolithiasis Guidelines

diagnosis: 24-hour urine uric acid; serum uric acid; urine pH (acidic favors uric acid stones); HPRT enzyme activity; stone analysis; dietary history

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — dilutes uric acid in urine; reduces supersaturation; 2–3 L/m²/day • Dietary purine restriction — reduce meat, organ meats, shellfish, legumes; moderate animal protein • Urinary alkalinization — potassium citrate; target urine pH 6.0–6.5; uric acid stones dissolve in alkaline urine; caution not to over-alkalinize (increases calcium phosphate risk) • Allopurinol — xanthine oxidase inhibitor; reduces uric acid production; for persistent symptomatic hyperuricosuria unresponsive to dietary measures; 10 mg/kg/day; monitor CBC and liver function • Febuxostat — alternative XO inhibitor; adult data; limited pediatric data; used if allopurinol intolerant • Diagnose secondary causes — Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, glycogen storage disease, tumor lysis syndrome, high purine diet, hemolytic anemia; treat etiology

name: Xanthinuria / Xanthine Stones (XDH)
description: Xanthine oxidase deficiency (XDH mutations) causing hypouricemia and xanthinuria; xanthine stones (radiolucent); rarely causes AKI

frequency.us: Very rare; ~150 cases
frequency.global: Very rare globally; ~150 total reported cases; XDH mutations; type I isolated, type II combined with sulfite oxidase deficiency
frequency.sources: Ichida et al. J Clin Invest 1997; Simmonds et al. J Inherit Metab Dis 1995

diagnosis: Serum uric acid (very low); urine xanthine and hypoxanthine; stone analysis (xanthine stones); XDH genetic testing; SO activity (type II)

treatment.standardOfCare: • High fluid intake — dilutes xanthine in urine; prevents xanthine crystallization; 2–3 L/m²/day; cornerstone • Low purine diet — reduces xanthine production; limit meats, organ meats, shellfish; vegetarian or low-purine diet • Avoid allopurinol — allopurinol CONTRAINDICATED in xanthinuria Type I (XDH deficiency); increases xanthine accumulation; worsens xanthinuria; important drug- disease interaction • Urinary alkalinization — potassium citrate; increases xanthine solubility; target urine pH 7.0+ • Monitor renal function — xanthine stones can cause obstructive nephropathy; renal ultrasound annually • Genetic counseling — XDH (xanthine dehydrogenase) mutations; autosomal recessive; usually benign if dietary measures followed • Type II xanthinuria — combined xanthine + sulfite oxidase deficiency; more severe; neurological involvement; sulfite restriction; no specific therapy

name: 2,8- Dihydroxyadenine Urolithiasis (APRT deficiency)
description: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency causing 2,8-DHA crystalluria; stone formation and AKI from crystal deposits in kidney

frequency.us: Rare
frequency.global: ~1/50,000–100,000 globally; Icelandic founder mutation well- studied; 2,8-DHA crystals on urine microscopy pathognomonic
frequency.sources: Bollée et al. Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012; Edvardsson et al. KI 1993; APRT Deficiency Registry

diagnosis: Urine microscopy (reddish- brown 2,8-DHA crystals); urine amino acids; APRT enzyme activity (erythrocytes); APRT genetic testing; stone analysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Allopurinol — ESSENTIAL and highly effective; inhibits xanthine oxidase → reduces production of 2,8-DHA by blocking adenine conversion; normalizes urinary 2,8-DHA; must be started as soon as diagnosis made and continued lifelong; dose 10–20 mg/kg/day; prevents stone Methods recurrence and CKD progression; delayed diagnosis leads to irreversible CKD • High fluid intake — dilutes 2,8-DHA; 2–3 L/m²/day; adjunct to allopurinol • Dietary restriction of adenine — reduce organ meats, red meats; low-purine diet adjunct • Febuxostat — alternative to allopurinol if intolerant; reduces DHA production; use with monitoring • Urinary alkalinization — limited benefit (2,8-DHA has low solubility across all pH ranges); potassium citrate as adjunct • Dialysis and transplant — for ESKD from DHA nephropathy; allopurinol continues post-transplant to prevent graft DHA crystalline nephropathy • Genetic counseling — APRT mutations; autosomal recessive; most common in Japan and Iceland

name: Struvite Urolithiasis (infection stones)
description: Magnesium ammonium phosphate stones caused by urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella) alkalinizing urine; associated with recurrent UTIs and structural anomalies

frequency.us: ~5–10% of pediatric stones in US; recurrent UTI and neurogenic bladder predispose; staghorn calculi
frequency.global: ~5–10% globally; Proteus mirabilis and urease-producing organisms predominant; higher in developing world with untreated UTI
frequency.sources: Griffith & Osborne Kidney Int 1987; EAU Urolithiasis Guidelines 2022

diagnosis: Stone analysis (struvite composition); urine culture; renal imaging (CT preferred for stone mapping); urodynamics if neurogenic bladder suspected

treatment.standardOfCare: • Complete stone removal — CRITICAL; struvite stones harbor bacteria within the stone matrix; antibiotic therapy alone cannot sterilize stone; percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) preferred for large/staghorn struvite stones; ureteroscopy for ureteral stones; ESWL less effective for large struvite • Antibiotic therapy — culture-directed; treat before and after stone manipulation; long-term suppressive antibiotics post-procedure to prevent recurrence if predisposing conditions persist • Identify and treat predisposing conditions — neurogenic bladder (CIC + anticholinergics); foreign body (catheter, stent); anatomical obstruction; VUR; underlying UTI source • Urease inhibitor (acetohydroxamic acid, AHA) — inhibits bacterial urease; reduces struvite stone growth; significant toxicity (hemolytic anemia, DVT); rarely used in pediatrics; adults with recurrent staghorn calculi • Bladder catheter management — change catheters regularly; maintain sterile technique • Irrigation/dissolution — urinary alkalization; Renacidin irrigation through nephrostomy tube (PCN drain) for residual stone dissolution • Prevention — adequate hydration; urine culture surveillance; treat bacteriuria promptly

name: Nephrocalcinosis — Prematurity / Furosemide- associated
description: Calcium deposits in renal parenchyma in premature infants receiving furosemide; hypercalciuria from immature tubular function and diuretic use

frequency.us: ~10–40% of premature US infants receiving furosemide; often resolves; risk with repeated dosing
frequency.global: ~10–40% of premature infants globally receiving furosemide; consistent rates across Western neonatal ICUs
frequency.sources: Jacinto et al. Pediatrics 2000; Hufnagle et al. Pediatrics 1982; Neonatal nephrocalcinosis review

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (echogenic medullary pyramids); urine calcium:creatinine ratio; serum calcium, phosphate; review furosemide exposure

treatment.standardOfCare: • Minimize furosemide exposure — furosemide is primary cause of nephrocalcinosis in premature infants; use thiazide diuretics instead when chronic diuretic needed for CLD; furosemide → hypercalciuria → medullary nephrocalcinosis Methods • Switch to chlorothiazide/hydrochlorothiazide — for chronic diuretic requirement; significantly reduces hypercalciuria; prevents nephrocalcinosis progression • Spironolactone — combined with thiazide; potassium- sparing; used in BPD management • Adequate calcium and phosphate nutrition — prevent metabolic bone disease of prematurity • High fluid intake — dilutes urinary calcium; adequate hydration; 150–180 mL/kg/day in NICU • Vitamin D — standard supplementation; avoid over- supplementation (hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria) • Serial renal ultrasound — monitor nephrocalcinosis resolution (most resolves by 6–12 months) • Monitor renal function — occasional CKD if extensive nephrocalcinosis; annual creatinine surveillance

name: Distal RTA- associated Nephrocalcinosis
description: Nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis as complication of untreated or undertreated distal (Type 1) RTA; hypocitraturia + alkaline urine promote calcium phosphate deposition

frequency.us: Common complication when dRTA is unrecognized in US; nephrocalcinosis distinguishes Type 1 from others
frequency.global: Common globally when dRTA is untreated; medullary nephrocalcinosis on imaging key distinguishing feature
frequency.sources: Alper JASN 2002; Karet et al. Nat Genet 1999; RTA and Nephrocalcinosis review Ped Nephrol

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound; urine citrate (low); urine calcium; blood gas; urine pH; identify underlying dRTA cause

treatment.standardOfCare: • Same as Distal RTA Type 1 treatment — potassium citrate is cornerstone; treats acidosis AND prevents nephrocalcinosis progression AND prevents new stone formation • Potassium citrate (Polycitra-K, Urocit-K) — 1–3 mEq/kg/day; long-term; prevents calcium crystallization; most important intervention • Early and sustained alkali therapy — critical; nephrocalcinosis can stabilize or partially regress with aggressive alkali therapy; starts at diagnosis • Monitor nephrocalcinosis — renal ultrasound every 6–12 months; document stability or regression • Calcium and vitamin D — for bone disease; balanced supplementation; avoid excessive calcium (exacerbates calcium deposition if acidosis not corrected) • Monitor renal function — nephrocalcinosis → potential CKD; eGFR annually

name: Atypical HUS (aHUS) — CFH/CFI/C3/CFB/MCP mutations
description: Complement dysregulation causing TMA with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and AKI; highly recurrent without treatment

frequency.us: ~2/million/year in US; CFH mutations most common (~20– 30%); ESKD in ~50% without eculizumab
frequency.global: ~2/million/year globally; European aHUS Registry well- characterized; CFH most common mutation; eculizumab transformed outcomes
frequency.sources: Fremeaux-Bacchi et al. JASN 2013; Loirat & Fremeaux- Bacchi Orphanet J Rare Dis 2011; aHUS Registry

diagnosis: CBC (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia); renal function; complement panel (C3, C4, CH50, factor H/I); genetic panel; anti-CFH antibodies; ADAMTS13 (exclude TTP)

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Eculizumab (Soliris, Alexion) — anti-C5 complement
inhibitor; FDA approved 2011 for aHUS; preferred for
ACUTE episode (most evidence; faster onset); biweekly
IV infusions; requires mandatory meningococcal
vaccination ≥2 weeks before initiation; lifelong in most
patients with high-risk mutations (CFH, CFI, C3, CFB,
THBD)
• Ravulizumab (Ultomiris, Alexion/AstraZeneca) — next-
generation anti-C5; FDA approved for aHUS (adults and
pediatric ≥1 month) 2019; extended dosing: every 4
weeks (<20 kg) or every 8 weeks (>20 kg); 3–4× longer Methods half-life than eculizumab; complete TMA response in 78% of children in Phase 3 trials; increasingly preferred for MAINTENANCE over eculizumab; 2-year Phase 3 data (2024) confirm sustained hematologic and renal improvement • Plasma infusion — bridge therapy before complement inhibitor available; fresh frozen plasma contains normal complement factors; less effective than C5 inhibitors • Kidney transplant — for ESKD; requires peri-transplant complement inhibition to prevent recurrence (risk varies by mutation: CFH >50% recurrence without eculizumab, CFI >30%, MCP <5%) • Meningococcal + encapsulated bacteria prophylaxis — mandatory vaccinations and/or prophylactic penicillin/amoxicillin before and during complement inhibition Note: Genetic testing for CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, MCP/CD46, THBD, CFHR1–5, anti-CFH antibodies mandatory before or at initiation of treatment; guides duration and discontinuation decisions
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Iptacopan (Fabhalta, Novartis) — Factor B inhibitor (proximal alternative pathway); FDA approved for C3G 2025; investigational for aHUS; Phase 2/3 trials ▶ Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor) — oral; Phase 2/3 in aHUS/C3G ▶ Subcutaneous C5 inhibitors — improved convenience; in development ▶ Crovalimab (Veopoz, Roche) — novel anti-C5 antibody; FDA approved for PNH 2023; investigational for aHUS; enables SC self-injection ▶ Cemdisiran — siRNA targeting complement C3 in liver; investigational for aHUS ▶ Discontinuation protocols — evidence accumulating for selected low-risk patients (MCP/CD46 mutations); individualized approach per KIDRAP and SHARE guidelines

name: Atypical HUS — Anti- CFH Antibody Mediated
description: Acquired aHUS from autoantibodies against complement factor H; occurs predominantly in children aged 5–12; associated with CFHR1/3 deletion

frequency.us: ~5–10% of aHUS in US; most common in children 5–12 years; CFHR1/3 deletion in ~90%
frequency.global: 5–10% of aHUS globally in children; European cohort data; CFHR1/3 homozygous deletion most frequent finding
frequency.sources: Dragon-Durey et al. JASN 2005; Józsi et al. Blood 2008; aHUS Registry Europe

diagnosis: Anti-CFH IgG antibody titer; CFHR1/3 deletion by MLPA; C3 (low); complement panel; renal function; ADAMTS13

treatment.standardOfCare: • Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) — removes anti-CFH antibodies AND supplies normal CFH; preferred initial therapy; typically 5–10 sessions • Rituximab — depletes anti-CFH antibody-producing B cells; key adjunct; prevents recurrence; usually given early in course; repeat doses for relapse • Eculizumab / Ravulizumab — complement inhibition during acute phase; bridges to definitive immunosuppression effect; increasingly used with immunosuppression rather than alone Methods • Corticosteroids — immunosuppressive; reduces anti-CFH Ab titers; combined with rituximab • Mycophenolate mofetil — maintenance immunosuppression post-rituximab; long-term B cell suppression • Monitor anti-CFH antibody titers — guide treatment duration and identify relapse • CFHR1-3 deletion screening — anti-CFH Ab most common in patients with homozygous CFHR1-3 deletion; helps identify genetic risk

name: Shiga toxin HUS (STEC- HUS)
description: Most common HUS in children; Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7 or O104:H4 triggers endothelial TMA; diarrhea-associated HUS

frequency.us: ~2–3/100,000 children/year in US; peak age 1–5 years; summer predominance; ESKD in 5–10%
frequency.global: ~2–3/100,000 children/year in high-income countries; higher in Argentina (5–7/100,000) — world's highest rate; E. coli O157:H7
frequency.sources: Tarr et al. NEJM 2005; Garg et al. NEJM 2003; STEC-HUS International Registry

diagnosis: CBC (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia); stool culture/PCR for STEC; Shiga toxin PCR/EIA in stool; serum Shiga toxin- producing E. coli antibodies; renal function; LDH; complement (normal)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Supportive care — cornerstone; careful fluid management; avoid hypovolemia and hypervolemia; antihypertensive therapy; dialysis (peritoneal or hemo) for renal failure; red cell transfusion for severe anemia (caution: may exacerbate hypertension) • NO antibiotics — risk of increased Shiga toxin release from lysed STEC bacteria; antibiotics contraindicated in active STEC-HUS diarrheal illness; meta-analyses do not support benefit • NO antimotility agents (loperamide) — increases toxin absorption time; contraindicated • Early pediatric nephrology involvement — critical given rapid progression to renal failure Eculizumab Controversy: • Eculizumab use in STEC-HUS remains controversial; was used extensively after 2011 E. coli O104:H4 Germany outbreak; subsequent systematic reviews and RCT data show no consistent benefit over supportive care in typical STEC-HUS; 2024 guidelines do not recommend routine use; may have benefit in select cases with severe neurological involvement or refractory disease; individualized, expert-center decision only
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Anti-Stx2 monoclonal antibody (Urtoxazumab) — targets Shiga toxin 2; Phase 2 trials; reduces Stx2-mediated injury; investigational ▶ CBLB502 (entolimod, TLR5 agonist) — reduces complement-mediated TMA; preclinical/early clinical ▶ Dialysis optimization — continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in severe pediatric STEC-HUS; evolving protocols ▶ FimH antagonists — prevent STEC intestinal adherence; investigational prevention approach

name: DGKE-associated HUS
description: DGKE mutations causing infantile-onset recurrent TMA/HUS; not complement- mediated; diacylglycerol kinase epsilon deficiency activates platelets

frequency.us: Very rare; DGKE mutations described in ~20 families

diagnosis: Genetic testing (DGKE); normal complement; recurrent TMA episodes from infancy; renal function; ADAMTS13 normal

treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational: Eculizumab — less effective (non-complement mechanism); investigational use ongoing Methods

name: TTP — Congenital / Upshaw-Schulman Syndrome
description: ADAMTS13 deficiency from mutations causing congenital TTP; presents in neonatal period or childhood with TMA triggered by illness/pregnancy

frequency.us: Very rare; ~1/million in US; AR; episodes triggered by infection, fever, or pregnancy
frequency.global: ~1/million globally; ADAMTS13 deficiency; European TTP Registry; episodes from childhood with complement triggers
frequency.sources: Levy et al. Nature 2001; Upshaw NEJM 1978; International TTP Registry

diagnosis: ADAMTS13 activity (<10%); ADAMTS13 inhibitor absent (distinguishes from acquired); ADAMTS13 genetic testing; CBC (TMA); LDH

treatment.standardOfCare: • Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) — ADAMTS13 replacement; historically the primary treatment; on-demand for acute TTP events AND prophylactic infusions; achieves ~19% of normal ADAMTS13 activity; allergic reactions common; relied on donated plasma supply FDA-Approved (November 2023) — CRITICAL NEW THERAPY ▶ Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, Takeda) — FDA approved Nov 2023 for congenital TTP (adults + children); first disease-specific therapy for cTTP; 40 IU/kg IV; restores ~100% of normal ADAMTS13 activity vs. ~19% with FFP; Phase 3 crossover trial (NEJM 2024, Scully et al.): ZERO acute TTP events vs. 1 with FFP; adverse events 9% vs. 48% with FFP; no TTP events in Phase 3; no neutralizing antibodies detected; 2-year real-world data (Japan, 2025) confirm efficacy in ESRD patients; ISTH 2025 guidelines: STRONG recommendation for rADAMTS13 over FFP for cTTP prophylaxis in remission (moderate certainty evidence) Standard Approach with Adzynma: ▶ rADAMTS13 (Adzynma) 40 IU/kg IV — prophylactic every 2–3 weeks OR on-demand for acute events; replaces FFP as first-choice where accessible ▶ FFP — alternative if rADAMTS13 unavailable; still effective but inferior
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Extended-half-life recombinant ADAMTS13 — to allow less frequent prophylactic dosing; in development ▶ Gene therapy (ADAMTS13) — hepatocyte-targeted; preclinical ▶ Caplacizumab — off-label for acute cTTP episodes with severe symptoms (ISTH 2025: conditional recommendation to use caplacizumab for acute cTTP if available, as part of shared decision-making)

name: TTP — Acquired Pediatric
description: Autoimmune ADAMTS13 inhibitor causing TTP in children; rare compared to adults; requires urgent treatment

frequency.us: Rare in children in US; peak in adolescent females; anti- ADAMTS13 antibodies; systemic involvement
frequency.global: Rare globally in children; ADAMTS13 antibody-mediated; European Registry shows pediatric peak in adolescence
frequency.sources: Scully et al. Blood 2012; Veyradier et al. Blood 2004; International TTP Registry

diagnosis: ADAMTS13 activity (<10%); ADAMTS13 inhibitor (IgG); CBC (TMA); LDH; renal function; neurological assessment

treatment.standardOfCare: • Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) — cornerstone; removes anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies AND replaces functional ADAMTS13; daily until platelet count normalized; typically 5–10 sessions; median 5 exchanges required before platelet normalization (UK pediatric registry) Methods • Corticosteroids — high-dose IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisone; immunosuppression reduces autoantibody production; standard adjunct to TPE • Rituximab (anti-CD20) — B-cell depletion; reduces autoantibody production; added at diagnosis in many centers (particularly for severe/refractory disease); ~75% of patients in UK TTP Registry received rituximab FDA-Approved Pediatric Expansion (January 5, 2026) — CRITICAL NEW APPROVAL: • Caplacizumab (Cablivi, Sanofi) — anti-VWF nanobody; inhibits VWF-platelet interaction; FDA EXPANDED approval to pediatric patients ≥12 years (January 5, 2026) for acquired TTP in combination with TPE and immunosuppression; previously approved for adults only (2019); Orphan Drug Designation; pediatric approval supported by retrospective data (30 patients 2–18 yr): 80% remission; UK TTP Registry (16 peds <18 yr, including 4 under age 12): no refractory cases, 1 relapse; youngest treated 33 months (off-label) • Dosing: 10 mg IV loading then 10 mg SC daily; for <40 kg: 5 mg daily; continue for 30 days after last TPE; extend if ADAMTS13 activity remains severely deficient • Key benefit: faster platelet normalization; reduces TPE sessions; reduces hospital stay ADAMTS13 Monitoring: • Serial ADAMTS13 activity levels guide caplacizumab duration; ADAMTS13 recovery may be delayed by caplacizumab (median 35 days in UK registry) — this is normal and expected; extend treatment until ADAMTS13 ≥20% • ISTH 2025 focused update: no change to prior recommendations for iTTP management; caplacizumab endorsed as part of standard TPE+IS+rituximab protocol
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Caplacizumab without TPE — Phase 2/3 trials ongoing (CABLIVI TPE-free); some centers adopting for mild- moderate iTTP ▶ Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated TTP — increasing recognition; rituximab + caplacizumab regimens ▶ Tolerization approaches for anti-ADAMTS13 Ab — investigational

name: Cobalamin C Deficiency — TMA (MMACHC)
description: MMACHC mutations causing impaired cobalamin metabolism; presents as TMA in neonates/infants with elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine

frequency.us: Rare; most common organic acidemia
frequency.global: Rare globally; Cobalamin C the most prevalent intracellular cobalamin defect; TMA presentation distinguishes from HUS

diagnosis: Plasma amino acids (elevated homocysteine); urine organic acids (elevated methylmalonic acid); MMACHC genetic testing; complement (normal); ADAMTS13 (normal)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Hydroxocobalamin (OHCbl) — high-dose intramuscular or subcutaneous; first-line and most effective; crosses blood- brain barrier; preferred over cyanocobalamin; doses 1–2 mg/day IM in acute phase, then 1 mg 3× weekly maintenance; dramatically improves TMA and metabolic parameters

name: Interferon-pathway TMA (TMEM173 / STING)
description: Gain-of-function STING mutations (SAVI syndrome) causing type I interferon overactivation with vasculopathy, TMA, and pulmonary fibrosis

frequency.us: Very rare; <50 cases reported
frequency.global: Very rare globally; <50 reported cases; TMEM173/STING gain-of-function; type I interferonopathy spectrum
frequency.sources: Bertoli-Avella et al. NEJM 2018; Liu et al. Science 2014; STING-associated vasculopathy registry

diagnosis: STING/TMEM173 genetic testing; type I interferon signature; renal biopsy (TMA); pulmonary CT; skin biopsy (vasculopathy)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib,
baricitinib — target interferon signaling) — investigational
for STING-associated TMA

name: HUS — Secondary (drug / transplant-associated)
description: TMA caused by immunosuppressants (calcineurin inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors), quinine, gemcitabine, or post- transplant in setting of antibody-mediated rejection

frequency.us: Uncommon in US; CNI-TMA in ~3–5% of transplant recipients; dose-related and complement- mediated forms
frequency.global: 3–5% of transplant recipients globally; consistent across US, European transplant registries
frequency.sources: Noris & Remuzzi JASN 2010; Thadhani et al. Kidney Int 1996; ERA-EDTA transplant TMA data

diagnosis: TMA triad; drug exposure history; calcineurin inhibitor levels; renal biopsy; complement panel; anti- donor antibodies (transplant context)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Identify and remove causative agent — CRITICAL; calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine — TMA in 1–5% transplant recipients), mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus), gemcitabine, bevacizumab, quinine, cocaine, clopidogrel; dose reduction or switch immunosuppressant • Plasma exchange — for drug-associated TMA with severe TMA; effective for removing drug and/or pathogenic factors; daily until TMA resolves; LESS effective than for iTTP • Eculizumab / Ravulizumab — complement activation demonstrated in CNI-TMA and transplant-associated Methods TMA; complement inhibition increasingly used for severe transplant-associated TMA; evidence from case series; no RCT; individualized decision • Platelet transfusions — AVOID in active TMA (fuels microthrombus formation); only for life-threatening bleeding • Supportive care — dialysis for AKI; antihypertensives; transfusion for severe anemia • Post-stem cell transplant TMA — eculizumab evidence growing; ravulizumab; high mortality without treatment • Identify complement mutation — some "secondary" HUS patients have underlying complement mutations revealed by drug trigger; genetic testing for CFH/CFI/CFB/C3/MCP recommended in severe or relapsing drug-TMA

name: Essential / Primary Hypertension — Pediatric
description: Hypertension without identifiable secondary cause; increasingly common in adolescents with overweight/obesity; familial component

frequency.us: ~3–5% of US children; prevalence rising with obesity; primarily adolescents; rare in young children
frequency.global: ~3–5% globally; variability by country; higher in US/Australia due to obesity epidemic; rising worldwide
frequency.sources: Hansen et al. Hypertension 2007; Flynn & Kaelber AAP 2017 guidelines; NHANES data

diagnosis: Blood pressure ≥95th percentile on ≥3 occasions; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM); exclude secondary causes; echocardiogram; lipids; fasting glucose

treatment.standardOfCare: • Lifestyle modification first-line — DASH diet; sodium restriction; weight loss (if overweight/obese); exercise; 6- month trial for Stage 1 without comorbidities • Pharmacological therapy — initiate immediately for: Stage 2 HTN, symptomatic HTN, Stage 1 with end-organ damage (LVH), comorbid CKD/diabetes/proteinuria • First-line drug classes (evidence-based): - ACEi (lisinopril, fosinopril, enalapril) — preferred in CKD, proteinuria, diabetes - ARB (losartan, candesartan) — preferred if ACEi intolerant; same CKD indications - Long-acting calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) — preferred post-transplant (first 6–12 months); well-tolerated; no monitoring requirements - Thiazide/thiazide-type diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) — for volume-dependent or low-renin hypertension • BP targets (2017 AAP): <90th percentile for age/sex/height (children <13 yr); <130/80 mmHg (adolescents ≥13 yr) • ABPM (ambulatory BP monitoring) — recommended for confirmation, white coat HTN, masked HTN, CKD surveillance; BP load and nocturnal dipping assessment • Beta-blockers — NOT first-line in pediatric primary HTN; used for specific indications (migraine, portal hypertension) • ACEi/ARB contraindicated in adolescent females with child-bearing potential — teratogenicity warning
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — growing evidence for renal hemodynamic BP-lowering effects; relevant in obese adolescents with metabolic syndrome; off-label use Methods ▶ GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide) — weight loss– mediated BP reduction; approved for pediatric obesity; indirect BP benefit ▶ Telehealth + home BP monitoring — improving adherence and treatment titration; clinical effectiveness research ongoing ▶ Finerenone — non-steroidal MRA; BP lowering in CKD/diabetes context; pediatric trials emerging ▶ Renalase modulation — novel pathway; early preclinical for pediatric renal hypertension

name: Obesity-related Hypertension — Pediatric
description: Hypertension directly attributable to obesity; insulin resistance, increased sympathetic activity, and renin-angiotensin activation; common metabolic syndrome component

frequency.us: ~30–40% of obese US children have hypertension; increasing prevalence with obesity epidemic
frequency.global: ~30–40% globally in obese children; metabolic syndrome association consistent across populations
frequency.sources: Dietz & Robinson NEJM 1998; Reinehr et al. Int J Obes 2006; WHO Global Obesity data

diagnosis: Anthropometric measures (BMI, waist circumference); fasting insulin, glucose (insulin resistance); lipids; ABPM; echocardiogram (LVH)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Weight loss — primary and most effective intervention; 5– 10% reduction lowers BP significantly; lifestyle, behavioral, dietary interventions • DASH diet + sodium restriction — especially effective in obesity-related HTN; reduces diet-induced renin- angiotensin activation • Physical activity — aerobic exercise ≥1 hour/day; reduces BP by 3–5 mmHg • Screen for sleep-disordered breathing — obstructive sleep apnea common in pediatric obesity; OSA treatment reduces BP • Pharmacotherapy per 2017 AAP guidelines — if lifestyle fails after 6 months or if Stage 2/end-organ damage; ACEi/ARB, CCB, or thiazide per renal/metabolic comorbidities
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ GLP-1 receptor agonists: - Liraglutide (Saxenda, Novo Nordisk) — FDA approved for obesity ≥12 yr (2020); significant weight loss + BP reduction; 3 mg SC daily - Semaglutide SC (Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) — FDA approved for obesity ≥12 yr (2022); superior weight loss to liraglutide; FLOW trial demonstrates renal and BP protection in adults; 2.4 mg weekly - Tirzepatide (Zepbound, Lilly) — GLP-1/GIP dual agonist; SURMOUNT-2 data; FDA approved obesity in adults (2023); adolescent trials underway ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — renal hemodynamic BP lowering; weight loss benefit; off-label in obese hypertensive adolescents ▶ Bariatric surgery — highly effective for severe obesity (BMI ≥35 with comorbidities); sustained hypertension remission documented

name: Renovascular Hypertension — Fibromuscular Dysplasia
description: Arterial dysplasia causing renal artery stenosis and renin-dependent hypertension; most common cause of renovascular hypertension in children

frequency.us: ~0.5–1% of pediatric hypertension is renovascular; FMD more common than atherosclerosis in US children
frequency.global: ~0.5–1% of pediatric HTN globally; FMD and Takayasu arteritis major causes; genetic forms rare
frequency.sources: Tullus et al. Lancet 2008; Stanley et al. J Vasc Surg 1995; ASPIRE Registry

diagnosis: Doppler ultrasound renal arteries; MRA; CTA; captopril renogram; renal arteriography (gold standard); plasma renin activity; peripheral vein renin sampling

treatment.standardOfCare: • Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) — first-line treatment for pediatric FMD-related renovascular hypertension; balloon dilation without stenting preferred in Methods children (stents poorly tolerate growth); 70–80% cure or significant improvement in BP; single dilations or serial dilations • ACEi/ARBs — for BP control and renal protection; reduce renin-driven hypertension; monitor renal function closely (risk of acute bilateral RAS-associated AKI with RAAS blockade) • Surgical revascularization — aortorenal bypass (saphenous vein, autologous artery graft) for: failed angioplasty, long-segment disease, ostial lesions, very young children; excellent long-term outcomes in specialized pediatric vascular surgery centers (Cincinnati Children's, CHOP, Great Ormond Street) • Calcium channel blockers — amlodipine for BP control when RAAS blockers not tolerated or pre-angioplasty; well-tolerated; commonly used • Multivessel/bilateral screening — renal artery assessment; mesenteric/celiac vessels; fibromuscular dysplasia can be systemic • Captopril renography or renal vein renins — diagnose lateralizing renovascular hypertension

name: Renal Artery Stenosis — Takayasu / Vasculitis- associated
description: Large vessel vasculitis causing renal artery stenosis; Takayasu arteritis most common in young females; middle aortic syndrome in children

frequency.us: Rare; Takayasu most common large-vessel vasculitis in US children; RAS in 30–70% of Takayasu
frequency.global: Rare globally; highest prevalence in Japan, India, Middle East; pediatric Takayasu well- described in Asian registries
frequency.sources: Ozen et al. ARD 2010; Eleftheriou et al. Rheumatology 2015; TAKI Consortium

diagnosis: MRA; CTA angiography; FDG-PET (active inflammation); ESR/CRP; ANCA; renal arteriography; captopril renogram; ophthalmology

treatment.standardOfCare: • Immunosuppression for active Takayasu — corticosteroids (prednisone 1–2 mg/kg/day); first-line for acute inflammatory phase; methotrexate, azathioprine, or mycophenolate as steroid-sparing agents • Biologics for refractory Takayasu — tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) FDA approved for adult GCA/Takayasu; increasingly used for pediatric Takayasu; abatacept (CTLA4-Ig); TNF inhibitors (infliximab); rituximab • BP management — ACEi/ARBs; calcium channel blockers; monitor renal function; bilateral RAS risk with RAAS blockade • Surgical/endovascular revascularization — reserved for quiescent disease; active inflammation precludes safe repair; PTA or bypass grafting for significant RAS causing uncontrolled HTN, renal ischemia, or renovascular HTN • Surveillance — MRA or CTA annually; PET-CT for activity assessment; inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, IL-6) • Antiplatelet therapy — aspirin for ischemic risk reduction in vessel disease Emerging ▶ Secukinumab (IL-17 inhibitor) — investigational for refractory Takayasu ▶ Ustekinumab (IL-12/23) — case reports for refractory large vessel vasculitis Methods

name: Renal Artery Stenosis — Neurofibromatosis- associated
description: NF1 causes RAS through neurofibromas or dysplastic arteriopathy of renal arteries; important and often underrecognized cause of renovascular hypertension in children with NF1

frequency.us: ~1% of NF1 patients develop renovascular HTN; NF1 frequency ~1/3,000 in US
frequency.global: ~1/3,000 globally for NF1; vascular complications in ~5%; renovascular HTN ~1% of NF1 patients; US and European data
frequency.sources: Friedman et al. Am J Med Genet 2002; Oderich et al. J Vasc Surg 2007; NF1 Registry

diagnosis: NF1 clinical diagnosis (café- au-lait spots, Lisch nodules); Doppler ultrasound; MRA; renal arteriography; captopril renogram; peripheral renin studies

treatment.standardOfCare: • ACEi/ARBs — for BP control; renovascular mechanism; monitor renal function (bilateral NF1-RAS risk with bilateral disease) • Surgical revascularization — NF1-associated renal artery stenosis requires surgery (not PTA/angioplasty); NF1 vessels are friable, dysplastic, prone to restenosis after angioplasty; aortorenal bypass preferred; experienced pediatric vascular surgery center essential • Calcium channel blockers — amlodipine for BP; peri- operative control • Multi-organ NF1 management — NPI, bone disease, plexiform neurofibromas, learning difficulties; multidisciplinary • Surveillance — aortic involvement possible; renal artery imaging; abdominal imaging for pheochromocytoma (NF1 association) Emerging ▶ Selumetinib (Koselugo) — MEK inhibitor FDA approved 2020 for NF1 plexiform neurofibromas ≥2 yr; no evidence for vascular NF1 lesions; research stage

name: Glucocorticoid- Remediable Aldosteronism (CYP11B1/B2)
description: Chimeric gene fusion of CYP11B1/CYP11B2 causing aldosterone production under ACTH control; familial hypertension, hypokalemia, suppressed renin, elevated aldosterone

frequency.us: Rare; ~1% of primary aldosteronism cases in US; important cause of familial early- onset HTN
frequency.global: Rare globally; CYP11B1/B2 chimeric gene; autosomal dominant; HTN responsive to dexamethasone suppression
frequency.sources: Sutherland et al. Lancet 1966; Stowasser et al. JASN 2003; GRA Registry

diagnosis: Blood pressure; electrolytes (hypokalemia); renin/aldosterone (low renin, high aldosterone); dexamethasone suppression test; CYP11B1/CYP11B2 fusion gene detection (Southern blot or long-range PCR)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Low-dose dexamethasone — cornerstone; suppresses ACTH → suppresses aldosterone (produced by chimeric CYP11B1/B2 fusion gene driven by ACTH-responsive promoter); 0.125–0.25 mg/day; restores normoaldosteronism; corrects hypokalemia and hypertension; long-term maintenance; minimize dose to avoid glucocorticoid side effects (growth suppression) • Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) — add if BP not fully controlled on dexamethasone alone; eplerenone preferred in adolescent males (fewer anti-androgen effects) • Amiloride — blocks ENaC; potassium-sparing; adjunct or alternative to MRA • Potassium supplementation — hypokalemia correction; oral KCl • Genetic testing (CYP11B1/B2 chimeric gene) — Southern blot or long-range PCR; confirmatory in all suspected cases; distinguishes from other primary aldosteronism • Family screening — autosomal dominant; first-degree relatives at 50% risk; screen for hypertension and hypokalemia; genetic testing of relatives

name: Monogenic Hypertension — Other (Liddle, AME, Gordon)
description: Genetic causes of low- renin, low-aldosterone hypertension not separately listed; family history of early-onset hypertension key

frequency.us: Collectively rare in US; important because treatment differs from essential hypertension
frequency.global: Collectively rare globally; each condition responds to specific treatment targeting pathogenic mechanism
frequency.sources: Lifton et al. Cell 2001; Dluhy & Williams Kidney Int 1994; Monogenic HTN review Nat Rev Nephrol 2018

diagnosis: Electrolytes; renin/aldosterone; genetic panel (SCNN1B/G, HSD11B2, WNK1/4, KLHL3, CUL3); urine steroid profile; consider in children with treatment-resistant hypertension + low renin

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Liddle Syndrome — amiloride/triamterene; low sodium
diet (see Liddle entry #95) Methods • Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess — spironolactone/eplerenone; dexamethasone (see AME entry #96) • Gordon Syndrome (PHA2) — thiazide diuretics (see PHA2 entry #94) • GRA — dexamethasone + MRA (see GRA entry #124) • All forms: dietary sodium restriction; genetic confirmation of diagnosis; family screening; tailored pharmacotherapy based on specific molecular mechanism • General principle — mechanism-based treatment essential; wrong class of antihypertensive will be ineffective or harmful; genetic diagnosis guides therapy • Monitor electrolytes, renin, aldosterone — confirms correct diagnosis and treatment response

name: White Coat Hypertension — Pediatric
description: Elevated clinic blood pressure with normal ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM); not associated with end-organ damage; may progress to sustained hypertension

frequency.us: ~30–40% of children with elevated US clinic BP have white coat HTN on ABPM; important to diagnose
frequency.global: ~30–40% globally with elevated clinic BP have white coat HTN; ABPM essential for definitive diagnosis
frequency.sources: Flynn et al. Hypertension 2014; Lurbe et al. J Hypertens 2016; AAP 2017 Pediatric HTN Guidelines

diagnosis: ABPM (24-hour; daytime mean below 95th percentile); echocardiogram (normal LV mass); renal ultrasound; repeat clinic measurements; home monitoring

treatment.standardOfCare: • Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) — ESSENTIAL for diagnosis; 24-hour ABPM shows normal BP outside clinical setting; daytime and nighttime loads normal; distinguishes WCH from true hypertension; 2017 AAP guideline strongly recommends ABPM confirmation • No pharmacological treatment — WCH does not require antihypertensive medications; reassurance • Lifestyle counseling — DASH diet, reduced sodium, regular physical activity, healthy weight • Repeat ABPM every 1–2 years — monitor for progression to true hypertension (WCH is a risk factor for future sustained HTN); follow through adolescence • Address anxiety — explain white coat effect; reduce anxiety around measurements; home BP monitoring with validated oscillometric device; compare to ABPM • Reassurance — WCH in children generally benign; stress reduction; normalization of BP expected outside clinic

name: Masked Hypertension — Pediatric
description: Normal clinic blood pressure but elevated ABPM; associated with end- organ damage and cardiovascular risk; prevalence underestimated

frequency.us: ~6–10% of US children with normal clinic BP have masked HTN; higher in CKD, obesity
frequency.global: ~6–10% globally; consistently higher in CKD (~30– 40%) and obese children; associated with organ damage
frequency.sources: Lurbe et al. Hypertension 2005; Stabouli et al. Ped Nephrol 2011; Masked HTN meta-analysis 2019

diagnosis: ABPM (daytime mean ≥95th percentile with normal clinic); home blood pressure monitoring; echocardiogram; renal function

treatment.standardOfCare: • ABPM — diagnostic; normal or borderline clinic BP but elevated 24-hour or nighttime BP on ABPM; daytime mean ≥135/85 or 24-hour ≥130/80 in adolescents; subclinical target organ damage (LVH, microalbuminuria) risk similar to sustained HTN • Antihypertensive therapy — indicated if masked HTN confirmed; same drug classes as true HTN: ACEi/ARBs (especially if CKD), CCB, thiazide; lower threshold for treatment vs. WCH due to similar cardiovascular risk • Lifestyle interventions — weight loss, sodium restriction, DASH diet, physical activity; critical first-line measures • Monitor for end-organ damage — echocardiography for LVH annually; urinalysis for microalbuminuria; optic disc evaluation in severe cases Methods • Repeat ABPM — every 6–12 months to assess treatment response and disease evolution • High-risk groups — CKD, obesity, premature birth, coarctation history, sleep apnea — screen for masked HTN in all

name: Hypertensive Emergency — Pediatric
description: Severe hypertension with acute end-organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy, seizures, acute heart failure, retinopathy, AKI); requires immediate IV therapy

frequency.us: ~1–2% of US pediatric HTN referrals; secondary HTN most common; AKI and neurological complications common
frequency.global: ~1–2% globally of pediatric HTN referrals; consistent rates in US and European pediatric intensive care data
frequency.sources: Deal et al. J Pediatr 1992; Flynn et al. Hypertension 2007; Pediatric Emergency HTN Collaborative

diagnosis: Blood pressure (severely elevated ≥99th percentile + 12 mmHg); neurological assessment; echocardiogram; renal function; fundoscopy; CT/MRI brain; CBC (TMA)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Nicardipine IV — dihydropyridine CCB; preferred IV agent for pediatric hypertensive emergency; continuous infusion; titratable; does not cause reflex tachycardia; minimal adverse effects; preferred in renal/CKD-associated emergency • Labetalol IV — alpha/beta blocker; effective for catecholamine excess (pheochromocytoma, cocaine); safe in most pediatric emergencies; bolus or infusion • Hydralazine IV or IM — vasodilator; use in pregnancy- associated HTN; less titratable; alternative in resource- limited settings • Sodium nitroprusside IV — most rapidly titratable; reserve for extreme emergencies (hypertensive encephalopathy, severe aortic coarctation crisis); cyanide toxicity risk with prolonged use; requires intensive monitoring • Esmolol IV — ultra-short-acting beta-blocker; for acute aortic dissection, perioperative HTN, thyroid storm • Furosemide IV — if volume overload component (acute glomerulonephritis emergency) Key principles: • TARGET: Reduce MAP by 25% in first 6–8 hours; then gradually to normal over 24–48 hours; avoid precipitous drops (risk of ischemic stroke, vision loss) • Identify and treat underlying cause — do NOT lower BP before securing IV access and ruling out AKI/GN/pheochromocytoma/coarctation • Oral agents — NOT appropriate for true hypertensive emergency; use IV only • Transfer to PICU — all hypertensive emergencies; neurological monitoring essential
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Clevidipine IV — ultrashort-acting CCB (clevidipine); used in adult cardiac surgery; pediatric data emerging for intraoperative/postoperative hypertension ▶ Fenoldopam IV — dopamine receptor agonist; renal vasodilation; may offer renal protection vs. other agents; used in some pediatric centers ▶ Diagnosis-specific protocols — coarctation rescue (prostaglandin, balloon dilation), aortic surgery protocols; increasingly protocol-driven in pediatric centers Methods

name: Hypomagnesemia with Secondary Hypocalcemia (TRPM6)
description: TRPM6 mutations causing neonatal severe hypomagnesemia and secondary hypocalcemia; seizures in neonates if untreated

frequency.us: Very rare; ~50 cases reported
frequency.global: Very rare globally; ~50 total reported cases; TRPM6 mutations; autosomal recessive; responds to high-dose Mg supplementation
frequency.sources: Walder et al. Nat Genet 2002; Schlingmann et al. Nat Genet 2002

diagnosis: Serum magnesium (very low); serum calcium (low — secondary); PTH (elevated or normal); TRPM6 genetic testing; urine magnesium (tubular leak)

treatment.standardOfCare: • High-dose magnesium supplementation — LIFELONG; oral MgCl₂ or Mg gluconate; IV MgSO₄ for acute severe hypomagnesemia (seizures); goal serum Mg >0.65 mmol/L; TRPM6 mutations require supraphysiological Mg doses to overcome impaired absorption; divided doses (3–4x/day) improve absorption • Calcium supplementation + vitamin D — secondary hypocalcemia due to PTH resistance from hypomagnesemia; calcium normalizes as Mg is replenished; calcitriol if persistent hypocalcemia • IV magnesium for acute crisis — seizures, tetany; 0.2 mL/kg of 50% MgSO₄ IV slowly; follow with continuous infusion • Monitor neurological development — hypomagnesemia seizures in infancy can cause neurodevelopmental injury if diagnosis delayed; early treatment critical • Genetic counseling — TRPM6 (transient receptor potential melastatin member 6) mutations; autosomal recessive

name: Familial Hypomagnesemia with Hypercalciuria and Nephrocalcinosis (CLDN16/19)
description: CLDN16 or CLDN19 mutations disrupting paracellular magnesium/calcium reabsorption in thick ascending limb; nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, ocular coloboma (CLDN19)

frequency.us: Very rare in US; CLDN16/19 mutations; severe ocular involvement with CLDN19; progressive CKD
frequency.global: Very rare globally; CLDN16 more prevalent in Mediterranean; CLDN19 associated with severe macular coloboma
frequency.sources: Simon et al. Nat Genet 1999; Konrad et al. Nat Genet 2006; FHHNC Registry

diagnosis: Serum magnesium (low); urine magnesium/calcium (elevated); renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis); ophthalmology (CLDN19: coloboma); CLDN16/19 genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Magnesium supplementation — high-dose oral MgCl₂; improves symptoms but does NOT halt progression to ESKD; incomplete response due to tubular impermeability
(CLDN16/CLDN19 mutations affect tight junctions of thick ascending limb) • Thiazide diuretics — modest reduction in urinary calcium; slows nephrocalcinosis progression partially • Potassium citrate — urinary alkalinization; reduces nephrocalcinosis and stone burden • ACEi/ARBs — renoprotective; CKD management • Ophthalmological — CLDN19 mutations cause severe ocular involvement (macular coloboma, nystagmus, myopia); regular ophthalmology; CLDN16 mutations have less ocular disease • Kidney transplant — ~50% reach ESKD by adolescence/young adulthood; transplant corrects renal disease; tubular defect not present in donor kidney; excellent outcomes; Mg and Ca normalize post-transplant • Genetic counseling — CLDN16 or CLDN19 mutations; autosomal recessive; family screening

name: X-linked Hypophosphatemic Rickets (PHEX)
description: PHEX mutations causing increased FGF23 production leading to phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, and rickets; most common inherited form of rickets

frequency.us: ~1/20,000 in US; X-linked dominant; males more severely affected; most common genetic rickets in US
frequency.global: ~1/20,000 globally; highest in North America and Europe; PHEX mutations; burosumab (anti- FGF23) approved 2018
frequency.sources: HYP Consortium Nat Genet 1995; Carpenter et al. JASN 2011; Imel et al. Lancet 2019

diagnosis: Serum phosphate (low); TmP/GFR (reduced); FGF23 (elevated); ALP (elevated); PTH (normal); wrist X-ray (metaphyseal changes); PHEX genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Burosumab (Crysvita, Ultragenyx) — anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody; FDA approved for pediatric XLH ≥1 year (2018); SC injection every 2 weeks (pediatric) or every 4 weeks (adult); directly addresses pathophysiology; superior to conventional therapy for rickets healing, linear growth, phosphate normalization Methods • Oral phosphate + active vitamin D (calcitriol / alfacalcidol) — conventional therapy; still used where burosumab unavailable; inferior to burosumab but widely used in resource-limited settings; risk of nephrocalcinosis with this approach • Growth hormone — for growth failure unresponsive to phosphate/burosumab; consider in pre-pubertal patients with severe growth impairment • Orthopedic management — corrective osteotomy for severe bowing; dental care (abscesses) • ENT — hearing evaluation; ossicular involvement in some
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Setrusumab (anti-sclerostin) — Phase 2 ORBIT trial for OI; potential relevance to bone disease in XLH ▶ Long-term burosumab data in adults — maturing; transition from pediatric protocols ▶ Burosumab in pregnancy — case reports accumulating; safety data emerging ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-PHEX) — preclinical

name: Autosomal Recessive Hypophosphatemic Rickets (DMP1/ENPP1)
description: DMP1 or ENPP1 mutations causing FGF23 excess and hypophosphatemic rickets; ENPP1 mutations also cause calcification of soft tissues (GACI)

frequency.us: Very rare in US; ENPP1 mutations cause GACI in infancy transitioning to hypophosphatemia later
frequency.global: Very rare globally; DMP1 and ENPP1 mutations; GACI-to- ARHR2 phenotypic transition established
frequency.sources: Lorenz-Depiereux et al. Nat Genet 2006; Nitschke et al. Nat Genet 2012

diagnosis: Serum phosphate; FGF23 (elevated); ALP; DMP1/ENPP1 genetic testing; X-ray; vascular imaging for GACI (ENPP1)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Burosumab (Crysvita) — anti-FGF23; FDA approved for XLH (PHEX); expanding evidence base for ARHR1 (DMP1) and ARHR2 (ENPP1); use is off-label for ARHR but increasingly adopted given shared FGF23-excess pathophysiology • Oral phosphate + active vitamin D — conventional therapy for ARHR when burosumab not available/approved • ENPP1 deficiency (ARHR2) — may co-present with generalized arterial calcification of infancy (GACI); complex management
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Asfotase alfa (Strensiq) — enzyme replacement for hypophosphatasia (ALPL); different condition but relevant to mineralization; approved for hypophosphatasia including pediatric ▶ Bisphosphonates — used for GACI (ENPP1 deficiency) to reduce arterial calcification; emerging data ▶ Inositol hexaphosphate — ENPP1 substrate; may reduce PPi deficiency-related ectopic calcification; early stage ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-DMP1, AAV-ENPP1) — preclinical

name: Autosomal Dominant Hypophosphatemia (FGF23)
description: FGF23 gain-of-function mutations or KL mutations causing hypophosphatemia; milder than XLH but similar mechanism; variable penetrance

frequency.us: Rare; autosomal dominant FGF23 mutations; variable penetrance; spectrum from mild to rickets
frequency.global: Rare globally; FGF23 gain- of-function mutations; autosomal

diagnosis: Serum phosphate; FGF23 (elevated); PHEX (normal); FGF23/KL genetic testing; ALP; X-ray if symptomatic

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Burosumab (Crysvita) — anti-FGF23; FDA-approved for
XLH; off-label use in ADHR (FGF23 gain-of-function) with
same rationale; increasingly used in symptomatic ADHR

name: Tumoral Calcinosis — Hyperphosphatemic (GALNT3/FGF23/KL)
description: Loss-of-function in FGF23/KL pathway causing reduced FGF23 activity; hyperphosphatemia and ectopic calcification (tumoral calcinosis); periarticular calcium deposits

frequency.us: Very rare in US; autosomal recessive; childhood onset; deposits around large joints
frequency.global: Very rare globally; GALNT3, FGF23, and KL (klotho) mutations; higher in Arab populations; calcification deposits pathognomonic
frequency.sources: Topaz et al. Nat Genet 2004; Ichikawa et al. J Clin Invest 2007

diagnosis: Serum phosphate (elevated); FGF23 (inappropriately normal or low); TmP/GFR; genetic testing (GALNT3, FGF23, KL); X-ray; ultrasound of deposits

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Novel therapies under
investigation — anti-FGF23 agents paradoxically
contraindicated; targeted approaches in development
