name: Idiopathic Infantile Hypercalcemia (CYP24A1 / SLC34A1)
description: CYP24A1 mutations causing impaired vitamin D catabolism; SLC34A1 mutations causing phosphate transport defect; both result in hypercalcemia in infancy with nephrocalcinosis

frequency.us: Rare; ~1/30,000 in US for CYP24A1 deficiency; worsened by vitamin D supplementation
frequency.global: ~1/30,000 globally for CYP24A1 deficiency; SLC34A1 mutations cause fetal variant; ascertainment improving with genetic testing
frequency.sources: Schlingmann et al. NEJM 2011; Dinour et al. NEJM 2010; IIH Registry

diagnosis: Serum calcium (elevated); PTH (suppressed); 25-OH vitamin D; 1,25 vitamin D; CYP24A1/SLC34A1 genetic testing; renal ultrasound (nephrocalcinosis)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Fluconazole (inhibits CYP24A1
— reduces 1,25 vitamin D production) — off-label emerging
use

name: Familial Hypocalciuric Hypercalcemia (CASR)
description: Heterozygous inactivating CASR mutations causing mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia with low urine calcium; usually benign; important to distinguish from primary hyperparathyroidism

frequency.us: ~1/78,000 in US; CASR loss-of- function mutations; often incidental hypercalcemia; neonatal form severe
frequency.global: ~1/78,000 globally; FHH types 1–3 (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1); hypercalciuria low; NSHPT (homozygous) serious
frequency.sources: Pollak et al. Cell 1993; Carel et al. Eur J Endocrinol 2010; FHH International Consortium

diagnosis: Serum calcium (mildly elevated); PTH (high normal or mildly elevated); urine calcium:creatinine ratio (low — FECa <0.01); CASR genetic testing; family history of hypercalcemia

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Cinacalcet for symptomatic FHH
— off-label, emerging indication

name: Urinary Tract Infection — Febrile (first / recurrent)
description: Bacterial infection of upper urinary tract in children; important to differentiate from lower UTI; risk of renal scarring with recurrent febrile UTIs

frequency.us: ~1–3% of boys, 3–8% of girls by age 7 in US; recurrent in ~30%; most common serious bacterial infection in young children
frequency.global: ~1–3% of boys, 3–8% of girls globally; E. coli >80%; higher recurrence rates in girls; AAP and NICE guidelines
frequency.sources: Roberts & Downs Ped Rev 2005; Shaikh et al. Arch Dis Child 2016; UTI-LTF Study NEJM 2010

diagnosis: Urine dipstick (leukocyte esterase, nitrite); urine culture (catheter specimen or SPA in young children); renal ultrasound; DMSA for scarring; VCUG after first febrile UTI in young children

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Antibiotic prophylaxis for VUR —
role debated; current RIVUR and CUTIE trial guidance
informing practice

name: Pyelonephritis — Acute
description: Bacterial upper tract infection causing fever, loin pain, and renal parenchymal inflammation; risk of renal scarring and CKD

frequency.us: Common; ~5% of febrile US children <2 years; E. coli most common; DMSA scintigraphy standard
frequency.global: Common globally; prevalence varies with circumcision rates and VUR screening practice
frequency.sources: Hoberman et al. NEJM 2003; RIVUR Trial NEJM 2014; NICE UTI Guidelines 2007

diagnosis: Urine culture; blood culture if systemically unwell; DMSA scan (2–3 months after episode for scarring); renal/bladder ultrasound; inflammatory markers

treatment.standardOfCare: • IV antibiotics (inpatient) — for: infants <3 months, ill- appearing, vomiting, urosepsis; ceftriaxone or ampicillin- gentamicin; oral step-down after 48–72 hours of afebrile clinical improvement • Oral antibiotics (outpatient) — for older children without systemic illness; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or cephalosporins; 10–14 days total; culture-guided • E. coli most common — gram-negative coverage essential; adjust when culture sensitivities return • Imaging — renal ultrasound at diagnosis or during admission; VCUG at 4–6 weeks post-fever to evaluate for VUR in children <2 years or recurrent UTI; DMSA scan 4– 6 months post-APN for renal scar detection • Fever management — antipyretics; assess for urosepsis; blood cultures if febrile and ill-appearing • Antibiotic prophylaxis — for VUR if detected on post-APN workup; evidence-based per 2011 AAP guidelines • AAP 2011 guideline — recommends VCUG only for febrile UTI with abnormal renal ultrasound; revised 2017 to expand back to all febrile UTI <2 yr; culture-confirmed UTI required before workup

name: Xanthogranulomatous Pyelonephritis
description: Rare chronic renal infection with granulomatous destruction of renal parenchyma; associated with staghorn calculi, obstruction, and Proteus/E. coli infection; mimics renal tumor

frequency.us: Rare in US children; ~1.4% of renal infections; <200 pediatric cases reported
frequency.global: Rare globally; <200 total pediatric cases in literature; mimics renal mass; Proteus most common pathogen
frequency.sources: Kim et al. J Urol 2001; Loffroy et al. Eur Radiol 2007

diagnosis: Renal imaging (CT: characteristic appearance with enlarged kidney containing 'bear paw' calculi and hypodense areas); urine culture; surgical pathology (foamy macrophages, lipid- laden)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Nephrectomy — definitive treatment; XGP is a destructive chronic granulomatous infection; kidney rarely salvageable; open or laparoscopic nephrectomy; specimen reveals staghorn calculus, pus, xanthoma cells (lipid-laden macrophages) • Antibiotics — preoperative and postoperative; treat Proteus, E. coli, Pseudomonas (most common organisms); 4–6 weeks of antibiotics peri-operatively; fluoroquinolones or culture-directed therapy • Percutaneous drainage — for abscess or perinephric involvement; temporizing before surgery Methods • Diagnose staghorn calculus — almost universal trigger; struvite stones; obstruction • Imaging — CT abdomen/pelvis preferred; demonstrates "bear paw sign" (multiple renal abscesses) • Fistula management — if XGP fistulizes to bowel or retroperitoneum; complex surgical repair

name: Renal Abscess — Pediatric
description: Focal bacterial infection forming purulent collection within renal parenchyma or perinephric space; may follow UTI or hematogenous spread

frequency.us: Rare in US children; ~1–2% of serious UTIs; S. aureus hematogenous; gram-negative rods ascending
frequency.global: Rare globally; structural anomalies major predisposing factor; S. aureus and gram- negatives predominant pathogens
frequency.sources: Coelho et al. J Urol 2007; Mangat & Nagler Ped Nephrol 2012

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (hypoechoic collection); CT (ring-enhancing lesion); urine and blood cultures; urinalysis; inflammatory markers

treatment.standardOfCare: • IV antibiotics — empirical broad-spectrum (cefazolin or ceftriaxone ± metronidazole for anaerobes); culture- guided adjustment; Staphylococcus aureus, gram- negative enteric organisms; 4–6 weeks total antibiotics • Percutaneous drainage (interventional radiology) — for abscesses ≥3 cm; CT-guided drainage; relieves obstruction and obtains culture specimen; most can be managed without surgery • Surgical drainage — for: failed percutaneous drainage, multiloculated abscess, perinephric extension, necrotizing fasciitis; open or laparoscopic • Blood cultures — bacteremia common; IV antibiotics until defervescence then oral step-down • Identify predisposing factors — VUR, urinary obstruction, instrumentation, skin infection hematogenous seeding (S. aureus), immunosuppression, diabetes • Imaging — ultrasound for initial diagnosis; CT for staging and drainage guidance; repeat imaging at 48–72 hours to assess treatment response

name: Schistosomiasis — Renal
description: Schistosoma haematobium infection causing obstructive uropathy, bladder fibrosis, hydronephrosis, and renal impairment; endemic in Africa and Middle East

frequency.us: Rare in US (no endemic S. haematobium); occurs in immigrants from endemic regions
frequency.global: ~200 million worldwide affected; S. haematobium causes urogenital schistosomiasis; endemic in Africa, Middle East
frequency.sources: Colley et al. Lancet 2014; WHO Schistosomiasis data 2022; Kjetland et al. Lancet Infect Dis 2012

diagnosis: Urine microscopy (terminal hematuria, S. haematobium eggs); serology; renal and bladder ultrasound (thickened bladder wall, hydronephrosis); cystoscopy for bladder disease

treatment.standardOfCare: • Praziquantel — drug of choice; curative for active Schistosoma haematobium infection; 40 mg/kg/day divided in 2 doses × 1 day; kills adult worms; highly effective; repeat dose at 4–6 weeks • Prevention of secondary infection — education; avoid freshwater exposure in endemic areas • Surgical management — for obstructive uropathy (ureteral fibrosis, bladder contracture, uretero-vesical junction obstruction); ureteral reimplantation; bladder augmentation; ureterolysis • Bladder carcinoma surveillance — S. haematobium carcinogen; squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder risk in chronic infection; cystoscopy in adults with long history; not routine in pediatric acute infection • Kidney involvement — glomerulonephritis from immune complex deposition; S. mansoni more commonly causes glomerulonephritis; ACEi/ARBs for proteinuria; CKD monitoring • World Health Organization (WHO) mass drug administration programs — praziquantel preventive

name: Renal Tuberculosis — Pediatric
description: Hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis to kidneys; typically presents years after primary infection with frequency, hematuria, pyuria, and progressive renal destruction

frequency.us: Rare in US children due to low TB burden; primarily in immigrant/refugee populations
frequency.global: Significant in high-TB-burden regions; renal TB in ~4–8% of pulmonary TB; endemic in South Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa
frequency.sources: Global TB Report WHO 2022; Abbara & Davidson Nat Rev Urol 2011

diagnosis: Urine TB culture (early morning specimens ×3); TB PCR (urine); renal ultrasound/CT (cavitation, calcification); chest X-ray; Mantoux/IGRA; IVU (calyceal destruction)

name: BK Virus Nephropathy (non-transplant)
description: BK polyomavirus reactivation causing tubulointerstitial nephritis in immunocompromised non- transplant patients (primary immunodeficiency, chemotherapy, HIV)

frequency.us: Rare outside transplant or immunocompromised settings in US; increasing recognition in chemotherapy patients
frequency.global: Rare globally outside transplant; primary BKV infection nearly universal; nephropathy requires immunosuppression
frequency.sources: Hirsch et al. NEJM 2002; Randhawa & Khaleel Virchows Arch 2004

diagnosis: Urine BK virus PCR (>7 log copies/mL suggests nephropathy); serum BK PCR; kidney biopsy (BK virus inclusions, tubulitis); urine decoy cells (screening)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Cidofovir (use with extreme
caution — nephrotoxic); brincidofovir — investigational

name: COVID-19 / MIS-C- associated Nephropathy — Pediatric
description: Kidney involvement in COVID-19 (AKI, collapsing FSGS) and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) with TMA, AKI, hypovolemia

frequency.us: ~5–10% of hospitalized pediatric COVID-19 have AKI in US; MIS-C ~1/3,000–4,000 infected; renal in 60–70% of MIS-C
frequency.global: ~5–10% globally; MIS-C rates similar across high-income countries; renal involvement in 60– 70% of MIS-C cases
frequency.sources: Feldstein et al. NEJM 2020; Götzinger et al. Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2020; CDC MIS-C surveillance

diagnosis: Urinalysis; creatinine; AKI staging; SARS-CoV-2 PCR/serology; inflammatory markers (ferritin, CRP, IL-6); MIS-C diagnostic criteria; TMA screen for severe cases; kidney biopsy if proteinuria persists

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Biologics (anakinra, infliximab)
for refractory MIS-C — emerging use

name: AKI — Sepsis-associated
description: Acute kidney injury caused by sepsis-induced hemodynamic compromise, endothelial injury, and inflammatory mediators; most common AKI cause in PICU

frequency.us: ~10–15% of PICU patients in US; AKI in ~30–50% of septic shock; S. aureus and gram- negatives predominant
frequency.global: ~30–50% globally in septic shock; consistent rates in high- income country ICUs; mortality increases 2–8× with AKI
frequency.sources: Symons et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2007; Goldstein & Devarajan Ped Nephrol 2011

diagnosis: Serum creatinine (KDIGO staging); urine output; blood and urine cultures; inflammatory markers; urinalysis; renal ultrasound; novel biomarkers (NGAL, KIM-1)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Furosemide continuous infusion
for fluid management — role refined by SPARK/FISST trials Methods

name: AKI — Nephrotoxin- induced
description: AKI caused by direct tubular toxicity from drugs or contrast agents; aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast media, NSAIDs, and chemotherapy most common in children

frequency.us: ~20–30% of pediatric AKI in US; aminoglycosides ~10% of hospital-acquired AKI; vancomycin toxicity increasing
frequency.global: ~20–30% globally in pediatric AKI cohorts; drug exposure varies by local antimicrobial patterns
frequency.sources: Schneider et al. JASN 2010; Blowey et al. Ped Nephrol 2019; Goldstein nephrotoxin score 2011

diagnosis: Creatinine trend after drug exposure; urinalysis (granular casts in ATN); drug levels (aminoglycosides, vancomycin); novel biomarkers (NGAL, KIM-1, TIMP-2×IGFBP7); renal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • Identify and discontinue nephrotoxin — IMMEDIATE; aminoglycosides, vancomycin, NSAIDs, contrast agents, cisplatin, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors, acyclovir, tenofovir; most important intervention • IV fluid resuscitation — maintain renal perfusion; avoid over-hydration; goal: normovolemia; urine output ≥0.5–1 mL/kg/hr • Drug level monitoring — aminoglycoside peak/trough; vancomycin AUC-guided dosing (2019 consensus recommends AUC-guided over trough monitoring to reduce nephrotoxicity); adjust dosing interval for reduced renal function • Alternative antibiotics — aztreonam or cephalosporins instead of aminoglycosides; rifamycins instead of vancomycin when possible; isolate sensitivities • Contrast-associated AKI prevention — IV pre-hydration with NS or sodium bicarbonate; N-acetylcysteine (controversial; reasonable in high-risk patients); low- osmolar/iso-osmolar contrast; minimize contrast volume • Cisplatin nephroprotection — aggressive IV hydration pre- and post-cisplatin; magnesium supplementation (cisplatin causes Mg wasting); sodium thiosulfate (cytoprotective); PREVENT with high diuresis Emerging ▶ Sodium thiosulfate — nephroprotection with cisplatin; Phase 3 data in pediatric oncology (Children's Oncology Group ACCL1031); reduces cisplatin-induced hearing loss AND nephrotoxicity

name: AKI — Ischemic / Hypoxic (cardiac surgery, birth asphyxia)
description: AKI from renal hypoperfusion during cardiac surgery (on-pump procedures), birth asphyxia, or severe hypovolemia; tubular injury from ischemia- reperfusion

frequency.us: ~30–40% of post-cardiac surgery US children; ~60–70% with severe birth asphyxia/HIE; high AKI mortality
frequency.global: Consistent globally; post- cardiac surgery AKI rates ~40% across international registries; HIE- associated AKI similar
frequency.sources: Sethi et al. J Am Heart Assoc 2017; Askenazi et al. Ped Nephrol 2019; TOBY Trial HIE data

diagnosis: Creatinine and urine output post-operatively or post- asphyxia; KDIGO staging; urinalysis; renal Doppler ultrasound; novel biomarkers (urine NGAL)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Mild therapeutic hypothermia for
HIE — not contraindicated; neonatal RenalGuard and
delayed cord clamping under study

name: Cortical Necrosis — Neonatal
description: Irreversible ischemic necrosis of renal cortex in neonates; caused by severe birth asphyxia, septic shock, or DIC; leads to permanent renal insufficiency

frequency.us: Rare; ~2% of neonatal AKI in US; bilateral leads to ESKD; devastating outcomes
frequency.global: Rare globally; bilateral cortical necrosis most often from perinatal asphyxia and renal vein thrombosis
frequency.sources: Lerner et al. Pediatrics 1992; Askenazi et al. Ped Nephrol 2019

diagnosis: Renal ultrasound (echogenic cortex, loss of corticomedullary differentiation); CT (cortical enhancement loss); DMSA scan (no function); creatinine; coagulation studies

treatment.standardOfCare: • Supportive care — primarily palliative/supportive; cortical necrosis represents irreversible ischemic destruction of renal cortex; prognosis guarded • Renal replacement therapy — acute dialysis (peritoneal dialysis in neonates) for severe AKI; bridge to recovery if partial cortical injury Methods • IV fluids and vasopressors — manage underlying cause (septic shock, severe asphyxia, severe dehydration); restore perfusion pressure • Treat underlying cause — maternal placental abruption, HUS, severe birth asphyxia, septicemia • Anticoagulation — renal vein thrombosis as comorbidity; heparin if thrombosis identified and clinical stability permits • Long-term monitoring — partial cortical necrosis may result in CKD; hypertension; renal function surveillance throughout childhood; ACEi/ARBs if hypertension/proteinuria develops

name: Renal Vein Thrombosis — Neonatal
description: Thrombosis of renal vein in neonates; presents with hematuria, renal mass, and thrombocytopenia; risk factors include dehydration, sepsis, maternal diabetes, polycythemia

frequency.us: ~2.2/100,000 live births in US; most common neonatal vascular emergency; left kidney more common
frequency.global: ~2.2/100,000 globally; consistent data from neonatal registries; thrombophilia screen and maternal conditions key
frequency.sources: Zigman et al. Arch Dis Child 2000; Schmidt et al. Ped Nephrol 2004

diagnosis: Renal Doppler ultrasound (absent venous flow, enlarged kidney); CT/MRI angiography; blood count (thrombocytopenia); coagulation studies; thrombophilia screen

treatment.standardOfCare: • Anticoagulation — LMWH (low-molecular-weight heparin: enoxaparin) for non-bilateral RVT without significant hemorrhage; duration 6–12 weeks minimum; CHEST 2012/2018 and ASH 2018 guidelines recommend therapeutic anticoagulation for bilateral RVT or unilateral RVT extending into IVC • Supportive care — hydration; electrolyte correction; blood transfusion for severe hemorrhagic anemia; dialysis if renal failure • Conservative observation — for unilateral RVT without IVC extension in stable neonate; monitor with serial ultrasound • Systemic thrombolytics (tPA) — for life-threatening bilateral RVT with massive renal failure; use cautiously given neonatal bleeding risk; specialist consultation • Serial renal ultrasound with Doppler — monitoring for thrombus resolution; assess renal blood flow recovery • Long-term monitoring — renal atrophy common; CKD risk; hypertension; annual BP, urinalysis, creatinine through childhood

name: Renal Vein Thrombosis — Non-neonatal Pediatric
description: Renal vein thrombosis in older children; usually associated with nephrotic syndrome, hypercoagulable states, dehydration, or central venous catheters

frequency.us: Uncommon in US; mostly in nephrotic syndrome (especially membranous) and Factor V Leiden thrombophilia
frequency.global: Uncommon globally; hypercoagulable states major risk; nephrotic syndrome patients at highest risk
frequency.sources: Llach et al. Ann Intern Med 1980; Kerlin et al. Blood 2003

diagnosis: Renal Doppler ultrasound; CT/MRI venography; thrombophilia screen (protein C/S, antithrombin, APLA, Factor V Leiden); coagulation studies; urinalysis

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Thrombolysis for massive
bilateral RVT with AKI — limited pediatric data

name: Renal Artery Thrombosis — Neonatal / Catheter-associated
description: Thrombosis of renal artery from umbilical arterial catheter positioning at aortic bifurcation; also from polycythemia, hypercoagulable states; causes renovascular hypertension

frequency.us: ~3–5% of UAC placements develop aortic/renal thrombosis in US NICUs; majority asymptomatic

diagnosis: Renal Doppler ultrasound; CT/MRI arteriography; blood pressure monitoring; DMSA scan (differential function); thrombophilia screen; UAC position review

treatment.standardOfCare:
• Remove umbilical artery catheter — immediate; UAC-
associated RAT accounts for majority of neonatal cases;

name: Hepatorenal Syndrome — Pediatric
description: Functional AKI in children with severe hepatic failure; intense renal vasoconstriction without structural kidney injury; reversible if liver recovers or transplant performed

frequency.us: Uncommon in US; complicates severe liver failure from biliary atresia, acute liver failure, cirrhosis
frequency.global: Uncommon globally; pathophysiology involves arterial vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction; liver transplant definitive treatment
frequency.sources: Ginès et al. NEJM 2009; Nayar & Bhardwaj Ped Gastroenterol 2019

diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis: AKI in setting of liver failure + ascites; exclude hypovolemia (fluid challenge); urine sodium (<10 mEq/L); creatinine; liver function tests; renal Doppler (normal)

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Liver transplant (definitive —
resolves HRS); midodrine + octreotide as bridge where
terlipressin unavailable

name: Neonatal AKI (NAKI) — Prematurity-associated
description: AKI in premature neonates from immature nephron development, reduced GFR, and frequent exposure to nephrotoxins, hemodynamic compromise, and infection

frequency.us: ~30% of VLBW infants in US; AKI in ~18% of all NICU admissions; independent predictor of CKD in adulthood
frequency.global: ~30% of VLBW infants globally; consistent rates across high-income country NICUs; adult CKD risk from neonatal nephron endowment deficit
frequency.sources: Jetton et al. NEJM 2017 (AWAKEN study); Askenazi et al. CJASN 2011; Selewski et al. Ped Nephrol 2019

diagnosis: Modified neonatal KDIGO staging (serum creatinine + urine output); serial creatinine trend (accounts for maternal creatinine at birth); urinalysis; renal Doppler ultrasound; novel biomarkers (NGAL, KIM-1)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Diagnose using neonatal-specific criteria — serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL rise in 48 hours, OR ≥1.5× reference SCr rise, OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for >6 hours; cord blood creatinine as baseline for first 24–48 hr • Treat underlying cause — sepsis (antibiotics, vasopressors), asphyxia (therapeutic hypothermia), hemodynamic instability (fluids, inotropes), nephrotoxin removal • IV fluid optimization — normovolemia; avoid both dehydration and fluid overload; fluid overload independently worsens outcomes • Diuretics (furosemide) — for volume overload only; does NOT convert oliguric to non-oliguric AKI; does NOT improve outcomes; use for fluid management only Methods • Dopamine — low-dose "renal dose" dopamine NOT proven effective in neonates; not routinely recommended • Peritoneal dialysis — treatment of choice for NAKI requiring RRT; access and circuit; flexible volume removal; safe in small neonates • Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) — increasingly available for NAKU in NICUs; higher-volume clearance; specialized circuits for neonates (<3 kg challenging) • Drug dosing adjustment — pharmacokinetics altered in neonatal AKI; dose all renally cleared drugs per eGFR • Long-term follow-up — NAKI survivors have elevated CKD and HTN risk; annual BP and urinalysis surveillance recommended per Neonatal Kidney Collaborative

name: Neonatal Hypertension
description: Blood pressure >95th percentile for corrected gestational age in neonate; often secondary to renovascular disease (UAC), CLD, PDA ligation, renal anomalies, or medications

frequency.us: ~0.2–3% of US NICU patients; higher in premature infants; UAC most common cause in preterm
frequency.global: ~0.2–3% globally in NICU; consistent rates in Western neonatal registries; echocardiographic assessment recommended
frequency.sources: Dionne et al. Pediatrics 2012; Blowey et al. Ped Nephrol 2011; Neonatal HTN Consensus 2017

diagnosis: Accurate blood pressure measurement (oscillometric + Doppler confirmation); renal Doppler ultrasound; renal function; catecholamines (exclude pheochromocytoma); drug history; echocardiogram

treatment.standardOfCare: • Identify and treat underlying cause — renovascular (UAC- associated RAT, renal artery stenosis), CKD, renal parenchymal disease, coarctation, volume overload, pheochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, medication- related (steroids, pressors, caffeine) • Antihypertensive pharmacotherapy — infants have limited medication options; first-line agents: - Isradipine — calcium channel blocker; oral or NG; first-line for most neonatal HTN; 0.05–0.15 mg/kg/dose q6–8h - Amlodipine — CCB; longer duration; oral; convenient once/twice daily - Hydralazine IV — acute management; vasodilator; IV bolus - Esmolol / labetalol IV — for hypertensive urgency; titratable - Captopril / enalaprilat — ACEi; USE WITH EXTREME CAUTION in neonates; risk of acute oliguric AKI; neonatal kidneys highly RAS-dependent; avoid in first month of life or bilateral RAS • Remove umbilical artery catheter — if RAT/renovascular cause • Serial BP monitoring — oscillometric per limb; confirm with Doppler; target BP <95th percentile for gestational and postnatal age • Echocardiogram — assess LVH, PDA, coarctation; cardiomegaly as marker of severity

name: Oligohydramnios — Renal Cause
description: Reduced amniotic fluid from impaired fetal urine production; caused by bilateral renal agenesis, severe bilateral obstruction (PUV), or ARPKD; leads to pulmonary hypoplasia

frequency.us: ~0.5–1% of US pregnancies have oligohydramnios; renal causes ~15–20% of all oligohydramnios
frequency.global: ~0.5–1% of pregnancies globally; renal agenesis and LUTO predominant renal causes; prognosis based on residual renal function
frequency.sources: Chamberlain et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol 1984; Shipp et al. AJOG 1996

diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound (AFI, renal evaluation); fetal MRI; amnioinfusion (therapeutic and diagnostic); genetic evaluation; postnatal renal ultrasound and function assessment

treatment.emerging:
Emerging/Investigational: Serial amnioinfusion —
experimental (may improve pulmonary development) Methods

name: Fabry Disease — Renal (GLA)
description: X-linked lysosomal storage disorder (alpha- galactosidase A deficiency) causing glycosphingolipid accumulation; proteinuria, CKD, and cardiomyopathy in males; later onset in females

frequency.us: ~1/40,000–117,000 in US; X- linked; classic males severely affected; females increasingly recognized
frequency.global: ~1/40,000–117,000 globally; higher in Sardinia (1/1,400); X- linked; female carriers ~50% symptomatic
frequency.sources: Eng et al. NEJM 2001; Schiffmann JASN 2009; Fabry Registry International data

diagnosis: Alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity (low in males); GLA genetic testing; lyso-Gb3 (sensitive biomarker); kidney biopsy (zebra bodies on EM, podocyte inclusions); echocardiogram; MRI brain

treatment.standardOfCare: • Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT): - Agalsidase beta (Fabrazyme, Sanofi) — FDA approved 2003; 1.0 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks; approved for adults and children ≥2 years - Agalsidase alfa (Replagal, Takeda) — 0.2 mg/kg IV every 2 weeks; approved in Europe/internationally; NOT FDA-approved in US; available via compassionate use - Pegunigalsidase alfa (Elfabrio, Chiesi/Protalix) — PEGylated ERT; FDA approved May 2023 for adults; reduced immunogenicity; prolonged half-life; BALANCE Phase 3 trial vs. agalsidase beta • Migalastat (Galafold, Amicus) — oral pharmacological chaperone; FDA approved Aug 2018 for adults (≥18 yr) with amenable GLA variants; stabilizes endogenous α-Gal A; ASPIRE Phase 3b trial (2025) confirms safety/efficacy in adolescents 12–17 yr with amenable variants — pediatric regulatory approval expected • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — for proteinuria; standard regardless of ERT/chaperone status • Pain management (gabapentin, carbamazepine, pregabalin) — for neuropathic pain/acroparesthesias • Renal transplant — for ESKD; does not cure systemic disease
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Gene therapy (4D-310, ST-920, FLT190) — AAV- mediated in vivo GLA gene delivery; Phase 1/2 trials ongoing ▶ Substrate reduction therapy (venglustat, lucerastat) — reduces GL-3 synthesis; Phase 2/3 trials; oral administration advantage ▶ Chaperone + ERT combination — investigational for non- amenable or partially amenable variants ▶ Next-gen ERT biosimilars — in development globally

name: Glycogen Storage Disease Type Ia — Renal (G6PC)
description: G6PC mutations causing hepatic glycogen accumulation; renal involvement from glycogen deposition, FSGS, and progressive CKD in second decade

frequency.us: ~1/100,000 in US; GSD Ia most common GSD; renal involvement in >75%; hypercalciuria and proteinuria by adolescence
frequency.global: ~1/100,000 globally; G6PC mutations; GSD Ia distribution worldwide; renal FSGS-like lesions; dietary treatment cornerstone
frequency.sources: Weinstein et al. Nat Genet 2000; Chen JASN 1991; GSD Ia Registry data

diagnosis: Genetic testing (G6PC); kidney biopsy (glycogen deposition, FSGS); urinalysis (proteinuria); urine calcium; eGFR; hepatic imaging; liver biopsy

treatment.standardOfCare: • Continuous glucose supplementation — cornerstone; uncooked cornstarch (oral); continuous nasogastric feeds overnight in infants; glycemic control prevents secondary complications including renal disease • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — for proteinuria; slows nephropathy progression • Allopurinol — for hyperuricemia (secondary to glucose-6- phosphate accumulation) • Low-fat diet — reduces hyperlipidemia; reduces hepatic steatosis Methods • Citrate supplementation — if renal stone risk (lactic aciduria and hypocitraturia) • Liver transplant — corrects metabolic defect; secondary prevention of renal complications; used for liver failure, HCC, or extreme metabolic instability
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — emerging evidence for renal protection in GSD Ia; reduces glomerular hyperfiltration and proteinuria; off-label use in adolescents being studied ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-G6PC) — Phase 3 STEADFAST trial (AT-307, Ultragenyx); monthly SC injection showed normalization of glucose in fasted patients; potential to eliminate cornstarch dependence; most advanced genetic therapy for GSD Ia ▶ mRNA therapy (mRNA-3745, Moderna) — Phase 1/2; hepatic G6PC delivery ▶ Hepatocyte transplantation — bridge to liver transplant; limited centers

name: Methylmalonic Acidemia — Renal (MMUT)
description: MUT/MMAB/MMAA mutations causing methylmalonic acid accumulation; CKD from tubulointerstitial injury is major long-term complication even after hepatic-renal transplant

frequency.us: ~1/80,000–100,000 in US; MMA; renal failure in >60% by adulthood; mut0 genotype worst prognosis
frequency.global: ~1/80,000–100,000 globally; mut0 (MMUT deficiency) and CblA/CblB types; ESKD major morbidity; liver/kidney transplant improves metabolic control
frequency.sources: Hörster et al. JIMD 2007; Baumgartner et al. Ped Nephrol 2014; MMA Natural History Study

diagnosis: Urine methylmalonic acid (markedly elevated); plasma amino acids; ammonia; renal function (progressive CKD); kidney biopsy (interstitial fibrosis); MMUT genetic testing

treatment.standardOfCare: • Low protein diet — limits propionate precursor amino acids (isoleucine, valine, threonine, methionine) • L-carnitine supplementation — conjugates toxic propionylcarnitine; facilitates urinary excretion • RAAS blockade — for proteinuria/CKD progression • Vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin, high-dose IM) — for B12-responsive forms (cblA, cblB subtypes); limited effect in isolated MMUT deficiency • Metabolic crisis management — IV glucose, carnitine; protein restriction during illness; avoid catabolism • Dialysis — for severe metabolic crises (removes MMA acutely) • Combined liver-kidney transplant — liver transplant reduces MMA production significantly; kidney transplant for ESKD; combined approach addresses both organ failure and partially corrects metabolic defect
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ mRNA therapy (mRNA-3705, Moderna) — encoding MMUT; Phase 2 trials; monthly IV infusion; reduces plasma MMA; potential to prevent long-term organ complications ▶ Propionate scavenging approaches (NKTT320) — reduces systemic propionate load; early stage ▶ Gene therapy (AAV-MMUT) — Phase 1/2 studies; selective hepatic expression; preclinical data promising ▶ Renal-specific approaches — mitochondrial targeted antioxidants for tubular protection Methods

name: Mitochondrial Nephropathy (MELAS / Pearson / CoQ10 deficiency)
description: Mitochondrial DNA or nuclear gene mutations causing renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi, RTA) or glomerulosclerosis as part of multisystem mitochondrial disease

frequency.us: ~1/5,000–10,000 for all mitochondrial disease in US; renal in ~20–30%; CoQ10 deficiency treatable
frequency.global: ~1/5,000–10,000 globally for mitochondrial disease; renal involvement variable by syndrome; MELAS, Pearson, MERRF each affect kidneys differently
frequency.sources: Menezes et al. Ped Nephrol 2012; MELAS Consortium; Rötig et al. Nat Genet 1990

diagnosis: Urinalysis (tubular dysfunction markers); plasma lactate; muscle biopsy (mitochondrial morphology); mitochondrial DNA analysis; nuclear gene panel; respiratory chain enzyme activity; renal biopsy

treatment.standardOfCare: • CoQ10 supplementation — dramatically effective for primary CoQ10 biosynthesis defects (ADCK4/COQ6/COQ2/PDSS2 mutations); less effective for respiratory chain complex disorders • L-carnitine — for secondary carnitine deficiency; mitochondrial energy support • Thiamine (vitamin B1) — for PDHC deficiency subtype; complex I-related • Riboflavin (vitamin B2) — for complex I/II deficiency; riboflavin-responsive MADD • Avoid mitochondrial toxins — metformin (complex I inhibitor), valproate, aminoglycosides, NSAIDs • Renal transplant — for ESKD; metabolic disease continues in transplanted kidney if not CoQ10-responsive; select carefully • Supportive management — electrolytes, Fanconi syndrome management (phosphate, bicarbonate, potassium)
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ KL1333 — NAD+ precursor; Phase 2 trials in mitochondrial myopathy ▶ Bezafibrate — PPAR-γ agonist; promotes mitochondrial biogenesis; clinical trials ongoing in MELAS ▶ Elamipretide (SS-31) — mitochondrial membrane peptide; Phase 2/3 trials in Barth syndrome and cardiac mitochondrial disease ▶ Gene therapy for specific respiratory chain defects — highly early stage; limited by heteroplasmy ▶ mRNA-based mitochondrial gene delivery — investigational

name: Wilson Disease — Renal Tubular (ATP7B)
description: ATP7B mutations causing copper accumulation in liver, brain, and kidneys; renal manifestations include Fanconi syndrome, hematuria, and nephrolithiasis

frequency.us: ~1/30,000 in US; AR; renal tubular disease common with liver disease; Kayser-Fleischer rings pathognomonic
frequency.global: ~1/30,000 globally; ATP7B mutations; most common in Sardinia (1/7,000) and some Asian populations; copper chelation treatment
frequency.sources: Bull et al. Nat Genet 1993; European Wilson Disease Study Group 2012; EAU/EASL Guidelines

diagnosis: Serum ceruloplasmin (low); 24-hour urine copper (elevated); slit-lamp (Kayser- Fleischer rings); liver biopsy (copper quantification); ATP7B genetic testing; urine amino acids if Fanconi suspected

treatment.standardOfCare: • D-Penicillamine — copper chelating agent; traditional first- line treatment; removes copper; urinary copper monitoring confirms response; maintenance 10–20 mg/kg/day; significant adverse effects (proteinuria, lupus-like, aplastic anemia — rare); most frequently initiated treatment historically • Trientine (triethylenetetramine) — copper chelator; first- line alternative to D-penicillamine; better tolerated; fewer autoimmune adverse effects; FDA approved; increasingly preferred over D-penicillamine • Trientine tetrahydrochloride (Cuvrior) — FDA approved 2022 for Wilson disease in adults; tablet formulation; more stable than trientine HCl; expanding to pediatric use • Zinc acetate (Galzin) — blocks intestinal copper absorption; approved for maintenance phase and Methods presymptomatic patients; first-line for presymptomatic or maintenance after initial chelation; generally safest • Combination therapy — chelator + zinc for severe initial disease; then zinc alone for maintenance • Liver transplant — for fulminant hepatic failure, decompensated cirrhosis unresponsive to chelation; normalizes copper metabolism; renal Fanconi syndrome resolves post-transplant • Renal Fanconi syndrome management — bicarbonate, phosphate, potassium supplementation during active copper-driven tubular injury; resolves with chelation therapy • Dietary copper restriction — avoid shellfish, nuts, chocolate, liver; cooking in copper pots Emerging ▶ Bis-choline tetrathiomolybdate (WTX101/ALXN1840) — hepatic copper chelator; Phase 3 trials for neurological Wilson; reduces copper rapidly; promising for neurological disease ▶ Gene therapy (AAV8-ATP7B) — hepatocyte-targeted; corrects copper metabolism; Phase 1/2 trials (GATEWAY trial, Passage Bio); early results

name: Sickle Cell Nephropathy
description: Renal complications of sickle cell disease including hyposthenuria, hematuria, papillary necrosis, FSGS, and progressive CKD from repeated sickling-ischemia cycles

frequency.us: ~1/500 African Americans; ~8% of US Black children carry HbS gene; renal involvement universal in SCD
frequency.global: ~1/1,000–1,500 in some African populations; highest burden in Sub-Saharan Africa; microalbuminuria from early childhood
frequency.sources: Powars et al. NEJM 1991; Ataga et al. JASN 2019; SCD Nephropathy Consensus 2015

diagnosis: Urinalysis (microhematuria, proteinuria); urine osmolality (low — hyposthenuria); eGFR; kidney biopsy (FSGS in proteinuric cases); urine protein:creatinine; renal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • Hydroxyurea — increases HbF; reduces sickling; reduces proteinuria and hyperfiltration; slows nephropathy progression; recommended for all moderate-severe SCD including SS and Sβ0 • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — for proteinuria and microalbuminuria; initiated when UACR ≥30 mg/g • L-glutamine (Endari) — FDA approved Jul 2017 for SCD ≥5 yr; reduces oxidative stress; reduces acute pain crises • Renal transplant — for ESKD; acceptable outcomes; sickle cell in allograft can occur in non-SS donor kidneys (screen donors) • Crizanlizumab (Adakveo, Novartis) — anti-P-selectin; FDA approved Nov 2019; reduces vaso-occlusive crises; renal microvascular benefit theoretical FDA-Approved Gene Therapies (December 2023): • Exagamglogene autotemcel / exa-cel (Casgevy, Vertex/CRISPR Therapeutics) — CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing; FDA approved Dec 8, 2023 for SCD (SS and Sβ0) ≥12 yr with recurrent VOCs; reactivates HbF via BCL11A erythroid enhancer disruption; ~90%+ free of severe VOC in trials; potentially curative; one-time treatment • Lovotibeglogene autotemcel / lovo-cel (Lyfgenia, bluebird bio) — lentiviral gene therapy; FDA approved Dec 8, 2023 for SCD ≥12 yr with VOC history; encodes anti-sickling HbAT87Q; 88% complete resolution of VOC events in trials; potentially curative Methods Note: Gene therapies require myeloablative conditioning (busulfan); significant infrastructure needed; risks include infertility and secondary malignancy monitoring; accessible at select specialized centers
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Voxelotor (Oxbryta) — HbS polymerization inhibitor; FDA approved Nov 2019 (VOLUNTARY WITHDRAWAL by Pfizer Sept 2024 due to mortality signal in Phase 3 trial — no longer available); removed from market ▶ Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (allogeneic) — curative for matched sibling donors; increasing use of haploidentical protocols ▶ Mitapivat — pyruvate kinase activator; reduces sickling; Phase 3 trials ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — renal hemodynamic effects; early trials in SCD nephropathy ▶ Omidubicel — enhanced cord blood transplant; Phase 3 for SCD

name: Diabetic Nephropathy — Type 1, Pediatric Onset
description: Progressive CKD from glomerular hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion, and glomerulosclerosis in children/adolescents with long-standing T1DM; microalbuminuria is early marker

frequency.us: ~1/300–500 US youth have T1DM; microalbuminuria in ~8–25% after 10 years; macroproteinuria in minority during childhood
frequency.global: ~1/300–500 in high-income countries; lower in developing countries; microalbuminuria risk factors include HbA1c and duration
frequency.sources: DCCT/EDIC Research Group NEJM 1993; T1D Exchange Registry; IDF Diabetes Atlas 2021

diagnosis: Annual urine albumin:creatinine ratio (from 5 years diabetes duration or age 11); eGFR; blood pressure; HbA1c; lipids; ophthalmic screening (retinopathy correlates with nephropathy)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Optimal glycemic control — HbA1c <7% (ISPAD target); continuous glucose monitoring; insulin pump; most powerful intervention for nephropathy prevention and progression • RAAS blockade — ACEi/ARB first-line when UACR ≥30 mg/g (microalbuminuria) or elevated blood pressure; slows progression • Blood pressure control — target <90th percentile for age; RAAS blockade preferred • Lipid management — statins for adolescents with dyslipidemia • Lifestyle modification — low-sodium diet, weight management, smoking avoidance
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — growing evidence in adolescents; empagliflozin (Jardiance) FDA approved for adult CKD Sept 2023; dapagliflozin approved for adults; pediatric trials (BUTTERFLY, DERIVE-KIDS) underway; off-label use in motivated adolescents with T1D microalbuminuria at some centers ▶ Finerenone (Kerendia, Bayer) — non-steroidal MRA; Phase 3 FIDELITY-DM1 trial for T1D nephropathy; cardiorenal benefits in T2D (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO- DKD); T1D-specific data pending ▶ GLP-1 receptor agonists — semaglutide injectable FDA approved Jan 2025 for CKD in adults with T2D (not T1D); T1D renal data limited but mechanisms of renal protection relevant Methods ▶ Atrasentan (endothelin A antagonist) — Phase 3 trials in diabetic kidney disease ▶ Sparsentan — DUPLEX trial includes T2D; T1D interest growing

name: Obesity-related Glomerulopathy — Pediatric
description: Glomerular hyperfiltration and glomerulomegaly from obesity-driven hemodynamic changes; presents with proteinuria and mild microhematuria; can progress to FSGS

frequency.us: Increasing incidence in US with childhood obesity epidemic; ~2% of obese children have proteinuria
frequency.global: Increasing globally with obesity; ~2% of obese children have proteinuria; distinct FSGS-like glomerulomegaly on biopsy
frequency.sources: D'Agati et al. JASN 2016; Praga et al. JASN 2001; Obesity- related glomerulopathy review KI 2008

diagnosis: Urinalysis (proteinuria, minimal hematuria); urine protein:creatinine; eGFR (often supranormal initially — hyperfiltration); BMI; kidney biopsy (glomerulomegaly, secondary FSGS)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Weight loss — primary and most powerful intervention; sustained 5–10% weight loss reduces proteinuria significantly; lifestyle, dietary, and behavioral interventions • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — for proteinuria reduction; mainstay regardless of weight loss progress
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — empagliflozin (Jardiance) FDA approved for adult CKD Sept 2023; reduces glomerular hyperfiltration; emerging evidence for renal protection in obese/diabetic adolescents; trials ongoing ▶ GLP-1 receptor agonists: - Semaglutide SC (Ozempic/Wegovy, Novo Nordisk) — FDA approved Jan 2025 for CKD in adults with T2D; profound weight loss + renal protection (FLOW trial: 24% reduction in kidney disease composite endpoint); increasing off-label interest in obese adolescents with glomerulopathy - Liraglutide (Saxenda) — FDA approved for obesity in adolescents ≥12 yr; indirect renal benefit via weight loss - Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) — GLP-1/GIP dual agonist; SURMOUNT trials; emerging renal protection data; adolescent obesity trials underway ▶ Bariatric surgery — for severe obesity (BMI ≥35 with comorbidities) in adolescents; most effective weight reduction; sustained remission of glomerulopathy documented

name: Amyloidosis — Renal (AA in autoinflammatory / JIA / familial)
description: AA amyloid deposition from chronic inflammation (JIA, FMF, autoinflammatory conditions) or AL amyloid (rare pediatric plasma cell dyscrasia); nephrotic syndrome and CKD

frequency.us: Rare in US children; AA amyloidosis in ~5–10% of long- standing JIA; FMF-associated in untreated Mediterranean patients
frequency.global: Rare globally in children; AA amyloidosis predominant form; FMF-associated highest in Middle East without colchicine treatment
frequency.sources: Lachmann et al. NEJM 2007; Berntson & Fasth Acta Paediatr 2001; FMF International Registry

diagnosis: Kidney biopsy (Congo red — apple green birefringence, SAA immunostaining for AA); serum amyloid A (elevated in AA); SAA gene (FMF: MEFV); urinalysis (nephrotic range proteinuria)

name: Oxalosis — Systemic (primary hyperoxaluria end-stage)
description: Systemic oxalate deposition in multiple organs (bone, heart, retina, peripheral nerves) occurring when GFR falls <30 and renal clearance of oxalate is impaired; complication of PH1/2

frequency.us: Develops in PH1 patients with advanced CKD/ESKD in US; systemic oxalate deposition in bones, heart, eyes
frequency.global: Globally; systemic oxalosis develops in PH1 ESKD; combined

diagnosis: Plasma oxalate (markedly elevated); bone biopsy; echocardiography (cardiac oxalate); retinal exam; plasma oxalate >50 μmol/L indicates systemic deposition; genetic confirmation of PH

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods

name: Pediatric Kidney Transplant — Acute Cellular Rejection
description: T cell-mediated immune response against allograft; presents with rising creatinine, oliguria, graft tenderness in days to weeks post-transplant; Banff grade I–III

frequency.us: ~10–15% of US pediatric kidney transplants; highly sensitized recipients higher risk; treatable if caught early
frequency.global: ~10–15% of pediatric transplants globally; T-cell mediated; steroid pulses effective; European Pediatric Transplant Registry
frequency.sources: Dharnidharka et al. JASN 2015; NAPRTCS Transplant Report; ERA-EDTA pediatric transplant registry

diagnosis: Allograft biopsy (Banff classification: tubulitis, interstitial infiltration, intimal arteritis); serum creatinine; DSA testing; tacrolimus levels; urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: • Pulse IV methylprednisolone — first-line for all acute cellular rejection (ACR); 3–5 days; effective for Banff IA/IB • Rabbit antithymocyte globulin (rATG / Thymoglobulin) — for steroid-resistant ACR or Banff ≥IIA (vascular rejection); 7–14 days; depletes T cells • Optimize maintenance immunosuppression — ensure therapeutic tacrolimus levels; review adherence; consider conversion if CNI toxicity • Adjust mycophenolate and steroids — dose optimization as adjunct • Biopsy surveillance — protocol biopsies at 1, 3, 12 months at many pediatric centers; subclinical rejection detected in 15–30% • Donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) — emerging non-invasive biomarker for rejection surveillance; increasingly used in pediatric transplant programs
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Extended-release tacrolimus (LCPT / Envarsus XR) — once-daily formulation; improving adherence in adolescents; growing pediatric evidence (Tönshoff 2025 Pediatric Transplantation review) ▶ Tegoprubart (AT-1501) — anti-CD40L monoclonal antibody; Phase 2 BESTOW trial for kidney transplant completed enrollment Sept 2024; topline results expected 2025; novel CNI-free maintenance strategy ▶ Costimulation blockade optimization — belatacept increasingly used as CNI-sparing maintenance in select pediatric patients (EBV-positive recipients); FDA approval study in pediatric kidney Tx underway ▶ Precision biopsy scoring tools — AI-augmented Banff scoring under development

name: Pediatric Kidney Transplant — Antibody- Mediated Rejection (AMR)
description: Donor-specific antibody (DSA)-mediated allograft injury; acute or chronic; characterized by microvascular inflammation and C4d deposition; leading cause of late graft loss

frequency.us: ~10–20% of US pediatric transplants; increasing recognition; re-transplants and sensitized patients highest risk
frequency.global: ~10–20% globally of pediatric transplants; chronic AMR major cause of late graft loss; DSA monitoring essential
frequency.sources: NAPRTCS Transplant Report 2011; Dharnidharka et al. JASN 2015; Solez et al. Am J Transplant 2007

diagnosis: DSA by Luminex single antigen bead assay; allograft biopsy (Banff: microvascular inflammation, C4d, arterial intimal fibrosis); eGFR trend; urinalysis Methods

name: Chronic Allograft Nephropathy
description: Progressive allograft fibrosis and dysfunction from multiple immune (chronic rejection, subclinical AMR) and non-immune (CNI toxicity, recurrent disease) causes; leading cause of late graft failure

frequency.us: ~50% of allografts show chronic histological changes by 10 years in US; late graft failure ~3–5%/year
frequency.global: ~50% globally show chronic allograft changes by 10 years; consistent across transplant registries; Banff criteria used
frequency.sources: Nankivell et al. NEJM 2003; Solez et al. Am J Transplant 2007; ERA-EDTA transplant outcomes

diagnosis: Allograft biopsy (Banff: interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy (IFTA), arterial intimal thickening); eGFR trend; DSA; tacrolimus levels; proteinuria; urinalysis

treatment.standardOfCare: Methods • Optimize tacrolimus exposure — minimize trough variability (high variability = worse outcomes); consider extended-release tacrolimus for adherence • Treat subclinical rejection — protocol biopsies identify subclinical AMR/TCR; early treatment slows progression • Minimize nephrotoxins — tacrolimus dose reduction where possible; avoid nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, contrast without hydration, aminoglycosides) • RAAS blockade — for proteinuria and blood pressure; slows CKD progression in allograft • Manage modifiable CKD risks — dyslipidemia, anemia, CKD-MBD, blood pressure, obesity • Conversion from CNI to mTOR inhibitor (everolimus/sirolimus) — reduces CNI nephrotoxicity component; beneficial in some patients; risk of rejection with conversion • Convert to belatacept — CNI-free maintenance; requires EBV-positive recipient (risk of PTLD if EBV-negative); growing evidence for long-term renal function preservation
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Rituximab / obinutuzumab — for antibody-mediated chronic allograft nephropathy (transplant glomerulopathy driven by DSA) ▶ Belatacept — industry-sponsored Phase 3 pediatric trial (BENEFIT-PEDS) ongoing as of 2025; CNI-free protocol ▶ Felzartamab (anti-CD38) — Phase 2 data for late AMR; potential application in cAMR-driven CAN ▶ Tocilizumab — cAMR stabilization; ongoing clinical use at some centers ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors — emerging evidence for renoprotection in allografts; reducing hyperfiltration in functioning grafts; off-label use growing ▶ Non-invasive biomarkers (dd-cfDNA, urinary CXCL9/CXCL10) — for surveillance of subclinical rejection in stable allografts

name: Recurrent FSGS Post-transplant
description: Return of circulating permeability factor causing immediate post-transplant proteinuria in recipients with primary FSGS; risk ~30– 50% for first transplant, >80% for second

frequency.us: ~30–50% of US pediatric primary FSGS recipients develop recurrence; rapid ESKD and young age risk factors
frequency.global: ~30–50% globally; circulating permeability factor pathogenic; plasmapheresis partially effective; European data consistent
frequency.sources: Senggutuvan et al. Ped Nephrol 1990; Dall'Amico et al. JASN 1999; FSGS-Recurrence Registry

diagnosis: Heavy proteinuria (often within hours-days post- transplant); allograft biopsy (FSGS on LM, foot process effacement on EM); urine protein:creatinine ratio; eGFR

treatment.standardOfCare: • Prophylactic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) — most effective intervention; 8–10 sessions peri-transplant, continuing post-operatively; reduces recurrence risk from ~50% to ~25%; especially important for prior allograft loss to recurrent FSGS • Rituximab (peri-transplant) — depletes B cells; reduces circulating permeability factor; used with or without PE; typical protocol: 375 mg/m² pre-transplant ± 1–2 doses post-transplant • High-dose cyclosporine — used at some centers for receptor-blockade / lipid raft stabilization; less common since rituximab data Methods • RAAS blockade — antiproteinuric maintenance • LDL apheresis — for refractory proteinuria; reduces circulating lipid-bound permeability factor
treatment.emerging: Near-Approval (as of March 2026) ▶ Sparsentan (Filspari, Travere) — dual endothelin A/AT1R antagonist; PDUFA date April 13, 2026 for FSGS (FDA extended from January 13, 2026 requesting additional clinical benefit data); Phase 3 DUPLEX trial; DUET Phase 2 included podocyte gene mutation patients; if approved, first FDA-approved FSGS-specific therapy; already approved for IgAN Emerging/Investigational ▶ Inaxaplin (VX-147, Vertex) — oral APOL1 channel inhibitor; FDA Breakthrough Therapy + Rare Pediatric Disease Designation for APOL1-mediated FSGS; Phase 3 AMPLITUDE trial (NCT05312879) includes adolescents 10–17; relevant for APOL1 high-risk genotype (G1/G2) recurrent FSGS ▶ Obinutuzumab — for rituximab-refractory recurrent FSGS; improved B-cell depletion; case reports emerging ▶ Abatacept / CTLA4-Ig — Phase 2 data (B7-1/CD80 podocyte expression mechanism); NCT02078895; variable results ▶ Anti-CD20 alternatives (ofatumumab, ublituximab) — rituximab-resistant cases ▶ Povetacicept (BAFF/APRIL dual inhibitor) — early investigation

name: Recurrent C3 Glomerulopathy / aHUS Post-transplant
description: Recurrence of complement- mediated disease in allograft; C3GN and DDD recur in ~50–80%; aHUS recur without anti- complement prophylaxis

frequency.us: C3GN: ~50% recurrence; DDD: ~80–90% recurrence; aHUS: near 100% without eculizumab prophylaxis
frequency.global: Consistent rates globally; C3G and aHUS recurrence data from European and North American registries; eculizumab dramatically reduces aHUS recurrence
frequency.sources: Medjeral-Thomas et al. JASN 2014; Zuber et al. NEJM 2008; aHUS Post-transplant Registry

diagnosis: Allograft biopsy; complement studies; DSA; anti-CFH antibodies; genetic testing; urinalysis; eGFR

treatment.standardOfCare: • Eculizumab (anti-C5) — CRITICAL for aHUS prevention; prophylactic eculizumab started peri-transplant and continued post-transplant; prevents complement-mediated allograft loss; lifelong in most patients with high-risk complement mutations (CFH, CFI, C3, CFB) • Ravulizumab — extended-dosing anti-C5; FDA approved for aHUS; monthly dosing; increasingly preferred over eculizumab in maintenance phase for adherence • Mycophenolate mofetil ± low-dose steroids — for recurrent C3G without identified complement dysregulation; evidence base limited • Rituximab — for anti-CFH antibody-mediated recurrent disease; combined with immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate) • Monitor complement biomarkers — C3, C4, CH50, AH50, sC5b-9, complement genetics pre-transplant; guides prophylaxis intensity • Meningococcal + encapsulated bacteria vaccination — mandatory before complement inhibition
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational Methods ▶ Pegcetacoplan (Empaveli, Apellis) — FDA approved July 2025 for C3G (≥12 yr); proximal C3 inhibitor; highly relevant for recurrent C3G post-transplant; upstream blockade may provide more complete complement suppression than eculizumab for C3G subtype ▶ Iptacopan (Factor B inhibitor) — Phase 2/3 trials ongoing in C3G including post-transplant recurrence ▶ Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor) — Phase 2 trials for C3G ▶ Targeted complement strategy — matching inhibitor to specific complement pathway defect (e.g., proximal C3 inhibitor for C3G; terminal C5 inhibitor for aHUS with CFH mutation)

name: Post-transplant Lymphoproliferative Disease (PTLD) — Renal
description: EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disorder in immunosuppressed transplant recipients; ranges from benign hyperplasia to aggressive lymphoma; can involve renal allograft

frequency.us: ~1–5% of US pediatric kidney transplant recipients; EBV- seronegative recipients at highest risk
frequency.global: ~1–5% globally of pediatric kidney transplants; PTLD rates higher in pediatric vs. adult transplant; EBV drive paramount
frequency.sources: NAPRTCS Transplant Report; Dharnidharka et al. Transplantation 2002; European PTLD Registry

diagnosis: EBV viral load monitoring; CT scan (lymphadenopathy, organ involvement); PET scan; tissue biopsy (EBER staining, CD20); bone marrow biopsy if systemic

treatment.standardOfCare: • Reduction of immunosuppression (RIS) — cornerstone; first intervention for all PTLD; reduce or stop MMF first; reduce tacrolimus target; may induce remission in 20– 40% of early/low-grade PTLD; balance against rejection risk • EBV PCR monitoring — routine surveillance; pre-emptive rituximab in EBV-seronegative recipients with rising EBV viremia (evidence: Pollack et al. 2025; Ashoor et al. PNRC 2024); prevents PTLD development • Rituximab (anti-CD20) — for CD20+ B-cell PTLD (>90% of pediatric cases are EBV+ CD20+); monotherapy after RIS fails; 75–90% response in polymorphic PTLD; escalate to chemoimmunotherapy if incomplete response • R-CHOP (rituximab + cyclophosphamide + doxorubicin + vincristine + prednisone) — for monomorphic PTLD (DLBCL histology) or rituximab-refractory disease; standard chemoimmunotherapy regimen • R-EPOCH — alternative to R-CHOP for high-grade/CNS- involved disease • Surgical resection — for localized, resectable disease (e.g., GI PTLD) • WHO/ICC 2022 classification — guides treatment decisions: nondestructive vs. polymorphic vs. monomorphic PTLD require different approaches; histological subtyping essential New Emerging Data (2024–2025): • Polatuzumab vedotin (Polivy, Genentech) — anti-CD79b antibody-drug conjugate; FDA approved for DLBCL IPI ≥2; case report of Pola-R-CHP for EBV+ PTLD DLBCL (Paranji 2024); non-GCB subtype (majority of EBV+ PTLD) shows greater benefit from pola-R-CHP vs R- CHOP; increasing off-label use in monomorphic PTLD • Brentuximab vedotin (anti-CD30, Seagen) — ~70–85% of PTLD express CD30; Phase 1/2 trial (rituximab + brentuximab): ORR 75%, CR 60%; significant neutropenia/infection toxicity; option for refractory/relapsing PTLD Methods • EBV-specific T-cell adoptive immunotherapy — transfers EBV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs); Phase 2 data for refractory EBV+ PTLD; centers with off-the-shelf EBV-CTL products increasing • CAR-T cell therapy — 76.5% success rate in 17 patients with refractory PTLD across real-world data; anti-CD19 CAR-T used in pediatric Burkitt-PTLD (case series); increasing use at specialized centers • Nanatinostat + valganciclovir — EBV lytic reactivation strategy for refractory EBV+ PTLD; Phase 1b/2 final results (VT3996-201) published; novel mechanism • Pre-emptive rituximab prophylaxis for EBV-seronegative recipients — growing adoption per 2022 IPTA Nashville pediatric PTLD consensus guidelines

name: Calcineurin Inhibitor Nephrotoxicity
description: Tacrolimus or cyclosporine- induced renal injury from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction (acute, reversible) and tubular toxicity/interstitial fibrosis (chronic, potentially irreversible)

frequency.us: Near-universal histological CNI changes with long-term use; clinically significant CKD in ~10– 30% of US pediatric recipients
frequency.global: Near-universal globally with chronic CNI exposure; ~10–30% develop significant CKD; CNI- sparing protocols emerging
frequency.sources: Nankivell et al. NEJM 2003; Solez et al. Am J Transplant 2007; CNI Toxicity Consensus Report 2018

diagnosis: Allograft biopsy (arteriolar hyalinosis, tubular vacuolization, striped fibrosis); drug levels (tacrolimus/cyclosporine); eGFR trend; exclude rejection

treatment.standardOfCare: • Minimize CNI exposure — reduce tacrolimus doses to lowest effective level; low-exposure protocols using C0 trough ≤5–7 ng/mL in maintenance phase • Extended-release tacrolimus (LCPT / Envarsus XR) — once-daily dosing; lower peak-to-trough variability; improved CNI-nephrotoxicity profile in adults; growing pediatric use; approved US 2015; pediatric PK/PD data maturing • Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) — regular tacrolimus and cyclosporine levels; area under curve (AUC)-based dosing more accurate than trough-only • Avoid combined nephrotoxins — NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides, antifungals (fluconazole/voriconazole elevate CNI levels) • RAAS blockade — for proteinuria and hypertension related to CNI arteriolopathy • Conversion to mTOR inhibitor (everolimus, sirolimus) — reduces CNI nephrotoxicity when conversion safe (post- 12 months, stable allograft, no significant proteinuria); BENEFIT-EXT and Symphony trials data • Conversion to belatacept — CNI-free regimen; FDA approved 2011; requires EBV-seropositive recipient; BENEFIT trials: superior eGFR at 7 years vs. CNI; increasing use at pediatric centers for CNI-intolerant patients
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Tegoprubart (anti-CD40L) — Phase 2 BESTOW trial completed enrollment 2024; CNI-free induction/maintenance; topline results 2025 ▶ Voclosporin — calcineurin inhibitor approved for LN; potentially more nephrotoxicity-favorable profile in transplant context; investigational Methods ▶ CYP3A5 pharmacogenomics testing — guides initial tacrolimus dosing to reduce early toxicity; increasing clinical adoption ▶ Kidney organoid models — preclinical tools for CNI nephrotoxicity mechanistic studies

name: BK Virus Nephropathy — Post-transplant
description: BK polyomavirus reactivation causing tubulointerstitial nephritis in kidney transplant recipients; major cause of graft loss if untreated

frequency.us: ~5–10% of US kidney transplant recipients; most in first 2 years; children have higher primary BKV infection rates
frequency.global: ~5–10% globally of kidney transplant recipients; children have higher rates than adults due to primary BKV infection peri- transplant
frequency.sources: Hirsch et al. NEJM 2002; Ramos et al. Transplantation 2002; BKV Nephropathy Consensus Report

diagnosis: Serum/plasma BK virus PCR (>10,000 copies/mL high- risk); urine decoy cells (screening); allograft biopsy (SV40 immunostaining for definitive diagnosis)

treatment.standardOfCare: • Reduce immunosuppression — primary and most effective intervention; reduce MMF dose first (by 25– 50%), then tacrolimus target; balance against rejection risk; serial BK PCR monitoring guides titration • Switching tacrolimus to cyclosporine — reduces immunosuppressive burden via different CNI profile; used in some centers for persistent BKVN despite IS reduction • IVIG — immunomodulation; off-label; used in refractory BKVN with persistent viremia or declining graft function; limited evidence • Leflunomide — antiviral/immunomodulatory properties; used in refractory BKVN; active metabolite teriflunomide has anti-BKV activity in vitro; limited randomized trial evidence; some centers use as adjunct • Protocol biopsy / BK PCR surveillance — routine plasma BK PCR every 3 months for 2 years post-transplant per AST guidelines; allows pre-emptive IS reduction before established nephropathy
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ Brincidofovir (hexadecyloxypropyl cidofovir) — oral lipid conjugate of cidofovir; greater intracellular concentration; less nephrotoxicity than parenteral cidofovir; Phase 2 data for BK viremia; off-label use in severe/refractory BKVN at select centers ▶ Cidofovir (IV) — use with extreme caution; significant nephrotoxicity; reserved for life-threatening BKVN with no alternatives; dose and frequency reduced in transplant recipients ▶ Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — inhibit BK viral replication in vitro; prevention studies conflicting; not recommended as routine prophylaxis; debated ▶ Artesunate — antiparasitic with antiviral BK properties; isolated case reports; very limited evidence ▶ BKV-specific T-cell immunotherapy — adoptive transfer of BKV-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes; emerging; clinical trials (e.g., NCT03267134); most relevant for patients unable to tolerate IS reduction ▶ Vaccines targeting BKV VP1 capsid protein — preclinical development ▶ CMX001 / brincidofovir real-world data accumulating — Phase 3 experience in hematopoietic SCT informing BK use Methods

name: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) — Pediatric
description: Sustained reduction in kidney function or structural kidney damage for >3 months in children; etiologies include CAKUT, glomerulonephritis, hereditary nephropathies, and sequelae of AKI

frequency.us: ~15–75/million children in US (CKiD Study); 56% CAKUT, 14% FSGS, 5% SLE as leading causes
frequency.global: ~15–75/million children globally; higher rates in lower- income countries due to post- infectious GN; CAKUT predominant in high-income countries
frequency.sources: Warady & Chadha Ped Nephrol 2007; ESPN/ERA-EDTA registry; CKiD Study CJASN 2008

diagnosis: eGFR calculation (Schwartz formula); urinalysis; serum electrolytes; hemoglobin; PTH; phosphate; 25-OH vitamin D; echocardiogram; growth chart; renal ultrasound

treatment.standardOfCare: • RAAS blockade (ACEi/ARB) — cornerstone; antiproteinuric and antihypertensive; slows CKD progression • CKD-MBD management — phosphate binders; active vitamin D (calcitriol, alfacalcidol); calcimimetics (cinacalcet) for secondary HPT • Anemia — erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (EPO, darbepoetin alfa); iron supplementation; HIF-PHI agents (daprodustat, roxadustat) emerging for dialysis patients • Growth failure — recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH); nutritional optimization; early nutritional support • Nutrition — low-phosphate diet; adequate caloric/protein intake for growth; sodium restriction • Prepare for RRT — peritoneal dialysis (preferred in children); hemodialysis; pre-emptive transplant planning • Renal transplant — preferred RRT modality; improves growth, neurodevelopment, and QoL FDA-Approved (2023–2025) ▶ Empagliflozin (Jardiance, BI/Lilly) — SGLT2 inhibitor; FDA approved Sept 2023 for adult CKD to reduce eGFR decline and kidney failure; EMPA-KIDNEY trial; pediatric CKD trials ongoing ▶ Semaglutide SC (Ozempic, Novo Nordisk) — GLP-1RA; FDA approved Jan 2025 for CKD in adults with T2D; FLOW trial; pediatric applicability limited but relevant for adolescents with diabetic CKD
treatment.emerging: Emerging/Investigational ▶ SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) — growing pediatric trial data; DERIVE-KIDS and BUTTERFLY trials ▶ Finerenone — non-steroidal MRA; Phase 3 trials across CKD spectrum; favorable cardiac and renal outcomes vs. spironolactone ▶ GLP-1 agonists (tirzepatide, liraglutide) — for CKD with obesity/metabolic syndrome component in adolescents ▶ Sparsentan — endothelin/AT1R antagonist; reduces proteinuria across proteinuric CKD beyond IgAN ▶ Novel EPO alternatives (HIF-PHI) — daprodustat FDA approved Feb 2023 for dialysis patients; may offer advantages in pediatric anemia management
